ci: Stories are shared in different ways.
lo: Imagining stories together; Ways stories are shared; Connecting with stories

s.d: Students record a short story about a lost toy using voices, footsteps, claps and classroom objects. Hearing a story without pictures shows how sound can carry characters, settings and events. Pairs swap recordings and draw what they imagined before seeing each other's original story plan. Students then ask a family member to add a familiar song, saying or sound from home. Each pair finishes with a sound story that can be played to the class with everyone's eyes closed. GarageBand makes it possible to record voices, layer sounds and compose simple music in one place.

Students paint three digital pictures showing the beginning, middle and end of an imagined story. They see that colour, shape and expression can tell events without written words. Partners exchange the middle pictures and invent different events that could connect the same beginning and ending. Students choose one version and explain how the pictures helped them understand it. Each child finishes with a three-picture story displayed in sequence. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with separate layers that can be changed as ideas grow.

Students lay coloured tiles across the carpet to guide Sphero Indi through the beginning, middle and end of a familiar story. The ordered path makes story sequence something children can build, walk beside and test. Another pair receives the same character and ending but chooses a different tile route to show a new version of the story. Students move, replace and reorder tiles when the car's journey does not match their planned events. Each group finishes with a working story path and an oral telling timed to Indi's movement. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students record three short scenes showing a family story, using drawings, toys, movement or spoken words. They explore how the same memory can be shared through pictures, actions and voice. Families can suggest one important detail or home-language phrase for children to include in the retelling. Students arrange the scenes in order and choose simple titles that help viewers follow the events. Each child finishes with a short family-history film for a class viewing. iMovie allows the clips, titles and transitions to be edited together in one tool.

Students choose puppet characters and record an imagined story that begins with two characters wanting different things. This helps children tell stories together while listening to another person's ideas. Halfway through, pairs swap their unfinished puppet show with another pair, who decides what happens next. The original storytellers then record an ending that connects both groups' ideas. Each pair finishes with a narrated puppet show containing a clear beginning, problem and ending. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students empathise with Prep listeners by asking what helps them follow a story, then define the need for a small theatre that makes event order clear. Using cardboard, recycled boxes, split pins, paper tabs, fabric and modelling clay, groups sketch ideas and build a theatre with three changeable scenes. They prototype moving characters and paper mechanisms, then use Stop Motion Studio to test whether each movement and scene change is easy to understand. After classmates watch the first animation, groups rebuild unclear parts, strengthen mechanisms and photograph the improved sequence frame by frame. Each group demonstrates a working physical story theatre and a short stop-motion story with a clear beginning, middle and end.

plannerText: The 'How We Express Ourselves' Prep unit explores how stories are shared in diverse ways, focusing on imagination, creativity, and personal/cultural expression. Students connect with their own and others' stories through oral storytelling, drawing, play, and digital media. The unit emphasises sequencing events, sharing family histories, and using different modes (words, pictures, movement) to communicate. Learning is play-based, teacher-guided, and encourages students to express identity, respect diversity, and connect with local and global communities through storytelling.

apply what they were learning in real situations.

Group games and activities where students had to
cooperate and take turns really helped them develop the
learner profile traits, like caring and open-mindedness. By

reflective, which tied into the social skills approach to

feel more confident about school life.

s.d: Students photograph school staff and record each person explaining one way they help the school community. This shows that the school works because many people carry out connected roles. Children choose one helpful question to ask, then play their page to the person they interviewed so they can check it together. They end up with a class book that families can use to meet the people and places in the school. Book Creator keeps photographs, recorded voices and children's drawings together on each page. Pairing children for the recording keeps screen time brief and makes the interview the main experience.

Students add drawings of familiar school people and places to a shared Freeform board. They draw lines between people who work together, such as the teacher, office staff and nurse helping a child who feels unwell. Pairs study another pair's connection and ask them to explain why it matters. The class ends up with one large visual web showing how the school community fits together. Freeform's open canvas gives the web room to grow as children notice more connections. The teacher can revisit the board after each community walk and add children's new ideas.

Students draw a cutaway view of the school and place staff members where their work usually happens. This helps children connect community roles with the places that support them. Each child hides one visual clue in the drawing, then a partner works out which staff role it represents. They end up with a detailed illustrated school scene for a classroom display. Sketchbook's drawing tools let children revise colours, shapes and details without starting again. Printed drawings can prompt conversations with visiting staff and families.

Students paint a digital portrait of a school community member doing one important part of their role. This makes each person's contribution visible rather than showing only a face or uniform. Children choose a meaningful object to include, such as a library book, garden tool or first-aid bag, and classmates work out what it tells them. They end up with a gallery of original role portraits. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with separate layers for the person, place and helpful object. The class can arrange the portraits by places or by the ways people help others.

Students lay coloured tiles across the carpet to guide Sphero Indi between picture cards showing connected school roles. This models how a message, object or request moves through the school community. Groups swap routes and work out which tile needs changing when Indi does not reach the next person. They end up with a tested physical pathway that tells a simple story, such as a lost hat travelling from the playground to lost property and back to its owner. Indi follows the coloured tiles without an app or screen. Children explain each stop as the robot car travels through their community story.

Students empathise by asking a staff member which school journey is difficult for young children, then define one route that needs to be clearer. They ideate with paper sketches and prototype a large floor map using cardboard rooms, recycled-material landmarks, arrows and textured path markers. They program a Bee-Bot with directional buttons to test the route, watch where it goes wrong, and move or redesign parts of the map before testing again. Each group finishes by demonstrating a reliable journey to the staff member or another Prep class. The physical model shows how people, places and clear directions work together to help the school community.

plannerText: The Prep 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores the concept that everyone has a role to play in the community, focusing on the school as a system made up of different people and places. Students inquire into who is in their school community, what roles staff members have, and how these roles connect and contribute to the functioning of the school. Learning experiences include guided walks, interviews, drawing, mapping, and sharing through digital media. The unit emphasises communication, collaboration, and early systems thinking, with opportunities for students to represent their understanding through play, storytelling, and creative construction.

s.d: Students magnify an ice cube every two minutes and draw the tiny cracks, bubbles and puddles they observe on paper. This makes careful observation the starting point for predicting, testing and drawing a conclusion. Partners compare drawings and decide which change happened first, next and last. They repeat the test with one cube in shade and one in sunlight to see whether their prediction holds. Each pair ends with a sequenced observation strip beside the two melting trays. The magnified view reveals changes that are difficult to notice with eyes alone.

Students record balls, blocks and toy cars moving down ramps, then watch each movement in slow motion. This helps them observe closely before deciding which object moved fastest or travelled furthest. Pairs swap one ramp feature, predict what will change and film the test again. Another Prep class watches the clips and votes on which evidence best supports each conclusion. Students end with paired slow-motion recordings showing what changed between two fair tests. Slow playback makes brief movements available for repeated observation.

Students photograph plants, animals and fungi during a nature walk and use Seek to suggest what each living thing might be. This shows that scientists observe carefully, use tools and check possible answers. Children compare two suggested identifications with the real colours, shapes and textures they can see. Each pair chooses one identification they trust and one they think needs more checking. The class ends with a paper display of observed living things labelled as checked or still wondering. Seek's camera-based identification gives children a useful starting point rather than a guaranteed answer.

Students record short weather reports after observing clouds, wind, sunlight and puddles outside. This gives them a clear routine of observe, predict, check and explain. Each group records a morning prediction, then returns later to add what actually happened. Families can watch the paired reports and hear children explain whether the evidence matched the prediction. Students end with a short weather clip containing both the prediction and conclusion. Live captions make their spoken scientific words visible for early readers.

Students program a character to move through four scenes showing a simple ice-melting investigation. This turns the scientific process into a sequence they can see, test and fix. Partners exchange projects and check whether observation, prediction, testing and conclusion appear in a sensible order. Children then change one scene so the character explains a different possible result. Each pair ends with a tappable animated explanation of how scientists find out new things. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young children debug the order without needing to read long instructions.

Students notice that a Bee-Bot scientist needs a safe path across a floor map to visit an observation site, testing table and conclusion board. They define the problem, sketch route ideas, then build raised map features from cardboard, blocks, paper and recycled lids. Groups program the directional buttons, test the route and move or rebuild features whenever the Bee-Bot misses a stop. They invite another group to run the route without help and use that test to improve the map and button sequence. Each group demonstrates a working physical route that shows the scientific process in order.

plannerText: The Prep 'How the World Works' unit focuses on introducing students to scientific thinking and the inquiry process through play-based, hands-on experiences. Students explore the roles of scientists, observe and record findings during nature walks, investigate weather patterns, and conduct simple experiments such as melting ice and testing how objects move. The unit emphasizes observing, predicting, testing, and communicating results, with strong links to literacy (storytelling, drawing, oral sharing) and maths (sequencing, sorting, counting). Learning is highly visual, collaborative, and connected to students' everyday experiences, supporting foundational skills in observation, reasoning, and communication.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students choose an animal character and record its voice explaining the important job it does in nature. This helps children notice that even small living things can pollinate plants, spread seeds, make soil or provide food. Students then improve their recording by adding one detail about how humans can share space with that animal. They end with a short talking-character explanation for another Prep class to watch. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to each child's recorded voice.

Students make a close-up digital drawing of a local living thing and the place where it finds food, water and shelter. This shows how plants and animals depend on the spaces around them. Children swap drawings and look for one helpful connection, such as a bee beside a flower or a worm beneath leaf litter. They then add that connection to their picture using a new layer. Each child finishes with a detailed habitat illustration that can prompt an oral explanation. Sketchbook's drawing tools and layers let children revise without covering their first ideas.

Students sort teacher-provided pictures of local plants, animals, fungi and people on a shared Freeform board. This helps them work out which living things share the same places and how their roles are different. Small groups draw lines between things that help one another, such as flowers and bees or trees and birds. Another group checks each connection and moves a picture if they can explain a better place for it. The class ends with one large visual web showing how life around Elsternwick is connected. Freeform's open canvas lets children move, group and connect pictures together.

Students arrange teacher-provided pictures to compare a healthy shared space with one that is difficult for living things. This makes human choices visible, including planting flowers, leaving water, dropping litter or removing shelter. Each pair chooses the three changes they think would help wildlife most and adds short spoken-to-the-teacher captions. Pairs exchange collages and point to one choice that could work at school. Students finish with a two-part visual display showing before, after and the changes between them. PicCollage's grids and captions keep the comparison clear for early readers.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a large floor mat showing trees, flowers, water, nests, paths and buildings. This lets children explore how animals and humans move through the same space to meet different needs. One group places an animal card at the starting point, while another chooses a safe destination and explains why it belongs there. Children press the directional buttons, run the route and debug it when the Bee-Bot stops at an unsafe or unsuitable place. Each group finishes with a tested sequence that connects a living thing to food, water or shelter. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make every route a hands-on sequence planned in advance.

Students empathise with a small local animal, then define one problem it may face when sharing the school grounds with people. Using cardboard, paper tubes, sticks, string, recycled containers and natural loose parts, they sketch ideas and build a shelter, crossing or feeding-space prototype. They test it with a toy animal, photograph each trial in Seesaw and record what worked or failed. Children change one part, test again and compare the new result with their first Seesaw entry. They finish by demonstrating the improved physical prototype and recording how it helps humans and another living thing share space.

plannerText: The Prep 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores identity, family, and community through personal histories and connections to place and time. Students engage in activities such as sharing family stories, sequencing life events, exploring artefacts, and reflecting on changes from past to present. The unit emphasizes oral storytelling, drawing, and hands-on inquiry, with strong links to literacy, mathematics (sequencing, patterns, measurement), and social studies. Learning is inquiry-driven, with provocations like baby photos and artefacts, and students are encouraged to express their understanding through creative, collaborative, and reflective tasks.

Students code two characters to show a playground interaction where one action changes how another character feels. This helps children notice how behaviour can support or harm wellbeing. Partners swap projects and suggest a different kind response for the second scene. Each pair ends with a short animated story that shows a problem and a helpful choice. Simple blocks let children sequence movement, speech and scene changes. The class can watch the stories and name the choices that build positive relationships.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a familiar character giving one clear tip for making friends or asking an adult for help. This gives children a safe way to talk about relationships, feelings and personal safety. Each child chooses whether the character speaks to a new Prep student, a worried friend or someone left out of play. The result is a short talking-character message for another Prep class. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to the child's voice. Teachers can replay the messages before transitions, buddy time or playground sessions.

Students build a class book by adding a drawing and recorded sentence about someone who helps them feel healthy, safe or included. This makes the link between caring relationships and wellbeing visible. Families can contribute a short child-recorded page about a caring routine used at home. The class ends with a narrated book showing many different ways people care for one another. Book Creator keeps pictures, text and voice recordings together on each page. Children can revisit the book when they need ideas for helping a classmate.

Students photograph a partner-made block scene of a friendship moment and record what each person might be feeling. This helps children connect visible actions with feelings that may not be easy to see. The partner listens, then records one helpful action that could improve the scene. Each child ends with a photo-and-voice reflection showing how behaviour can affect wellbeing. Seesaw keeps the photograph and both spoken reflections together in a portfolio entry. The teacher can use the entries to notice which children can name feelings, safe choices and sources of help.

Students empathise with classmates by discussing busy classroom moments, then define a need such as finding a friend, a quiet place or a trusted adult. Using cardboard, paper, blocks and recycled materials, teams design a floor map with safe destinations and ideate a clear route between them. They prototype by programming Beebot with its directional buttons, test whether it reaches the chosen support place and change either the route or commands after each attempt. At the end, each team demonstrates a working journey and explains when that destination could help someone's wellbeing. The physical map remains available for play-based practice with safe choices and help-seeking.

plannerText: The Prep 'Who We Are' unit explores identity, relationships, and wellbeing as students transition into school life. Through stories, discussions, and creative activities, students learn about friendship, emotions, and belonging. The unit emphasizes developing social skills, understanding feelings, and building positive classroom agreements. Learning is play-based and teacher-guided, with opportunities for drawing, storytelling, and reflecting on personal experiences. The focus is on helping students recognize their own identity, connect with others, and understand how relationships impact their wellbeing.

Partners swap soundscapes, name the emotion they hear and explain which sounds shaped their response. Students then revise one sound so their message is clearer to the listener. Each pair ends with four short emotion soundscapes for a class listening gallery. GarageBand lets students layer recorded sounds and musical loops.

Students build a face from paper shapes and photograph it changing from one emotion to another. This helps them notice how eyes, eyebrows and mouths can communicate feelings. Partners watch each animation without being told the emotion, then suggest what may have happened between the first and last face. Students add or remove frames to make the emotional change easier to interpret. Each pair finishes with a short stop-motion story showing an emotion developing over time. Stop Motion Studio combines their photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students record a short video showing an emotion through facial expression, posture and movement while keeping their voice silent. This helps them recognise that people can express feelings without words. A partner watches the video, records an interpretation and suggests a kind response to the feeling they noticed. The original student then adds a voice reflection explaining what the partner understood accurately or differently. Each student finishes with a portfolio entry containing an expression, an interpretation and a response. Seesaw keeps video, voice and reflection together in one journal post.

Students sort drawings and words for emotions onto a shared Freeform board. This helps them see that the same situation can lead to different feelings and that one expression can have several meanings. Small groups connect each emotion to possible body clues, facial clues and helpful responses. Groups then visit another section of the board and add a different interpretation rather than copying the first answer. The class ends with a connected emotion map that can support later picture-book and drama discussions. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and link ideas together.

Students draw the same simple face twice, using colour, line and texture to express two different emotions. This shows how visual choices can communicate feelings even when the facial features stay similar. Partners view the drawings without labels and describe what each colour or mark makes them think the character feels. Students choose one piece of feedback and adjust a layer to make their intended emotion clearer. Each student finishes with a paired digital artwork and a short spoken explanation given to the class. Sketchbook's drawing tools and layers make it easy to test changes without losing the first idea.

Students empathise by watching classmates try to identify emotions shown by handmade cardboard masks, then define which moving feature is hardest to notice. They ideate and prototype a mask with paper eyebrows, sliding mouths, split pins, tabs, elastic and recycled cardboard so one face can change expression. Pairs film each mechanism in slow motion, test whether viewers can identify the emotion, and look closely at where a tab jams or a feature moves too little. They strengthen, reposition or enlarge parts, then film the revised mask for another test. At the end, each student demonstrates a working mask that changes between two clearly readable emotions and explains the improvement made after testing.

plannerText: The Year 1 'How We Express Ourselves' unit explores how emotions can be recognized, communicated, and managed in diverse ways. Students inquire into their own and others' feelings, using picture books, art, music, and collaborative activities to build emotional literacy. The unit emphasizes creative expression through visual arts (such as masks and group collages), music (soundscapes for stories), and drama, while also integrating digital skills and wellbeing strategies. Students are encouraged to reflect on their emotions, share their perspectives, and use a variety of communication modes including body language, facial expressions, and digital tools to express themselves and understand others.

Year 1 students made great strides in understanding how
regular exercise contributes to a healthy lifestyle, both
physically and emotionally. During our soccer and football
activities, they began recognising how their stamina and
running speed improved as the term progressed. This led to
discussions about how exercise not only strengthens the body

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

Final notes and reflections

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.

ci: Services are established to help the needs of people in the community.
lo: Local services; Why we need local services in our community; How services meet personal and community needs

s.d: Students train Teachable Machine to recognise picture cards showing ambulances, fire engines and library services. They test whether the computer can match each image to a service that meets a community need. Students choose difficult pictures, swap them with another group and work out why the model makes mistakes. They improve the model by adding more varied examples and testing it again. The class ends with a working image classifier and a record of its correct and incorrect guesses. Similar image recognition helps council monitoring and emergency-dispatch systems identify vehicles and respond to community needs.

Students answer a picture survey about which local service they would contact for needs such as feeling sick, finding a lost pet or borrowing a book. They see that services are established because different people need different kinds of help. Each pair adds one new question based on a need they notice at school or in Elsternwick. Students compare the automatic charts and discuss why some services were chosen more often than others. They end with a class survey and charts showing patterns in community needs. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and turns the results into automatic charts.

Students record a puppet conversation between a community helper and a person asking for help. They show what the service provides, why it is needed and what happens when someone contacts it. Students swap planned situations so another pair must decide which helper belongs in the scene. They record clear questions and answers, then replay the show to check that the service process makes sense. Each pair finishes with a short animated puppet show for a younger class. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students record a short interview with a visiting community helper about the people, places and steps involved in their service. This makes the organisation behind a familiar service visible, rather than showing only the helper's job. Students choose the most useful answers for families new to Elsternwick and remove repeated or unclear sections. They arrange the clips so the film moves from a community need to the service's response. The class finishes with a set of short interview films featuring real local voices. iMovie lets students trim clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students collect a class tally of local services they have used, such as libraries, doctors, public transport and emergency services. They enter the totals into a simple teacher-prepared Excel table and create a column chart. The chart helps them see which services meet frequent needs and which are used only in special situations. Pairs choose one surprising result and explain it to the class using the numbers. Students finish with a labelled chart showing how often different services support their class. Excel keeps the tally, totals and chart together so changing a number updates the display.

Students empathise with a toy person who needs to reach a doctor, library or fire station, then define what would make the journey clear and safe. They ideate and build a large floor map from cardboard, recycled boxes, paper roads, signs and removable service buildings. Each group prototypes a route by programming a Bee-Bot's directional buttons, then tests whether another group can follow and explain the service sequence. After collisions, missing signs or unclear routes are noticed, students move the physical parts, shorten the program and test again. The final demonstration shows a Bee-Bot travelling from a community need to the correct service on a working model of an organised neighbourhood.

plannerText: The Year 1 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores how services are established to meet the needs of people in the community. Students inquire into local services, why they are needed, and how they function, with a focus on community helpers and systems. The unit emphasizes communication, research, and agency, incorporating guest speakers, read-alouds, student presentations, and hands-on activities. Learners develop an understanding of the roles different people play in supporting the community, make connections through real-world experiences, and demonstrate their learning through creative projects and digital portfolios.

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.

ci: Patterns help us to interpret the world around us.
lo: Patterns and cycles in our lives; Different patterns around us; How patterns can be created, interpreted and extended

s.d: Students record repeating movements around the school, such as swaying leaves, dripping water and a bouncing ball, then watch them in slow motion. Slowing each movement helps them notice the small steps that make a pattern repeat. Partners compare clips and choose the moment that best shows where one cycle ends and the next begins. They test whether the same pattern continues when the movement becomes faster or slower. Each pair ends with a short slow-motion clip and a spoken explanation of the repeating cycle. The slow-motion playback makes changes that are usually too quick to see available for close observation.

Students collect daily observations of the butterfly chrysalis, weather or daylight and enter simple words or numbers into Microsoft Excel. The growing table helps them work out which changes repeat and which changes belong to a life cycle. Small groups choose one question to investigate, such as whether warmer days appear together or how long each chrysalis stage lasts. They compare their chart with another group's chart and explain one pattern they notice. Each group ends with a clear table and chart showing change over time. Excel turns their collected data into a graph that makes patterns easier to see.

Students program a ScratchJr animation showing a repeating natural pattern, such as day and night, the seasons or a butterfly life cycle. Repeated blocks help them see that a cycle follows an order and returns to its beginning. Students swap projects, predict what should happen next and check the animation to test their prediction. They then debug any stage that appears in the wrong order or does not repeat clearly. Each student ends with a working animated cycle that classmates can interpret. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young students sequence movement and repetition without needing to type code.

Students build repeating colour and shape patterns on Geoboard by stretching virtual bands around the pegs. They explore how a pattern can change in size or direction while keeping the same repeating rule. Partners exchange unfinished patterns and work out which shape should come next. The original designer checks the extension and explains the rule using words such as repeat, turn, bigger and smaller. Each pair ends with a completed geometric pattern and a clear explanation of how it grows. The virtual bands can be moved quickly, so students can test several possible extensions before choosing one.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to identify plants, animals or fungi found during repeated walks through the same part of the school grounds. Returning to one place helps them notice seasonal patterns and changes in which living things appear. Pairs choose one identification they are unsure about and compare the living thing carefully with the app's suggestion before accepting it as a guide. The class compares observations from different days and discusses which living things appeared again. Students end with a checked set of local species observations that can be revisited later in the term. Seek uses the camera to suggest identifications, but students still need to look closely because a suggestion may not always be correct.

Students empathise with a younger child who needs help understanding the butterfly life cycle, then define the challenge of making every stage easy to follow. They ideate a floor path and build large stage tiles from cardboard, drawings and recycled materials, including egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly. They prototype by placing the tiles in sequence and programming the Bee-Bot's directional buttons to travel through the cycle. Another group tests the path without being told the order, then gives feedback about confusing turns, missing stages or unclear pictures. Students reposition tiles, debug the movement sequence and demonstrate a final physical model in which the Bee-Bot travels through the complete repeating cycle.

plannerText: The Year 1 'How the World Works' unit explores patterns and cycles in the natural world, focusing on life cycles, seasons, and other repeating phenomena. Students inquire into how patterns help us interpret the world, using observation, research, and creative activities to build understanding. The unit integrates science, literacy, and digital skills, with hands-on experiences like observing a butterfly chrysalis, researching with Epic, and building models. Emphasis is placed on student agency, reflection, and making connections between classroom learning and the world around them.

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.

lo: Products derived from plants; Plants all around us; The interconnectedness of plants

s.d: Students record 360-degree views beneath a tree, beside a garden bed and near plant-based materials around the classroom. Seeing the whole space helps them notice that plants support life and appear in places they may overlook. Pairs choose one view and challenge another class to find every plant, plant product and living thing that depends on plants. They replay the spherical footage and turn the view to check anything they missed. The class ends with an immersive tour of plants and plant products across the Elsternwick campus. The camera captures the full surroundings, so viewers can look in every direction.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a floor mat showing a plant's journey from seed to familiar product. This makes the links between plants, people and products such as paper, bread, cotton clothing and wooden furniture visible. Groups swap mats and work out the intended journey before checking it with the designers. They debug any route that skips a stage or places the stages in the wrong order. Each group finishes with a working sequence that connects a growing plant to something people use. Bee-Bot's directional buttons let students enter and revise each route step by step.

Students magnify leaves, seeds, wood, paper, cotton fabric and a piece of fruit to look for tiny patterns and structures. Close observation helps them compare plants with the products that come from plants. Each pair chooses one surprising detail and invites classmates to find it without first naming the object. Students sort the specimens by visible features such as fibres, veins, layers, pores or repeating shapes. They finish with a labelled comparison display of specimens arranged beside their magnified details. The magnification aid makes details visible that young eyes could not easily inspect unaided.

Students build a narrated digital book that follows one plant resource from where it grows to how people use it. This shows that food, fibres, paper, medicines and building materials begin with living plants. Each child chooses a different reader?another Year 1 class, a family member or a younger buddy?and explains unfamiliar words for that audience. Partners listen to each page and ask one question that the author answers in a final revision. Students finish with a class library of plant-to-product stories containing text, images and recorded voices. Book Creator keeps the writing, visuals and narration together in one book.

Students photograph leaves from three common school plants and train Teachable Machine to recognise each group. They look closely for patterns in shape, edge, colour and vein structure that help distinguish plants around them. Groups exchange one mystery leaf and test whether the model recognises it, then add better examples when it makes a mistake. This works like plant-identification apps such as Seek, which compare camera images with patterns learned from many examples. Students finish with a tested image-classification model and a record of which leaves confused it. Teachable Machine lets them retrain the model so they can see how the examples they choose affect its decisions.

Students empathise with a seed that must travel away from its parent plant, then define the need to move safely towards light, soil and water. Using paper, cardboard, wool, leaves, tape and recycled materials, they sketch ideas and prototype a wind-carried seed that falls slowly and travels sideways. They test each design in front of a fan or during a safe drop, film it in slow motion, and study spinning, gliding and landing. Students change one feature?such as wing size, weight or shape?and repeat the test to improve the design. At the end, each group demonstrates its best prototype and uses the slow-motion evidence to explain how the change helped seed dispersal.

plannerText: The Year 1 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores how patterns and cycles help us interpret the world, focusing on natural and human-made patterns such as life cycles, seasons, and the water cycle. Students inquire into changes in living things, observe cycles in their environment, and connect learning across science, literacy, and the arts. The unit emphasizes hands-on investigation, student agency, and transdisciplinary connections, with opportunities for digital documentation, creative expression, and collaborative learning. Reflection and sharing with families and the school community are key components, supporting students to build knowledge, communication skills, and a deeper understanding of patterns in their lives.

Year 1 students made great strides in understanding how
regular exercise contributes to a healthy lifestyle, both
physically and emotionally. During our soccer and football
activities, they began recognising how their stamina and
running speed improved as the term progressed. This led to

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

Final notes and reflections

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.
