th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Homes reflect our culture and environment.
lo: Different types of homes; Characteristics of a home; The importance of sustainable living spaces

s.d: Students photograph a model or drawing of a home and record the home explaining how its culture and environment shaped it. This makes features such as raised floors, thick walls, courtyards or steep roofs easier to connect with real needs. Students choose one feature the home is proud of and one change that could make it more sustainable. They swap recordings with a partner, who listens for clues about where the home might belong. Each student ends with a short talking-home recording based on researched details rather than stereotypes. ChatterPix Kids makes the image talk by adding a drawn mouth and a recorded voice.

Students sort teacher-provided pictures of homes from different places into a visual comparison grid. They add short captions showing how climate, local materials, family life or traditions may affect each home. Pairs then exchange grids and add one surprising similarity between two very different-looking homes. Students also choose one sustainable feature they would borrow for a Melbourne home and explain why. Each pair ends with a labelled collage that can be displayed as evidence for the central idea. PicCollage makes it quick to arrange pictures, captions and simple backgrounds on one page.

Students build a small home from classroom construction pieces and photograph each stage in Stop Motion Studio. Their animation shows the home changing from an older design to a present-day version with one sustainable improvement. Another group watches the unfinished animation and suggests a change that better suits the weather or the people's needs. Students revise the model, add the new frames and check that viewers can see why the design changed. Each group ends with a short stop-motion film showing how homes respond to place and time. Stop Motion Studio joins the photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students stretch virtual bands to make a simple bird's-eye floor plan of a home. They use shapes to show spaces for sleeping, preparing food, gathering, washing and staying safe. Partners swap plans and work out whose needs the layout meets well and whose needs may have been missed. Students then move one wall or doorway to make the home more welcoming, useful or efficient. Each student ends with an original floor plan that shows deliberate choices about the characteristics of a home. Geoboard allows bands to be moved quickly so students can test several layouts without redrawing everything.

Students lay coloured tiles to guide Sphero Indi through a large floor plan containing key parts of a sustainable home. They sequence a route past features such as a water tank, shaded window, recycling area and shared family space. Another pair changes the order of the tiles, and students work out how the new route affects Indi's journey through the home. They revise the path so every chosen feature is visited without unnecessary travel. Each group ends with a working coloured-tile route and a spoken explanation of its design choices. Sphero Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen.

Students empathise with a child, older person or wheelchair user who needs a safe, comfortable and sustainable home. They define one clear need, sketch several layouts, then build a large floor plan from cardboard, recycled packaging, paper doors, fabric shade and bottle-top furniture. A Bee-Bot is programmed in advance to travel from the entrance to essential spaces, revealing narrow paths, blocked turns or rooms that are difficult to reach. Students test the route, move physical walls or furniture, and debug the button sequence until the journey works. Each group demonstrates its improved home prototype and explains how testing changed both the layout and the Bee-Bot program.

plannerText: The Year 1 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit explores how homes reflect culture and environment, focusing on different types of homes, their characteristics, and the importance of sustainability. Students investigate homes from around the world, compare past and present structures, and consider how homes meet people's needs. The unit emphasizes inquiry, creative thinking, and communication, with opportunities for hands-on construction, digital research, and sharing learning through various media. Learner profile attributes and approaches to learning are woven throughout, supporting students to be knowledgeable, open-minded, and reflective as they explore global perspectives on homes.

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.

ci: The actions we take influence our safety and wellbeing.
lo: Safe environments; How our actions affect ourselves and others; Keeping our body and mind healthy

s.d: Students record two versions of the same doorway, playground or handwashing moment?one with an unsafe choice and one with a safer choice. Comparing the clips makes it clear that small actions can change everyone's safety and wellbeing. Each group chooses a real school routine that younger students or families would find useful. They finish with a short safety film that pauses before the choice and invites viewers to predict what should happen next. Live captions, stickers and titles help Year 1 students make the message easy to follow.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a heart, brain, stomach or pair of lungs explaining one daily action that helps it stay healthy. Giving the body part a voice helps children connect eating, movement, sleep and calming choices with how their bodies and minds feel. Students swap recordings and check whether the advice is clear, kind and possible for a Year 1 child to follow. They finish with a short talking-character health message for a class body display. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the character's mouth with each student's recorded voice.

Students paint a layered self-portrait showing how their body and mind might feel before and after a healthy action such as sleep, movement, water or quiet breathing. The two versions show that choices can affect both physical feelings and emotions. Each student chooses colours, marks and shapes that make sense to them, then asks a partner what changes they notice. They finish with a paired digital painting that can prompt a class conversation about different ways people care for themselves. Layers let students change the background, body outline and feeling marks without starting again.

Students watch a teacher-selected video about body care, emotions or staying safe and answer its built-in questions as they go. Stopping at key moments helps them notice how one person's action can help or harm themselves and others. Pairs compare one answer, replay the matching scene and decide whether the video gives enough evidence. They finish with a completed set of responses and one healthy or safe action they can test during the school week. Clickview's curated clips and built-in questions keep the viewing focused and manageable.

Students build and record a short puppet scene in which a character faces a choice about playground safety, personal space, rest or asking for help. Showing both the choice and its effect makes cause and consequence visible to young learners. Groups exchange unfinished scenes, predict the safest next action and let the original creators choose the ending. They finish with a narrated puppet show that models clear words and helpful actions. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students empathise with someone moving through a busy classroom, define one safety problem, and sketch ideas for a clearer route. Using a Bee-Bot, a large paper floor mat, cardboard furniture, recycled-material barriers and picture cards, they prototype a path to places such as the sink, bag area or calm corner. They program the route in advance, test whether it avoids hazards, then move or redesign the physical features when the Bee-Bot cannot travel safely. After repeated testing, each group demonstrates its improved environment and explains how the design and programmed sequence protect people's wellbeing. The Bee-Bot follows only the directional commands students enter, so successful navigation depends on careful planning and debugging.

Students investigate body systems, healthy routines, and choices that support physical and emotional health through hands-on activities, read-alouds, inquiry stations, and creative projects. The unit emphasizes student agency, reflection, and communication, with opportunities for students to document learning, build models, and share their understanding with peers and families. Transdisciplinary links include science, English, PE, and wellbeing, fostering a holistic understanding of how we care for ourselves and others.

Year 1 students made great strides in understanding how

physically and emotionally. During our soccer and football
activities, they began recognising how their stamina and
running speed improved as the term progressed. This led to
discussions about how exercise not only strengthens the body

on how consistent effort led to gradual improvement. In the
swimming program, students saw firsthand how regular
practice made swimming strokes and water safety skills
easier, reinforcing the idea that change takes time but leads
to positive outcomes when they stick with it.

REFLECTING
How can our reflections guide next steps in current and future learning and teaching?

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to
develop and evidence students? understanding of the
central idea?
The combination of nonfiction read-alouds, guest speakers, and
student-led presentations allowed students to engage with the
central idea in meaningful ways. The read-alouds provided
background knowledge and vocabulary, while the guest speaker
visit from the Royal Flying Doctor Service made the concept of
services more tangible. Student presentations demonstrated their
ability to apply and communicate their understanding of different
community helpers and their roles.

How did teachers design and plan for, recognize, and
support student agency in learning and teaching?
Student agency was encouraged through choice and voice in
learning. The student presentations allowed learners to select a
community helper of interest, research their role, and present
their findings in their own way. Open-ended discussions during
read-alouds also provided opportunities for students to ask
questions and make connections to their own experiences.
The community helper information report was another
transdisciplinary learning experience that allowed agency, when
students chose their helper to research and write about.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the
learner profile and approaches to learning?

The Year 1s prepared and presented an assembly item about the
Learner Profile attributes. They made connects between different
community helpers and the Learner Profile attributes.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings, and skills to
support the transfer of learning across, between, and
beyond subjects?

What are the students? perceptions of how the learning
experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the guest speaker session from the Royal Flying Doctor
Service particularly exciting because they could see how real people
help the community. Many students also enjoyed the nonfiction read-
alouds, as they helped them learn new facts in an interesting way. The
student presentations were engaging because they allowed them to
choose a community helper they were interested in and share their
knowledge with their peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals outlined for the
unit of inquiry?
Most students felt they had a good understanding of how services
support the community. They were able to name different community
helpers, explain why they are important, and give examples of how
they meet people's needs. Some students said they learned more
about helpers they had never thought about before, like emergency
responders and postal workers.

What are students? reflections on their understanding of the central
idea?
Students recognized that services are essential because they help
people in different ways. Some mentioned that they now understand
why their families rely on these services, such as doctors, teachers, and
shopkeepers. Others shared that they hadn't realized how many jobs
work together to support the community.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated the learner
profile attributes that were identified for this unit?
Yes ? through our assembly item.

What did students feel challenged by?
Some students found it difficult to remember all the details about their
chosen community helper during their presentations. Others said they
struggled with formulating good questions to ask the guest speaker. A
few students mentioned that learning about so many different services
at once was overwhelming at times.

Students made connections between nonfiction texts and real-
world experiences, showing an ability to apply learning.

What do students now know or understand that they didn't
before?

 Students now understand that community services are not just about
helping individuals but supporting the whole community. They also
learned about less obvious helpers, like waste collectors and librarians,
and how they play a role in keeping things running smoothly.

What will students do with their new learning?
Many students expressed a desire to show appreciation for community
helpers, with some suggesting writing thank-you letters. Others said
they now notice these services more in their daily lives and want to
learn more about different jobs in their community. Some students
even mentioned wanting to be a community helper when they grow up!

During the guest speaker session, students asked insightful
questions, demonstrating an understanding of the purpose of
services.

Their presentations showcased research skills, organization of
ideas, and communication strategies that align with literacy
development.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
The unit naturally integrated literacy (reading and presenting
information), social studies (understanding community needs),
and inquiry skills (researching and questioning). Collaboration
among teachers (mainly Library) ensured that the read-alouds
aligned with key concepts, discussions deepened understanding,
and assessment reflected both communication and content
knowledge.

What did we discover about the process of learning that
will inform future learning and teaching?

Students benefited from real-world connections, and guest
speakers significantly enhanced engagement and understanding.

Providing opportunities for student choice led to more meaningful
engagement with the content.

Future units could incorporate more hands-on or role-playing
experiences to deepen understanding of services and their impact.

ourselves healthy. Students were curious and motivated by the
hands-on and creative experiences, such as building life-size
models of the skeleton and organs. These activities made abstract
concepts more concrete and supported collaboration and problem-
solving skills.
The daily shared read-alouds were particularly valuable, as they
built background knowledge and vocabulary, which students were
then able to transfer into their writing. Informative writing
improved noticeably across the unit. Many students were able to
use text features such as headings, diagrams, and labels in their
Informative Books, demonstrating their growing understanding of
nonfiction writing. The creation of the Quiz Book for Student-Led
Conferences gave students ownership over their learning and an
authentic purpose for recalling and applying information.
Students showed high levels of engagement during the inquiry
stations on healthy habits. They made meaningful connections
between the body systems we studied and the lifestyle choices
that help maintain health, such as nutrition, exercise, and rest. It
was encouraging to see students reflecting on their own routines
and articulating changes they could make to improve their
wellbeing.
Some challenges included the range of prior knowledge students
had about the body. A few students initially found it difficult to
connect systems together, seeing them as separate rather than
interdependent. Through discussions, models, and experiments,
many were able to progress towards a more holistic view of how
the body functions.
Moving forward, I would like to include more opportunities for
student-led research, possibly through guided use of digital
resources or library texts, so they can further drive their own
inquiries. Additionally, providing more structured formative
checkpoints around body systems would help ensure all students
are consolidating understanding before moving on.
Overall, the unit was successful in fostering curiosity,
responsibility, and communication skills. Students demonstrated
both conceptual understanding and practical application, and they
were proud to showcase their learning through the Healthy Bodies
Museum at the end of the unit.

PE ? connecting to this unit allowed students to explore how their
actions influence their own safety and wellbeing through
movement-based activities. We engaged with key concepts such
as Form, Change and Perspective by exploring how our bodies

 grow and change, and how we can make safe, thoughtful choices
during physical activity. While students responded well to
activities that built coordination, strength and confidence, time
limitations meant some concepts were only touched on briefly
rather than explored in depth. Peer challenges and occasional
friendship conflicts made teamwork and supporting others difficult
at times.  However, these moments also provided authentic
opportunities to reinforce respectful behaviour, reflection and
problem-solving. Many students showed progress in understanding
how movement and behaviour choices affect not just themselves
but those around them. In future, more time and explicit
scaffolding around emotional regulation and group roles would
help further strengthen these connections.

Music ? The unit worked well, and the students enjoyed listening to this classical
work. We collectively identified things they see, feel, hear and do in during each
season and discussed if there were musical elements that helped us to imagine
those things. Following which students were put into groups and were given the
opportunity to choose their own season, come up with their own items for each
season and then create sounds that matched the season.

ci: Artistic appreciation and expressions inspire our imagination and creativity.
lo: Forms of expression; Expressing thoughts and ideas; Understanding and appreciating art

s.d: Students compose a short soundscape that expresses the colours, shapes and feelings they notice in a chosen artwork. This shows how one art form can spark imagination in another. Students swap artworks without explaining their choices, then compare how differently their partners translate the same image into sound. They choose and arrange sounds to create a clear beginning, change and ending. The class finishes with a listening gallery where the artwork is revealed after each composition plays. GarageBand makes this possible by letting students record and arrange music and sound effects.

Students draw an everyday object in Sketchbook, then transform it into something imagined through colour, pattern and added details. This helps them see that artistic expression can begin with close observation and grow through creative choices. Partners exchange unfinished drawings and suggest one surprising possibility without taking control of the artist's idea. Each student decides whether to accept, adapt or reject the suggestion. They finish with a detailed digital illustration and a short written artist statement. Sketchbook's drawing tools support careful sketching, colouring and visual experimentation.

Students animate cut-paper shapes to show the feeling and imagery in a short poem they have written. This lets them explore how words, movement and visual art can express the same thought in different ways. Another class watches the animations without seeing the poems and describes the feelings or ideas it notices. Students use that response to adjust the timing, movement or final frame. They finish with a short stop-motion poem that can be screened for the school community. Stop Motion Studio captures the paper pieces frame by frame so small changes appear to move.

Students record a short interview with a classmate about an artwork, song or poem that inspires them. This builds appreciation by asking children to listen closely to another person's ideas and feelings. Interviewers must include one follow-up question based on something their partner actually says. Students then edit the conversation so the speaker's voice and meaning remain clear. They finish with a brief podcast episode featuring an introduction, interview and closing reflection. Podcasting using Canva supports recording and editing the complete audio story on an iPad.

Students draw or write responses to several artworks on a shared Freeform canvas. This makes different forms of expression and personal interpretations visible in one place. Each student connects their response to a classmate's idea that surprises them, then adds a note explaining the connection. The class looks for artworks that produced similar feelings as well as completely different reactions. They finish with a connected visual wall of drawings, words, questions and appreciation notes. Freeform's infinite collaborative canvas lets ideas sit beside one another and grow over several lessons.

Students empathise with younger visitors who need a clear, playful way to move through a classroom art display, then define what would make the journey easy and enjoyable. They ideate routes with coloured tiles and prototype signs, arches and viewing stops from cardboard, paper, tape and recycled materials. Teams test whether Sphero Indi can travel the full route and pause attention at each artwork, then move tiles or rebuild structures when the journey is unclear. They invite another group to test the route without instructions and use the group's actions as feedback. Each team demonstrates an improved physical gallery path in which movement, colour and student-made art work together.

plannerText: The 'How We Express Ourselves' Year 2 unit explores artistic appreciation, creativity, and imagination through diverse forms of expression such as art, poetry, and music. Students investigate how thoughts and feelings can be communicated, develop empathy and social skills, and reflect on their own creative processes. The unit emphasizes risk-taking, balanced wellbeing, and responsible use of materials, with strong links to visual art, music, and literacy. Learning experiences include poetry writing, digital art, collaborative projects, and sharing creative work with the school community, all designed to foster self-expression and appreciation of others' creativity.

Throughout this unit, students explored the forces of push, pull,
gravity and momentum by engaging in movement-based
experiences such as gymnastics, skipping and striking games.
These activities allowed them to reflect on how their own body
and equipment could be used to create or respond to different
types of motion.  The Year 2 students demonstrated curiosity and
growing confidence when experimenting with balance, control and
coordination, especially during tasks that required prediction or
decision-making. The link to physical forces was highly successful.

prompts to reinforce the learning, perhaps incorporating more
visual tools (like diagrams or slow-motion video) to highlight
motion and force more explicitly.

Needs: Things we must have to live.
Examples: Food, water, shelter, clothing.

? Wants: Things we would like to have, but don't need to survive.

?

Basic Needs: The most important things we need to stay alive.

comfortable.

 ?

o

After the role-play, have a class discussion about what was
essential for the situation and what was just a nice addition.

Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

ci: Marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities.
lo: Needs and wants; The changing needs of communities; The design process

s.d: Students build a short survey that asks another Year 2 class to choose between community needs and wants in marketplace situations. The responses show that marketplaces change according to what people value, use and can afford. Students include one question about what a local support organisation should stock first when space is limited. They compare the live results, discuss surprising choices and revise any unclear questions. They end with a real set of community preference data and a ranked list of priorities. Microsoft Forms automatically collects the answers and displays simple charts.

Students enter class votes about essential and optional marketplace items into a simple spreadsheet. They use the totals to work out which items a small community stall should stock and how many of each it might need. Pairs receive the same limited stock budget but make different choices, then compare who they have served and who may miss out. They adjust quantities when the teacher announces a change such as hot weather, a new baby group or fewer available funds. They end with a stock table and a graph showing how community needs can change. Excel turns the entered totals into clear column or picture-style charts.

Students watch selected clips showing supermarkets, street markets and community food services, pausing to sort what each place provides into needs and wants. This helps them see that marketplaces are organised around the people who use them. The teacher adds questions that ask students to notice who is served, what is easy to access and what may be missing. Students revisit one clip after hearing about Sacred Heart Mission and change an answer when new evidence changes their thinking. They end with completed responses comparing several kinds of marketplaces. ClickView's built-in questions keep the viewing focused and make student thinking visible to the teacher.

Students record a 360-degree view of a classroom marketplace while classmates buy, sell, queue and restock essential and optional items. The whole-space recording helps them notice how layout and organisation affect whether community needs are met. Students watch from different directions and choose one change that would make the market easier for a young child, an older person or someone carrying several bags. They rearrange the stalls, record the market again and compare the two versions. They end with before-and-after 360-degree recordings of a redesigned marketplace. The spherical view captures the stalls, signs, queues and movement at the same time.

Students build possible floor plans for a small community market by stretching bands around the virtual peg grid. They explore how stall shape, pathway width and available space influence what the market can offer. Partners swap plans and test whether every essential stall can be reached without crossing another stall. Students revise their shapes when a new community need requires a food table, quiet waiting area or donation point. They end with a clear geometric market plan that balances limited space with community priorities. The virtual bands make it quick to move boundaries and compare area and perimeter.

Students empathise with people collecting essential items, then define the need for a safe route through a busy community market. Using cardboard stalls, recycled packaging, paper signs and Indi's coloured tiles, they sketch several ideas before building a physical marketplace and laying a delivery path. They test whether Indi can travel from the storeroom to the correct stalls, then move tiles, widen paths or change the layout whenever the route fails. Classmates test each prototype with a changed request, such as delivering food before toiletries or avoiding a crowded area. Students finish by demonstrating a reliable route and explaining how each redesign better meets a community need.

plannerText: The Year 2 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores how marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities, with a strong focus on distinguishing needs from wants and using the design thinking process to create solutions for real community challenges. Students investigate local and global perspectives, connect with organisations like Sacred Heart Mission, and engage in hands-on activities such as role-play, sorting games, and prototyping. The unit emphasises communication, reflection, and responsibility, integrating maths (data, measurement), English (persuasive writing, information reports), and social studies. Learners are encouraged to document their thinking, collaborate, and share their innovations with the school community, building empathy and practical problem-solving skills.

?

Needs: Things we must have to live.
Examples: Food, water, shelter, clothing.

? Wants: Things we would like to have, but don't need to survive.

?

?

Examples: Toys, games, fancy clothes, sweets.
Basic Needs: The most important things we need to stay alive.
Examples: Air, food, water, shelter, and sleep.
Luxury Wants: Things that are not necessary but make life more fun or
comfortable.
Examples: Video games, pets, swimming pools.

"I Want, I Need" Song or Chant

 ?

Activity:
o

Create a simple song or chant with the students about needs and
wants. You can use a familiar tune, like "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little
Star," or create your own.

o Here's an example of a simple chant:

?

"I need food, I need water, I need shelter, clothes to
wear, But I want toys and fancy shoes, Games and
candy, I could choose. Needs are first, wants are fun,
But needs come first, everyone!"

o

the ideas.

Needs and Wants Role-Play

Objective: Encourage students to think about needs and wants in real-life
situations.

?

o Divide students into pairs or small groups.

move, separating them into needs (like a tent, food, or warm
clothes) and wants (like toys, games, or decorations).
After the role-play, have a class discussion about what was
essential for the situation and what was just a nice addition.

PSPE
Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

s.d: Students photograph pushes, pulls and still objects, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images into three groups. This helps them work out how a computer can recognise evidence of force and motion. Pairs swap image sets to test whether each model can recognise unfamiliar examples from the playground. They finish with a working image-classification model and a list of mistakes that helped them improve it. Teachable Machine retrains the model when students add clearer or more varied examples. This works like sports-coaching apps that recognise movement from images to give feedback on technique.

Students photograph a playground object and record it explaining the pushes, pulls, gravity or friction acting on it. This gives young scientists a playful reason to use force and motion vocabulary accurately. Another class watches the talking objects and sends back one question each group must answer. Students finish with a collection of short explanations from swings, slides, balls and climbing equipment. ChatterPix Kids lets students draw a mouth on a photo and add a recorded voice. The short recording limit encourages one clear scientific explanation rather than a long script.

Students build a digital investigation book by adding results from rolling the same object across different surfaces. This shows how friction changes motion and why fair testing matters. Groups exchange books and repeat one another's investigation to see whether the results are similar. Each group finishes with a narrated book containing predictions, measurements, labelled evidence and a conclusion. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page. Families can use the finished books to try one safe force experiment at home.

Students film and edit short comparisons of objects moving down ramps with different heights or surfaces. This makes changes in speed and distance easier to see and discuss. Groups choose one surprising result and ask another group to explain it before revealing their own conclusion. They finish with a short science documentary using titles, spoken explanations and carefully selected clips. iMovie provides titles and transitions for joining several tests into one clear film. The final films can run beside the physical ramps during a community display.

Students arrange coloured tiles to make Sphero Indi start, change direction and stop along a floor path. This shows how technology can control motion through a planned sequence of causes and effects. Groups swap paths and work out the intended sequence before letting the car run. They finish with a tested route that carries the car between labelled examples of pushes, pulls, gravity and friction. Sphero Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen. Students improve the spacing and order of tiles when the movement does not match their plan.

Students empathise with a classroom visitor who needs a marble delivered across a table without touching it, then define the exact distance, finish point and safety rules on a Freeform board. They sketch several linked-force ideas before building a physical Rube Goldberg machine from cardboard ramps, tubes, cups, string, dominoes, recycled materials and masking tape. Teams prototype one section at a time, test where gravity, pushes and friction help or stop the motion, and record each change on the board. They combine the strongest sections, retest the full chain and adjust heights, joins and surfaces until the marble reaches its target reliably. At the final demonstration, students point out each force, explain one failed test and show how their improved machine solves the visitor's problem.

plannerText: The Year 2 'How the World Works' unit explores forces and motion through hands-on experiments, playground investigations, and simple machines. Students learn about push, pull, gravity, friction, and how materials and inventions solve problems. The unit emphasises inquiry, vocabulary development, and scientific thinking, with strong links to maths (measurement, data, time), English (non-fiction features, information reports), and the arts. Maker Space sessions and digital tools are used to deepen understanding, culminating in creative projects like Rube Goldberg machines and sharing learning with the community.

PSPE
Throughout this unit, students explored the forces of push, pull,
gravity and momentum by engaging in movement-based
experiences such as gymnastics, skipping and striking games.
These activities allowed them to reflect on how their own body
and equipment could be used to create or respond to different
types of motion.  The Year 2 students demonstrated curiosity and
growing confidence when experimenting with balance, control and
coordination, especially during tasks that required prediction or
decision-making. The link to physical forces was highly successful.
In future, I would continue using questioning and reflection
prompts to reinforce the learning, perhaps incorporating more
visual tools (like diagrams or slow-motion video) to highlight
motion and force more explicitly.

Music ? The students enjoyed this unit and used their iPads to
create short stories with accompanying pictures and sound
effects. They could choose body percussion, classroom
instruments or digital sounds accessed via a QR code.
Interestingly, only 2 students chose to use the digital sounds
with the majority choosing the classroom instruments. In
reflection, this activity was pitched a little too high for this

 particular cohort and would benefit from less steps.

Needs: Things we must have to live.
Examples: Food, water, shelter, clothing.

? Wants: Things we would like to have, but don't need to survive.

?

?

Examples: Toys, games, fancy clothes, sweets.
Basic Needs: The most important things we need to stay alive.
Examples: Air, food, water, shelter, and sleep.
Luxury Wants: Things that are not necessary but make life more fun or
comfortable.
Examples: Video games, pets, swimming pools.

"I Want, I Need" Song or Chant

 ?

Activity:
o

Create a simple song or chant with the students about needs and
wants. You can use a familiar tune, like "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little
Star," or create your own.

o Here's an example of a simple chant:

?

"I need food, I need water, I need shelter, clothes to
wear, But I want toys and fancy shoes, Games and
candy, I could choose. Needs are first, wants are fun,
But needs come first, everyone!"

o

Sing the song together and repeat it several times to reinforce
the ideas.

Needs and Wants Role-Play

Objective: Encourage students to think about needs and wants in real-life
situations.

?

o Divide students into pairs or small groups.

clothes) and wants (like toys, games, or decorations).
After the role-play, have a class discussion about what was
essential for the situation and what was just a nice addition.

PSPE
Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

ci: Taking care of our Earth starts with the choices we make.
lo: Earth's resources; How our actions affect the environment; Ways we can care for our planet

s.d: Students sort photographs of everyday lunchbox items into 'use once', 'use again' and 'recycle' groups. This makes the link between daily choices, Earth's resources and the rubbish we produce easy to see. Pairs then redesign one waste-heavy lunchbox by replacing three items with lower-waste choices. They swap collages and check whether each suggested change is realistic for a Year 2 family. Each pair finishes with a clear before-and-after lunchbox collage. PicCollage's grid layouts and short captions keep the comparison simple and visual.

Students count and enter the different types of rubbish found during a classroom bin audit. The numbers show how small daily actions can add up to a large effect on the environment. Groups choose one type of waste they believe the class could reduce, then compare their prediction with the data. They repeat the audit after a week of changed classroom habits to see whether their choice worked. The class ends with a table and two charts showing the before-and-after results. Excel turns the collected numbers into graphs that Year 2 students can read and discuss.

Students photograph a clean discarded object and record it explaining where it came from and what could happen to it next. Speaking as a bottle, wrapper or cardboard tube makes the path from resource to rubbish easier to understand. Students swap recordings and suggest one better choice that could change each object's ending. They then revise the voice clip so the object asks listeners to take one clear action. Each student finishes with a short talking-object message for a class recycling display. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and recorded voice directly to the photograph.

Students code two short animations showing what happens when a character makes a wasteful choice and a caring choice. The side-by-side outcomes show how one action can affect land, water, animals or the amount of rubbish produced. Partners exchange projects, follow each sequence and identify where the environmental outcome changes. Students debug any unclear movement or message so a younger class can understand the cause and effect. Each pair finishes with an animated choice story containing two different endings. ScratchJr's blocks let students sequence characters, speech and movement without needing to type code.

Students record short interviews with classmates about one Earth-friendly choice they already make and one they could improve. Hearing several answers shows that caring for the planet depends on many practical choices rather than one perfect solution. The class selects a few questions for a staff member who helps manage waste, gardens or resources at school. Students listen back and choose the clearest answers rather than recording every idea again. They finish with a set of brief audio interviews that can be played at a class action meeting. The microphones and recorders capture voices clearly enough for students to compare ideas and notice repeated themes.

Students empathise with school cleaners by examining a floor mat showing classrooms, bins, garden beds and places where litter often collects, then define the problem of moving rubbish to the correct place. Using cardboard, bottle tops, paper signs and other clean recycled materials, teams ideate and build movable bins, obstacles and collection points on the mat. They prototype a Bee-Bot route by planning and entering a sequence of directional button presses before the robot moves. Teams test whether every item reaches the correct bin, then change the mat or debug the sequence when the route is inefficient. Each team demonstrates a working waste-collection route and explains how its redesign saves movement, prevents contamination and supports better choices.

plannerText: The Year 2 'Sharing the Planet' unit focuses on students understanding Earth's resources, the impact of their actions on the environment, and practical ways to care for the planet. Through inquiry, students explore concepts like recycling, waste management, and sustainability, connecting local actions to global responsibility. The unit emphasizes communication, reflection, and action, with opportunities for students to document, share, and act on their learning using digital tools and hands-on Makerspace experiences.

PSPE
Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during
Athletics.

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Landmarks and places of significance tell stories about our history.
lo: The significance of places to different people and cultures; The connection between landmarks and identity; How landmarks and symbols represent our history

s.d: Students explore teacher-selected Australian and Aboriginal places of significance in Street View, looking closely at signs, symbols, paths and memorials. This shows how a place can hold stories that are not obvious from its appearance alone. Pairs compare two sites and choose which details help visitors understand each place's identity and history. They then guide another pair through the view and explain one visible story and one story that would need to be learned from Traditional Owners or trusted sources. Each pair finishes with an oral guided tour of a significant place. Street View lets students move through the surroundings without signing in or changing the map.

Students build a simple 3D scene showing a significant Australian place at two moments in time. This helps them show how landmarks can stay important even when their surroundings or uses change. Students swap scenes and ask whether the symbols, people and objects make the place's story clear. They revise one detail after hearing what their classmates understood or missed. Each student finishes with an interactive virtual scene that can be explored from different viewpoints. Delightex lets students place and arrange objects inside a three-dimensional world.

Students record a short puppet conversation between two people who value the same place for different reasons. This makes the significance of places to different people and cultures easier to hear and compare. Students choose a carefully researched local or Australian place, while teacher-approved sources guide any Aboriginal perspectives. Another class watches the puppet shows and identifies the clues that reveal each speaker's connection to the place. Each pair finishes with a narrated puppet show containing a clear setting, two viewpoints and a respectful ending. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a landmark or symbol speaking in the first person about one true event, memory or cultural connection linked to it. This gives them a clear way to explain how landmarks carry stories from the past. Students choose whether their speaker addresses a new visitor, a future child or someone who wants to change the site. Partners listen and check that the recording separates known facts from imagined words. Each student finishes with a short lip-synced character explanation suitable for a class exhibition. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the on-screen character's mouth with the student's voice.

Students make a digital field guide with one page for each significant Australian place they investigate. This brings maps, stories, symbols and reasons for preservation into one clear collection. Families or another Year 2 class can listen to the pages and leave students with questions to answer in a revised edition. Students include their own words, a labelled image and a recorded explanation of why each place matters. The class finishes with a narrated digital book that compares several places without ranking one culture's significance above another. Book Creator supports text, images and student-recorded narration on the same page.

Students empathise with young visitors who need a respectful, easy-to-follow path through a model heritage site, then define which important stories and protected areas the route must include. Using cardboard, paper signs, recycled materials, blocks and a large grid mat, they ideate several routes and build a physical model with symbols marking story stops and no-go areas. They prototype by programming the Bee-Bot's directional buttons, then test whether it reaches each stop in the intended historical order without touching protected spaces. After classmates try the route, students change the path, signs or command sequence and test it again. Each group demonstrates a working guided route and explains how its design helps visitors learn while caring for the significant place.

plannerText: The Year 2 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit explores how landmarks and places of significance tell stories about our history, with a focus on Australian and Indigenous sites. Students inquire into the significance of places to different people and cultures, the connection between place and story, and ways we preserve and remember historical sites. Learning experiences include mapping, storytelling, Dreaming stories, data collection, and the use of symbols, with strong links to literacy, geography, and Indigenous perspectives. The unit emphasizes hands-on learning, communication, and digital skills, culminating in creative projects that connect students' understanding of place, culture, and history.

gravity and momentum by engaging in movement-based
experiences such as gymnastics, skipping and striking games.
These activities allowed them to reflect on how their own body

Other student comments

PSPE
Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during
Athletics.

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

inspiringRegenAutoSwapped.toTool: Seesaw + Animating a Character with Adobe Express

ci: Our relationships with others impact our lives.
lo: Importance of relationships; Developing and maintaining healthy relationships; The impact of relationships on wellbeing

s.d: Students record a short interview with a trusted person about how their relationship has changed over time. This shows that caring relationships grow through shared experiences, listening and repair. Each student chooses one answer that could help the class build stronger relationships and records a voice reflection explaining why. Families can listen and add another example from home. Students end with a collection of short video or audio interviews and personal reflections. Seesaw keeps the recordings together in each student's portfolio.

Students photograph three clear body poses for calming down, such as stretching, star breathing and hands on heart, then train Teachable Machine to recognise them. This helps students explore how self-regulation can support healthy relationships during difficult moments. Pairs swap models and test whether each pose is recognised from different positions, then add better examples when the model makes mistakes. Similar pose recognition is used in physiotherapy and accessibility tools to notice body movements and give useful feedback. Students end with a tested model that identifies their chosen calming poses. The model improves as students add varied and accurate training examples.

Students plan and record a puppet scene in which two friends face a small disagreement and try two different responses. This makes the impact of words, listening and taking responsibility easy to see and discuss. Another pair watches the unfinished scene and chooses which healthy response the characters should try next. Students then record an ending that shows how the choice affects both characters' wellbeing. They end with a short animated puppet show that can be used during a class meeting. Puppet Pals lets students move characters across a backdrop while recording their voices.

Students paint two layered portraits showing how a person might feel before and after a caring interaction. This helps them notice that relationships can affect feelings, confidence and wellbeing. Students exchange paintings without explanations and ask a partner what colours, shapes or details helped them read each feeling. They then revise one layer so the emotional change is clearer without adding words. Students end with a paired digital artwork showing the impact of kindness, exclusion, apology or support. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting with separate layers that can be adjusted during revision.

Students photograph small classroom figures frame by frame to show a friendship changing over time. This makes maintaining relationships visible through actions such as inviting, listening, apologising and checking in. Groups swap half-finished animations and suggest one caring action that could change what happens next. The original group chooses whether to use that suggestion and explains its choice in the final scene. Students end with a short stop-motion story showing a relationship problem, a response and its effect on wellbeing. Stop Motion Studio joins the photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students empathise with two classroom figures who need a calm, welcoming place to reconnect after a disagreement, then define what the route and meeting space must provide. They ideate with sketches and prototype a physical pathway using Indi colour tiles, cardboard boundaries, recycled boxes, paper signs and a small meeting space. Teams test whether Indi travels through their planned sequence and reaches the meeting place, then move tiles or rebuild parts that do not work. They repeat the test with another team's figure and feedback so the design supports more than one person's needs. Students finish by demonstrating the improved route and explaining how each physical choice helps people reconnect safely and calmly.

plannerText: The Year 2 'Who We Are' unit explores how relationships impact our lives, focusing on developing caring, reflective, and open-minded learners. Students investigate the importance of relationships, how to maintain them, and how they change over time. The unit emphasizes social-emotional learning, empathy, and self-regulation, using strategies like Toolbox Education, Zones of Regulation, and the UR Strong Friendology program. Learning experiences include read-alouds, class meetings, role-play, and reflective journals, with strong links to PSPE and wellbeing. The unit encourages students to build positive relationships, understand emotions, and take responsibility for their actions within the classroom community.

PSPE
Throughout this unit, students explored the forces of push, pull,
gravity and momentum by engaging in movement-based
experiences such as gymnastics, skipping and striking games.
These activities allowed them to reflect on how their own body
and equipment could be used to create or respond to different
types of motion.  The Year 2 students demonstrated curiosity and
growing confidence when experimenting with balance, control and
coordination, especially during tasks that required prediction or
decision-making. The link to physical forces was highly successful.
In future, I would continue using questioning and reflection
prompts to reinforce the learning, perhaps incorporating more
visual tools (like diagrams or slow-motion video) to highlight
motion and force more explicitly.

Music ? The students enjoyed this unit and used their iPads to
create short stories with accompanying pictures and sound
effects. They could choose body percussion, classroom
instruments or digital sounds accessed via a QR code.
Interestingly, only 2 students chose to use the digital sounds
with the majority choosing the classroom instruments. In
reflection, this activity was pitched a little too high for this

 particular cohort and would benefit from less steps.

PSPE
Students explored a variety of athletic events, developing technique,
movement efficiency, and building awareness of personal progress.

 Alongside the physical skills, I intentionally supported transdisciplinary
thinking by weaving in the concepts of Responsibility and Connection
from the STP theme.
Regular check-ins and reflection questions were used to help students
make links between their choices in PE and their role in shared spaces.
Prompts like ?How did you help your team today?? or ?Why is it important
to share equipment fairly?? encouraged them to consider how their
behaviour impacted others and how we are all connected in a team
environment.
The approach worked well.  The language around fairness, teamwork and
encouragement became more natural as the weeks progressed. Some
students needed support to go beyond surface-level answers, so next
time I'd like to introduce some sentence starters or visual prompts to help
scaffold deeper responses. I also think it would be valuable to include a
mini reflection portfolio task at the end of the unit, so students can share
one example of how they showed responsibility or connection during
Athletics.

Mathematics. How do symbols help us read a map?

It is impossible to label every single feature in words on a map,
therefore we use map symbols. Both shapes and colours can be
used for symbols on maps. A small circle may mean a point of
interest, with a brown circle meaning recreation, red circle
meaning services, and green circle meaning rest stop. Colors
may cover larger areas of a map, such as green representing
forested land and blue representing waterways.

ci: Celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community.
lo: The ways personal and cultural events are celebrated; Our appreciation of the diversity of cultures; How celebrations shape community identity

s.d: Students arrange objects, colours and handmade signs that show how a family or cultural celebration brings people together, then record each display with the Insta360 camera. Seeing the whole setting helps them notice that space, decoration and gathering are part of how traditions shape community identity. Groups swap recordings and look around each other's displays, asking respectful questions about details they do not recognise. Families can also suggest one object or message that should appear in the display. Students finish with an immersive 360-degree gallery of celebrations represented across the class. The spherical recording lets viewers turn and explore every part of each setting rather than seeing one chosen camera angle.

Students write and send a short survey asking families which events they celebrate, what they do and why those traditions matter. The responses show both shared customs and important differences within one school community. Each group chooses one pattern in the auto-charts that surprised them and writes a new question to investigate. The class discusses how to report small cultural groups respectfully without treating one answer as typical of everyone. Students finish with a class data display showing how celebrations help shape the Elsternwick community. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and turns them into charts that Year 3 students can read and compare.

Students record a short interview with a family or community member about one celebration, including what has stayed the same and what has changed. Listening to a real voice helps students understand that traditions are carried, adapted and valued by people. Partners exchange recordings and choose one respectful follow-up question that would help the speaker explain the tradition more fully. Students edit the interview so the speaker's words remain the centre of the episode. They finish with a class podcast collection featuring different cultural and personal celebrations. Podcasting using Canva works on iPads and supports recording and editing the complete episode in one place.

Students design an exhibition panel comparing two celebrations through food, music, clothing, symbols, gathering places and purpose. The comparison helps them see diversity without deciding that one way of celebrating is normal and another is unusual. Each panel includes a question for visitors, such as 'What brings people together in both celebrations?' Visitors add spoken responses during a class gallery walk, and students revise any wording that could create a stereotype. Students finish with a clear visual display for families or another Year 3 class. Canva provides layouts for combining short text, images and headings on one exhibition panel.

Students paint a layered digital artwork that combines symbols, colours and patterns from celebrations that matter to their family or community. Choosing what to place in the foreground and background helps them show which parts of identity are public, shared or personally meaningful. Students exchange paintings without explanations first, then compare what viewers noticed with what the artist intended. The artist can change a layer when a symbol needs more emphasis or a clearer relationship to the whole image. Students finish with an original digital portrait of cultural identity for a class gallery. Brushes Redux supports layered painting, so students can revise one part without repainting the entire work.

Students empathise with younger visitors who may not know how to join a celebration, then define a need for a clear and welcoming interactive sign. Using cardboard, recycled materials, foil switches, crocodile clips and a battery-powered Micro:bit, they ideate and prototype a display that shows a simple welcome symbol or sequence on the LED grid when a visitor presses a labelled switch. Pairs test whether visitors can operate it without spoken instructions, then debug the code and reshape or relabel the physical controls. At the end, students demonstrate a sturdy working welcome display and explain how feedback made it easier for everyone to take part.

plannerText: The Year 3 'How We Express Ourselves' unit explores how celebrations and traditions shape culture and identity. Students investigate personal and cultural events, appreciate diversity, and reflect on what it means to be a global citizen. Through inquiry, research, and creative projects, they examine traditions in their own families and around the world, compare celebrations, and express their learning through presentations, art, and digital media. The unit emphasizes open-mindedness, caring, communication, and research skills, with strong links to English, Social Studies, Music, Visual Art, and Digital Technologies. Students share their cultural identities, create collaborative displays, and celebrate diversity through a range of hands-on and digital experiences.

 where students explored how small changes in technique, like
adjusting their grip, angle, speed or timing, can completely
change the outcome of a pass or shot. We looked closely at how
strategy and movement shift depending on space, teammates and
goals, and students used trial and error to figure out what worked.

refined their approach to improve performance.

humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take
action. From footwork adjustments to finding better angles on
court, the students began to see that success in sport (and in
learning) often comes from small tweaks and persistence, not just
natural skill. It was a great way to bring scientific thinking into PE,

Lesson 1: Learning engagements

Key question: What motivates people to explore?

Tuning in: Introduce push and pull factors for exploration. Model though shared reading how to find
the push and pull factors in a text (Ten Pound Pom). For example, trade, conquest, curiosity,
economics, financial opportunity, religion, persecution, fame, adventure, business, technological
advancement, health car. Model for students how to write a fact fragment, using bullet points and
key words only.

Learning Engagement: Students work in small groups to read a text and write fact fragments related
to the exploration in the text. Using a T-chart graphic organiser, students record the push and pull
factors related to exploration in the text. Bring students together at the end to share findings and
