Student perspective
During the WWAIPAT unit, students were actively engaged in the Drama Toolbox incursion. During
this excursion, the students enjoyed participating in role-plays of significant historical events
connecting to the unit (Burke and Wills, Gold Rush, First Fleet). The students also enjoyed the

 provocation using Scratch Jr to explore and discover. Throughout the unit, students were effectively
engaged in the case study of Captain Cook and enjoyed learning about other historical explorations
through reading material. The students felt liek they achieved the outline learning goals, as indicated
through their self-assessments of the SeeSaw formative assessment task. Students also displayed a
strong understanding of the Learner Profile attributes when completing the Explorer Project, by
identifying the LP attributes that the explorer demonstrated. Students were occasionaly challeneged
by the application of research skills. This was dependant on the chosen explorer, as some explorers
had a vast range of age-appropriate online resources, while others had fewer resources. Students
now have a very strong understanding of Australia's discovery and settlement and history. Students
have also gained a strong sense of the different motivations for exploration. With their new learning,
students will apply Research Skills in future learning.

The theme of the unit became We are one, we are many and the
song I am Australian helped frame the unit and the general

How did teachers design and plan for, recognise and support
student agency in learning and teaching?
Students were able to follow their interests with the choices they
were offered for exploration. Students each created a Powerpoint
and they had agency with how they put their Powerpoint
together. This way they learn the tools with PP and then we will
use Canva for the next unit then open it up for more agency in
the units that follow.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner

their development of conceptual understandings so incredible
links where made there. The lego experience where they viewed
the creations through different perspectives highlighted this.
ATL: Students set two ATL goals (communication and research
skills) as they worked on their research. The wrote how they
hoped to achieve the goal and then refflected on it with two stars
and a wish.

What evidence do we have that students are developing

transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
Collaboration with different specialists supported
transdisciplinary connections. Each teacher was really excited we
kept checking in on one another.
During Music classes we discussed the culture of singing and
performing at our school and in our JS assemblies; with the

 students able to perform the song they had worked on, during an
assembly towards the end of term. Students viewed different
performances from around the world, commenting on the use of
different musical elements and the subsequent effect on the
listeners. We collaboratively created a verse per class that
represented their own cultures weaving it into an arrangement of
?I Am Australian?. This was a very successful activity and one in
which the students were really invested and seemed to enjoy.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?
I felt that the process was supportive for students because we
started off wither a wider angle then students could refine the
skills when moving into smaller groups and more independent
inquiry. The flow of the unit worked so well. Having HWEO before
WWAIPAT provided great flow across the term.

PSPE

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different
environments).
Looking ahead, I'd like to build in even more time for student reflection and perhaps more
explicit links to visible thinking routines, and vocabulary shared in the homerooms.

ci: The rights and responsibilities of citizens are determined by the rules and laws of a community.
lo: The differences between rules and laws; People responsible for enforcing rules and laws; Rights and responsibilities of citizens; The consequences when rules, laws and rights are not met

s.d: Students program Sphero BOLT to travel through a floor course where signs represent community rules, laws and restricted areas. They work out why some instructions keep everyone safe while others simply help a group run smoothly. Teams exchange courses and test whether another group's instructions are clear, fair and possible to follow. When a route fails or breaks a stated rule, students revise the code and explain the likely consequence for the community. Each team ends with a working coded route and a short spoken explanation at each checkpoint. Sphero BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid let students show actions such as stop, wait and proceed.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion about whether a fictional community decision should be a rule or a law. This helps them examine who makes decisions, who enforces them and how citizens' rights may be affected. Halfway through, students must choose one new piece of information that could change their position, such as a safety risk or an unfair consequence. They compare their reasoning with a partner and identify where their answers became stronger. Each student finishes with a written conversation and a justified recommendation for the fictional community. The teacher can set up a Socratic Tutor scenario that asks open-ended questions without giving students the answer.

Students enter class responses into Microsoft Excel about which rights and responsibilities matter most at school. They turn the responses into charts and look for patterns, disagreements and responsibilities that support several rights. Small groups choose one surprising result and ask another class whether the same pattern appears there. They add the new responses and check whether the larger sample changes their conclusion. Students finish with a labelled chart and a short evidence-based statement about one right and its matching responsibility. Excel tables and charts make changes in the class data easy to see.

Students record and edit a short news report showing what happens when a community rule, law or right is not respected. Their report must explain the rule or law, identify who responds and show consequences for more than one person. Groups film two possible endings?one where the response is fair and one where it creates a new problem. Another class watches both endings and chooses which response best protects people's rights. Students finish with an edited news report containing titles, interviews and two contrasting outcomes. iMovie lets them combine recorded clips, titles and transitions in one film.

Students write a Kahoot quiz that asks classmates to decide whether each everyday example is a rule, a law, a right or a responsibility. They must explain the correct answer after each question so the quiz teaches rather than only tests. Groups swap quizzes and flag any question where the wording or answer seems unfair or unclear. The authors then revise those questions using the feedback and run the improved quiz with another group. Each team ends with a playable quiz built from realistic school and community situations. Kahoot's timed questions and response summaries quickly reveal which distinctions still need discussion.

Students empathise with pedestrians, drivers and crossing supervisors, then define what a fair and safe model crossing must help each person do. Using cardboard, tape, paper signs and toy figures, they sketch ideas before building a physical street prototype with a Micro:bit as the crossing signal. They program its buttons and LED grid to request a crossing and show clear stop-and-walk symbols. Other groups test the model with agreed scenarios, including impatient users and someone ignoring the signal, while the designers observe problems and debug the timing or instructions. Students finish by demonstrating the improved crossing and explaining how its rules balance rights, responsibilities and safety.

plannerText: The Year 3 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores the differences between rules and laws, the people responsible for enforcing them, and the rights and responsibilities of citizens. Students inquire into the function and purpose of social systems, the consequences of not meeting rules and laws, and the concept of citizenship. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, communication, and research skills, with learning engagements including card game design, persuasive writing, and collaborative projects. Students connect local and global perspectives, reflect on their roles as responsible citizens, and demonstrate understanding through creative, inquiry-based tasks.

 where students explored how small changes in technique, like
adjusting their grip, angle, speed or timing, can completely
change the outcome of a pass or shot. We looked closely at how
strategy and movement shift depending on space, teammates and
goals, and students used trial and error to figure out what worked.
Just like scientists, they tested ideas, made observations, and
refined their approach to improve performance.
This tied beautifully into the UOI, where students explored how
humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take
action. From footwork adjustments to finding better angles on
court, the students began to see that success in sport (and in
learning) often comes from small tweaks and persistence, not just
natural skill. It was a great way to bring scientific thinking into PE,
and highlight how discovery, change and growth go hand in hand.

Assessment Reflections

How effective was our monitoring, documenting and measuring of learning informing our understanding of
student learning?
Opportunities for teacher and student feedback.  Students were encouraged to use self-reflection tasks to demonstrate their
understanding of skills and strategies being taught.  When students needed assistance with friendship issues or needed help

 with resilience they needed to demonstrate their use of language with teachers. The unit was delivered on an ?as needs? basis.
As social issues/friendship fires arose, the well-being curriculum was addressed using the programs Grow Your Mind and UR
Strong. Cyber Safety was taught regularly throughout the year using The Cyber Safety Project videos and resources. An area
that could be improved in the future would be more regular assessment and feedback. Because the unit was delivered on an
?as need? basis, there wasn't a Formative or summative assessment shared on Seesaw.

What evidence did we gather about students? knowledge, conceptual understandings and skills?
Evidence of student knowledge and conceptual understanding and skills were captured through the discussion and informal
assessment. Evidence of learning was also captured through day-to-day teaching and observation. However, there was no
formal assessment for each line of inquiry.

How will we share this learning with the learning community?
Parents were invited to a Friendology and cyber safety workshop to learn the language and strategies that students would be
developing in class, so they can assist with conflicts and technology issues that may arise at home. Evidence of learning would
be shared with parents through their ability to self-regulate and resolve friendship fires. In future, we will provide students with
opportunities to share their learning with their through their SeeSaw portfolios.

Lesson 1: Learning engagements

Key question: What motivates people to explore?

Tuning in: Introduce push and pull factors for exploration. Model though shared reading how to find
the push and pull factors in a text (Ten Pound Pom). For example, trade, conquest, curiosity,
economics, financial opportunity, religion, persecution, fame, adventure, business, technological
advancement, health car. Model for students how to write a fact fragment, using bullet points and
key words only.

Learning Engagement: Students work in small groups to read a text and write fact fragments related
to the exploration in the text. Using a T-chart graphic organiser, students record the push and pull
factors related to exploration in the text. Bring students together at the end to share findings and
create a class T-chart of push and pull factors OR two groups share their findings with each other.

Student perspective
During the WWAIPAT unit, students were actively engaged in the Drama Toolbox incursion. During
this excursion, the students enjoyed participating in role-plays of significant historical events
connecting to the unit (Burke and Wills, Gold Rush, First Fleet). The students also enjoyed the

 provocation using Scratch Jr to explore and discover. Throughout the unit, students were effectively
engaged in the case study of Captain Cook and enjoyed learning about other historical explorations
through reading material. The students felt liek they achieved the outline learning goals, as indicated
through their self-assessments of the SeeSaw formative assessment task. Students also displayed a
strong understanding of the Learner Profile attributes when completing the Explorer Project, by
identifying the LP attributes that the explorer demonstrated. Students were occasionaly challeneged
by the application of research skills. This was dependant on the chosen explorer, as some explorers
had a vast range of age-appropriate online resources, while others had fewer resources. Students
now have a very strong understanding of Australia's discovery and settlement and history. Students
have also gained a strong sense of the different motivations for exploration. With their new learning,
students will apply Research Skills in future learning.

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different
environments).
Looking ahead, I'd like to build in even more time for student reflection and perhaps more
explicit links to visible thinking routines, and vocabulary shared in the homerooms.

lo: The work of scientists; The process of learning; How science brings about new understandings and changes

s.d: Students program a micro:bit to measure light levels and show an LED warning when a classroom space is using more light than it needs. This shows how scientists turn measurements into action that can reduce wasted energy. Groups test different thresholds, compare sunny and cloudy conditions, and swap devices to check whether another group's code works reliably. They adjust one variable at a time and debug warnings that appear too early or too late. Each group finishes with a working light-monitoring device and a tested recommendation for the classroom. The built-in light sensing, LED grid and battery pack allow the device to collect information and run away from the computer.

Students measure the time taken for ice cubes to melt under different fair-test conditions and enter their results in Microsoft Excel. This helps them see how controlled variables and repeated measurements lead to stronger scientific explanations. Groups exchange data so they can decide whether one unusual result should change the class conclusion. They make charts that reveal patterns across locations, coverings or container types. Each group finishes with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based conclusion about heat transfer and changes of state. Excel's tables and charts make patterns and unexpected results easy to compare.

Students build two small homes in Minecraft Education, changing one design feature at a time to show how shade, windows and building materials can affect heating and energy use. This makes scientific principles visible as choices that can improve how people live. Another group inspects each pair of homes and identifies the variable that changed before suggesting a more sustainable redesign. Students then rebuild one section to respond to that feedback while keeping the comparison fair. Each team finishes with a matched pair of models and signs explaining the scientific reason for each design choice. Minecraft's shared block-building world lets students construct, inspect and revise the models at full scale.

Students photograph clean examples of paper, plastic and general waste in Teachable Machine and train an image model to sort them. This shows how repeated examples help a computer learn patterns and how science can support responsible consumption. Groups test one another's models with crumpled, partly hidden and differently coloured items, then add better training examples when the model makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way by recognising materials before directing them into different streams. Each group finishes with a tested classification model and a record of which objects confused it. Teachable Machine's image classes and live camera testing make each improvement visible straight away.

Students record a narrated screencast that explains one fair test, drawing the setup and moving labels to show the independent, dependent and controlled variables. This makes the process of learning in science as important as the final result. Partners pause the explanation at the prediction stage and decide whether the test is fair before hearing what happened. Students revise any unclear section and add an annotation showing how the evidence changed or strengthened their thinking. Each student finishes with a short recorded explanation that can play beside the experiment at the science fair. Explain Everything records the student's voice, drawing and on-screen movements together.

Students empathise with people who need to move a small solar-panel cleaning robot safely along a narrow rooftop, then define the need for a reliable route that avoids fragile areas. Using cardboard, masking tape, recycled packaging and paper markers, they ideate and build a physical rooftop course before writing a Sphero BOLT program. They prototype one route, test its speed and direction, and change either the code or the cardboard design after every collision. Teams exchange courses so the robot must work in a setting its programmers did not build. Each team demonstrates a refined moving system and explains which test caused its most useful change.

plannerText: The Year 3 'How the World Works' unit explores how humans use scientific principles to take action, focusing on the work of scientists, the scientific method, and the impact of scientific and technological advances on society and the environment. Students investigate energy transformation, states of matter, fair testing, and variables through hands-on experiments and inquiry-based learning. The unit emphasizes research skills, critical thinking, and communication, with strong links to sustainability, responsible consumption, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Students engage in collaborative projects, digital presentations, and a science fair, connecting their learning to real-world challenges and community action.

PSPE
In PE this term, students will explore how small changes in
movement (like speed, force or timing) can lead to different
results. They'll experiment with technique, reflect on what works,
and refine their approach over time, just like scientists testing
ideas. We're also focusing on how movement, strategy and
technique shift depending on the situation, linking directly to the
movement conceptual understanding: The choice of movement,
technique and strategy is a response to the environment and
situation. It's a great way for students to see how learning and
discovery go hand in hand, supporting the unit's focus on
causation, change and transformation.

 where students explored how small changes in technique, like

Homeroom Teaching Reflection
Students unpacked what the growth mindset was at the
beginning of the year.  Words we use and characteristics that
help us successfully navigate challenges are consistently
used throughout the year as needed. Students had
cybersafety lessons every fortnight. After developing an iPad
essential agreement, elements of the cyber safety
programme got referred back to the agreement. Students
were involved in the Friendology Incursion which launched
the program in Semester 2. Students looked at different ways
friendship can be made and maintained and how to deal with
conflict when it arises. All three programs assisted with
strategies for feeling safe and creating a healthy classroom
community through building positive social skills. As issues
across the three areas arise, the strategies and skills are
implemented and with the consistent language students can
successfully work through conflicts and build resilience when
they face challenges.

Assessment Reflections

How effective was our monitoring, documenting and measuring of learning informing our understanding of
student learning?
Opportunities for teacher and student feedback.  Students were encouraged to use self-reflection tasks to demonstrate their
understanding of skills and strategies being taught.  When students needed assistance with friendship issues or needed help

 with resilience they needed to demonstrate their use of language with teachers. The unit was delivered on an ?as needs? basis.
As social issues/friendship fires arose, the well-being curriculum was addressed using the programs Grow Your Mind and UR
Strong. Cyber Safety was taught regularly throughout the year using The Cyber Safety Project videos and resources. An area
that could be improved in the future would be more regular assessment and feedback. Because the unit was delivered on an
?as need? basis, there wasn't a Formative or summative assessment shared on Seesaw.

What evidence did we gather about students? knowledge, conceptual understandings and skills?
Evidence of student knowledge and conceptual understanding and skills were captured through the discussion and informal
assessment. Evidence of learning was also captured through day-to-day teaching and observation. However, there was no
formal assessment for each line of inquiry.

How will we share this learning with the learning community?
Parents were invited to a Friendology and cyber safety workshop to learn the language and strategies that students would be
developing in class, so they can assist with conflicts and technology issues that may arise at home. Evidence of learning would
be shared with parents through their ability to self-regulate and resolve friendship fires. In future, we will provide students with
opportunities to share their learning with their through their SeeSaw portfolios.

students will apply Research Skills in future learning.

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different
environments).
Looking ahead, I'd like to build in even more time for student reflection and perhaps more
explicit links to visible thinking routines, and vocabulary shared in the homerooms.

sugs.d: Students become energy detectives by using the BBC micro:bit to gather real data about energy use in their classroom and homes, then analyse it to propose ways to reduce waste. This hands-on investigation directly explores how humans use scientific principles to take action for sustainability. Students take on the role of energy consultants, presenting their findings and recommendations to the school community to inspire positive change. Their final artefact is a data-driven digital report, including graphs, insights, and actionable steps, created and shared using the micro:bit's data logging and communication features. The micro:bit's built-in data logging and real-time sensor tracking allow students to collect, visualise, and analyse authentic environmental data in a way that feels like real scientific fieldwork. Students walk away empowered to see themselves as agents of change, ready to influence their families and peers to make smarter, more responsible energy choices.

Students design and experience interactive 3D models of energy transformations and states of matter using Merge Cubes, making abstract scientific concepts tangible in their hands. This activity brings the process of learning and the work of scientists to life by letting students manipulate virtual experiments from every angle. Students become science communicators, creating short video demonstrations to teach younger classes or families about energy changes using their Merge Cube models. The final artefact is a collection of student-created augmented reality models and narrated video walkthroughs, published to the school science fair website. Merge Cube's object annotation feature allows students to embed voice explanations and interactive hotspots directly into their models, adding depth and clarity to their scientific storytelling. By visualising the invisible and teaching others, students build confidence as scientific thinkers and communicators.

Students create eye-catching infographics in Canva that illustrate how scientific discoveries?like renewable energy innovations or recycling breakthroughs?have transformed society and the environment. This project dives deep into the line of inquiry about how science brings about new understandings and changes. Students collaborate as investigative journalists, researching real-world case studies and interviewing local experts or community members about the impact of science-driven action. Their final artefact is a set of professional-quality infographics, displayed around the school and shared with families to spark conversations about responsible consumption and the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Canva's Magic Write feature empowers students to generate compelling headlines and summarise complex information with clarity and flair. Students emerge as advocates for sustainability, equipped to communicate the power of scientific action to a wider audience.

Students author digital science journals in Book Creator, documenting their fair tests, hypotheses, and results as they experiment with variables in energy and matter. This immersive process models the authentic workflow of scientists and highlights the importance of careful observation and communication in the scientific method. Students step into the shoes of real researchers, publishing their journals as part of a collaborative Year 3 science anthology for the school library. The final artefact is a multimedia eBook, featuring photos, diagrams, voice recordings, and reflections, accessible to future students and families. Book Creator's comic templates and audio hotspots allow students to blend narrative, visuals, and spoken explanation in creative ways that deepen understanding. Through this process, students develop scientific literacy and pride in their ability to contribute to a lasting record of inquiry.

Students program Sphero BOLT robots to model energy transfer and fair testing by designing obstacle courses that demonstrate the effects of different variables?like surface texture or ramp angle?on motion. This hands-on coding challenge directly engages with the line of inquiry into how scientists use variables and fair testing to build new knowledge. Acting as engineers, students iterate on their course designs and compare results, then present their findings to a panel of 'expert judges' made up of teachers and visiting parents. The final artefact is a live demonstration and digital portfolio, including video evidence and coded programs, shared during the science fair. Sphero BOLT's live sensor data streaming and programmable LED matrix enable students to visualise speed, direction, and energy changes in real time, adding a layer of scientific analysis to their experiments. Students gain not only coding skills but also a sense of agency as experimenters and problem-solvers.

Students work in teams to design, prototype, and test their own sustainable energy devices?such as wind turbines, solar ovens, or water wheels?using recycled materials, simple circuits, and everyday classroom supplies. Following the design cycle (empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test), students identify a real-world energy challenge at school or home and brainstorm creative solutions. They iterate on their prototypes, collecting data on efficiency or output, and refine their designs based on peer feedback and test results. The project culminates in a hands-on demonstration at the Year 3 science fair, where students explain the scientific principles behind their inventions and advocate for responsible energy use. This experience empowers students to see themselves as inventors and changemakers, ready to take meaningful action in their community.

s.d: Students photograph and identify Victorian animals they can find around the Elsternwick campus. They check each identification against the app's species information and list the structural or behavioural features that may help the animal survive. This makes adaptation visible in places students usually walk past without noticing. Pairs compare animals found in sunny, shaded, built and planted areas, then suggest why each animal was there. They finish with a set of local species records and evidence-based survival explanations. The app's Victorian fauna guide keeps the investigation local and age-appropriate.

Students explore climate and terrain layers to compare the changing environments where selected animals live. They annotate regions with the adaptations that help each animal find food, shelter or safety there. Groups then swap maps and add one possible environmental change, such as reduced rainfall, warmer conditions or habitat loss. The original group decides whether its animal could survive that change and adds a supported prediction. Students finish with an annotated map showing how place, adaptation and survival are connected. MapMaker's layered geographic data lets them look for patterns rather than view a static map.

Students record a short digital field guide entry explaining how one living thing fits into an ecosystem. They combine text, labelled images and narration to show its adaptations, food relationships and role in keeping the ecosystem healthy. Each student also adds a page showing one human action that would help and one that would cause harm. Another class listens to the entries and records a question that the authors can answer through revision. Students finish with a narrated class book linked to Life on Land or Life Below Water. Book Creator keeps writing, images, audio and video together in one book.

Students design an infographic that follows one animal through an environmental change. They show the animal's useful features, its ecosystem role, the new threat and an action people could take to improve its chance of survival. Students choose whether their message is aimed at families, park visitors or other children, then adjust the words and images for that audience. Partners test each infographic by explaining its message after viewing it for only ten seconds. Students finish with a clear conservation display for a classroom or corridor exhibition. Adobe Express provides simple layouts for combining short text, images and diagrams.

Students build a 3D ecosystem containing producers, consumers, shelter, water and a human action that changes the environment. They code selected objects to move or respond so viewers can see relationships such as feeding, hiding or habitat loss. Groups exchange scenes and predict which living things will benefit, struggle or disappear after the change. The builders then revise their scene so the cause and effect can be understood without a long explanation. Students finish with an interactive ecosystem that compares a harmful choice with a more sustainable one. Delightex's CoBlocks make movement and responses part of the model rather than decoration.

Students empathise with a small local animal that needs shelter from bright, exposed conditions, then define what a safe refuge must provide. They sketch several ideas and build a physical prototype from cardboard, recycled containers, paper engineering, fabric and natural loose parts. They add a battery-powered micro:bit programmed to read light level and show an LED warning when the shelter becomes too exposed. Teams test their refuge under different light and shade conditions, then adjust the structure or debug the light threshold. Each team demonstrates a revised shelter and explains how its design supports survival while using materials responsibly.

plannerText: The Year 3 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores how adaptation and sustainability ensure the survival of living things in changing environments. Students investigate animal adaptations (physical and behavioral), the roles of living things in ecosystems, and actions that benefit or harm ecosystems. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, and collaboration, with students engaging in research, hands-on experiments, and digital projects. They connect their learning to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Life on Land and Life Below Water, and demonstrate understanding through creative outputs like documentaries, information reports, and model ecosystems. The unit fosters agency, teamwork, and transdisciplinary connections across science, English, digital skills, and the arts.

PSPE
In PE this term, students will explore how small changes in
movement (like speed, force or timing) can lead to different
results. They'll experiment with technique, reflect on what works,
and refine their approach over time, just like scientists testing
ideas. We're also focusing on how movement, strategy and
technique shift depending on the situation, linking directly to the
movement conceptual understanding: The choice of movement,
technique and strategy is a response to the environment and
situation. It's a great way for students to see how learning and
discovery go hand in hand, supporting the unit's focus on
causation, change and transformation.

Assessment Reflections

How effective was our monitoring, documenting and measuring of learning informing our understanding of
student learning?
Opportunities for teacher and student feedback.  Students were encouraged to use self-reflection tasks to demonstrate their
understanding of skills and strategies being taught.  When students needed assistance with friendship issues or needed help

 with resilience they needed to demonstrate their use of language with teachers. The unit was delivered on an ?as needs? basis.
As social issues/friendship fires arose, the well-being curriculum was addressed using the programs Grow Your Mind and UR
Strong. Cyber Safety was taught regularly throughout the year using The Cyber Safety Project videos and resources. An area
that could be improved in the future would be more regular assessment and feedback. Because the unit was delivered on an
?as need? basis, there wasn't a Formative or summative assessment shared on Seesaw.

What evidence did we gather about students? knowledge, conceptual understandings and skills?

assessment. Evidence of learning was also captured through day-to-day teaching and observation. However, there was no
formal assessment for each line of inquiry.

How will we share this learning with the learning community?
Parents were invited to a Friendology and cyber safety workshop to learn the language and strategies that students would be
developing in class, so they can assist with conflicts and technology issues that may arise at home. Evidence of learning would

Lesson 1: Learning engagements

Key question: What motivates people to explore?

Tuning in: Introduce push and pull factors for exploration. Model though shared reading how to find
the push and pull factors in a text (Ten Pound Pom). For example, trade, conquest, curiosity,
economics, financial opportunity, religion, persecution, fame, adventure, business, technological
advancement, health car. Model for students how to write a fact fragment, using bullet points and
key words only.

Learning Engagement: Students work in small groups to read a text and write fact fragments related
to the exploration in the text. Using a T-chart graphic organiser, students record the push and pull
factors related to exploration in the text. Bring students together at the end to share findings and
create a class T-chart of push and pull factors OR two groups share their findings with each other.

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different
environments).
Looking ahead, I'd like to build in even more time for student reflection and perhaps more
explicit links to visible thinking routines, and vocabulary shared in the homerooms.

through collaboration among members of the teaching team?
Cam in the library supported the unit through designing lessons that supported

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration leads to new discoveries that can shape and change society.
lo: The factors that motivate exploration (Causation); How people reflect on discoveries from the past to inform change (Change); How exploration brings about change and new understandings for people, places and society (Change)

s.d: Students map the First Fleet route and add notes showing key decisions, risks and motivations along the journey. They switch between terrain, climate and population layers to work out how place may influence exploration. Groups compare the British route with evidence of the ancient travel, trade and navigation networks of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Each group chooses one point where a different decision might have changed what happened next. Students finish with an annotated map that separates evidence, questions and possible consequences. MapMaker's geographic layers let them test ideas against real features of the Earth.

Students collect images, short notes and source details about an Australian journey or discovery on a shared canvas. They connect each motivation to an action and then to a change for people, places or society. Groups swap boards and add a question wherever the evidence does not fully support a claim. Students then rearrange the material to show that the same event can look different from British and First Nations perspectives. They finish with a visual evidence web ready to guide historical writing or discussion. Freeform's infinite canvas makes relationships and gaps easy to see.

Students build paper scenes and record a stop-motion explanation of how one discovery changed everyday life. They show the sequence from a problem or motivation, through exploration, to a discovery and its later effects. Another group watches the unfinished animation and identifies any missing cause or unexplained change. Students revise the sequence by adding frames, labels or a contrasting perspective rather than simply making the film longer. They finish with a short historical animation that makes cause and change visible. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame recording lets students slow down a complex chain of events.

Students interview a teacher-set historical character about why they supported, joined or were affected by an exploration. They ask follow-up questions about motives, choices and consequences while remembering that the chatbot is not a fact-checked source. Halfway through, students exchange their strongest question with a partner and use it to push the conversation beyond dates and events. They check important claims against class sources and note where the character's viewpoint may be limited. Students finish with a saved written conversation and a short list of claims to verify. The Character Interview scenario keeps the discussion structured while the teacher controls its rules and support.

Students watch selected clips about the First Fleet, Aboriginal histories and later Australian exploration, pausing to record what each clip says changed. They sort their responses into motivations, discoveries, benefits, harms and unanswered questions. Pairs compare two clips and look for differences in language, missing voices and evidence. Each pair chooses one claim that needs a different perspective before it can be accepted. Students finish with completed responses that show how accounts of the past can shape decisions today. ClickView's curated video library and built-in questions support close viewing without requiring students to make another media piece.

Students empathise with travellers who need to keep a direction during a journey, then define one navigation problem their device should solve. Using cardboard, string, recycled packaging and a battery-powered Micro:bit, they sketch and build a wearable or handheld case before adding any code. They ideate several displays, then program the compass direction and 5x5 LED grid to give a simple directional signal. Pairs test the prototype on a marked classroom route, record where the signal or case causes confusion, and improve the code or physical design. Students finish by demonstrating the revised navigation aid and explaining how tools can change what people are able to explore.

plannerText: The 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit for Year 3 explores how exploration leads to new discoveries that shape and change society. Students investigate the motivations behind exploration, the impact of historical journeys (such as the First Fleet), and how discoveries inform change for people, places, and society. The unit integrates research skills, historical inquiry, mapping, and creative expression, with strong links to Australian history, Indigenous perspectives, and global citizenship. Learners engage in collaborative projects, digital storytelling, and hands-on activities to deepen their understanding of causation, change, and the interconnectedness of individuals and civilizations.

 where students explored how small changes in technique, like
adjusting their grip, angle, speed or timing, can completely
change the outcome of a pass or shot. We looked closely at how
strategy and movement shift depending on space, teammates and
goals, and students used trial and error to figure out what worked.
Just like scientists, they tested ideas, made observations, and
refined their approach to improve performance.
This tied beautifully into the UOI, where students explored how
humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take
action. From footwork adjustments to finding better angles on
court, the students began to see that success in sport (and in
learning) often comes from small tweaks and persistence, not just
natural skill. It was a great way to bring scientific thinking into PE,
and highlight how discovery, change and growth go hand in hand.

Assessment Reflections

How effective was our monitoring, documenting and measuring of learning informing our understanding of
student learning?
Opportunities for teacher and student feedback.  Students were encouraged to use self-reflection tasks to demonstrate their
understanding of skills and strategies being taught.  When students needed assistance with friendship issues or needed help

 with resilience they needed to demonstrate their use of language with teachers. The unit was delivered on an ?as needs? basis.
As social issues/friendship fires arose, the well-being curriculum was addressed using the programs Grow Your Mind and UR
Strong. Cyber Safety was taught regularly throughout the year using The Cyber Safety Project videos and resources. An area
that could be improved in the future would be more regular assessment and feedback. Because the unit was delivered on an
?as need? basis, there wasn't a Formative or summative assessment shared on Seesaw.

What evidence did we gather about students? knowledge, conceptual understandings and skills?
Evidence of student knowledge and conceptual understanding and skills were captured through the discussion and informal
assessment. Evidence of learning was also captured through day-to-day teaching and observation. However, there was no
formal assessment for each line of inquiry.

How will we share this learning with the learning community?
Parents were invited to a Friendology and cyber safety workshop to learn the language and strategies that students would be
developing in class, so they can assist with conflicts and technology issues that may arise at home. Evidence of learning would
be shared with parents through their ability to self-regulate and resolve friendship fires. In future, we will provide students with
opportunities to share their learning with their through their SeeSaw portfolios.

Lesson 1: Learning engagements

Key question: What motivates people to explore?

Tuning in: Introduce push and pull factors for exploration. Model though shared reading how to find
the push and pull factors in a text (Ten Pound Pom). For example, trade, conquest, curiosity,
economics, financial opportunity, religion, persecution, fame, adventure, business, technological
advancement, health car. Model for students how to write a fact fragment, using bullet points and
key words only.

Learning Engagement: Students work in small groups to read a text and write fact fragments related
to the exploration in the text. Using a T-chart graphic organiser, students record the push and pull
factors related to exploration in the text. Bring students together at the end to share findings and
create a class T-chart of push and pull factors OR two groups share their findings with each other.

Student perspective
During the WWAIPAT unit, students were actively engaged in the Drama Toolbox incursion. During
this excursion, the students enjoyed participating in role-plays of significant historical events
connecting to the unit (Burke and Wills, Gold Rush, First Fleet). The students also enjoyed the

 provocation using Scratch Jr to explore and discover. Throughout the unit, students were effectively
engaged in the case study of Captain Cook and enjoyed learning about other historical explorations
through reading material. The students felt liek they achieved the outline learning goals, as indicated
through their self-assessments of the SeeSaw formative assessment task. Students also displayed a
strong understanding of the Learner Profile attributes when completing the Explorer Project, by
identifying the LP attributes that the explorer demonstrated. Students were occasionaly challeneged
by the application of research skills. This was dependant on the chosen explorer, as some explorers
had a vast range of age-appropriate online resources, while others had fewer resources. Students
now have a very strong understanding of Australia's discovery and settlement and history. Students
have also gained a strong sense of the different motivations for exploration. With their new learning,
students will apply Research Skills in future learning.

The theme of the unit became We are one, we are many and the
song I am Australian helped frame the unit and the general

How did teachers design and plan for, recognise and support
student agency in learning and teaching?
Students were able to follow their interests with the choices they
were offered for exploration. Students each created a Powerpoint
and they had agency with how they put their Powerpoint
together. This way they learn the tools with PP and then we will
use Canva for the next unit then open it up for more agency in
the units that follow.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?
LP: The learner profile attributes were brought to life through
their development of conceptual understandings so incredible
links where made there. The lego experience where they viewed
the creations through different perspectives highlighted this.
ATL: Students set two ATL goals (communication and research
skills) as they worked on their research. The wrote how they
hoped to achieve the goal and then refflected on it with two stars
and a wish.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understandings and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?
Collaboration with different specialists supported
transdisciplinary connections. Each teacher was really excited we
kept checking in on one another.
During Music classes we discussed the culture of singing and
performing at our school and in our JS assemblies; with the

 students able to perform the song they had worked on, during an
assembly towards the end of term. Students viewed different
performances from around the world, commenting on the use of
different musical elements and the subsequent effect on the
listeners. We collaboratively created a verse per class that
represented their own cultures weaving it into an arrangement of
?I Am Australian?. This was a very successful activity and one in
which the students were really invested and seemed to enjoy.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?
I felt that the process was supportive for students because we
started off wither a wider angle then students could refine the
skills when moving into smaller groups and more independent
inquiry. The flow of the unit worked so well. Having HWEO before
WWAIPAT provided great flow across the term.

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a future version of themselves giving advice about handling a setback, change or friendship problem. This opens a safe conversation about resilience because students can speak through a character rather than perform on camera. Students swap characters with a partner and record a second message showing how advice may change for different people. They end with two short character videos that model helpful self-talk and responsible choices. The character automatically lip-syncs to each student's recorded voice. A class viewing can begin a list of strategies students already use when life feels difficult.

Students build a shared map of actions that help or harm friendships online and face-to-face. This makes the links between choices, feelings, safety and trust easy to see. Small groups connect similar actions, then respectfully challenge one connection made by another group. They end with a colour-coded class canvas showing friendship problems, possible responses and likely outcomes. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes. The teacher can return to the board after stories or discussions and ask students to revise earlier ideas.

Students compose two short soundscapes showing how a setback can feel before and after someone uses a coping strategy. This helps them notice that feelings can change without labelling any emotion as wrong. Partners listen without seeing the title and explain what change they hear, prompting the composer to refine the music. Each student ends with a paired recording that moves from tension towards calm, courage or hope. GarageBand lets students arrange loops and record original sounds in separate tracks. A listening gallery gives the class many word-free ways to represent resilience.

Students post short responses to friendship and online-safety scenarios, naming a safe action and why it could help. This makes personal responsibility visible through everyday choices such as pausing, asking permission, including others or seeking adult help. Students reply to two classmates by offering another respectful option rather than judging the first response. The class ends with a practical wall of strategies that can be revisited when real problems arise. Padlet supports brief posts and peer replies in one shared space. The teacher can add new scenarios during the inquiry to see whether students' responses become more thoughtful.

Students create a choose-your-own-response story about a character facing a setback, change or friendship difficulty. This shows how one decision can affect safety, trust, feelings and what happens next. Students exchange books and record advice for the character at one important decision point. Each student ends with a multimodal book containing two possible responses, their consequences and a final reflection. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration on the same pages. Families or another Year 3 class can read the stories and discuss which choices protect both self and others.

Students empathise with classmates who sometimes need help pausing during a challenge, then define one moment when a quiet prompt could help. Using cardboard, felt, elastic and a battery-powered Micro:bit, they sketch and build a wearable or desk-based device that displays a chosen coping icon when button A or B is pressed. They test paper versions first, then program the 5x5 LED grid and improve the placement, comfort and clarity after partner feedback. Each student demonstrates a working prototype for a real situation such as taking a breath, asking for help or trying again. The final test checks whether another student can understand and use the device without spoken instructions.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' unit for Year 3 explores how individuals use different strategies to overcome challenges and keep themselves safe, with a strong focus on resilience, personal responsibility, and positive relationships. Students investigate ways people respond to setbacks, manage change, and build healthy friendships, both online and face-to-face. The unit emphasizes growth mindset, self-reflection, and social skills, using a variety of learning experiences including literature, collaborative discussions, digital storytelling, and hands-on projects. Connections are made across curriculum areas, with opportunities for students to express their learning through journals, digital media, and creative presentations.

 where students explored how small changes in technique, like

factors related to exploration in the text. Bring students together at the end to share findings and

now have a very strong understanding of Australia's discovery and settlement and history. Students
have also gained a strong sense of the different motivations for exploration. With their new learning,
students will apply Research Skills in future learning.

Our athletics unit provided a meaningful opportunity to explore the concept of adaptation
through movement. Using track and field events as our vehicle, I encouraged students to
think beyond simply ?doing the activity,? and instead focused on how and why movement
needs to change depending on the challenge.  Things like pacing for a longer distance
run, adjusting power in a throw, or using a more efficient take-off technique in jumping.  I
saw some great moments of student insight, particularly when they were given the
chance to reflect on what worked and what didn't. It was evident that many students
began to make connections between changing their movement strategy and achieving a
better outcome (a parallel to the way living things adapt to survive and thrive in different
environments).
Looking ahead, I'd like to build in even more time for student reflection and perhaps more
explicit links to visible thinking routines, and vocabulary shared in the homerooms.

through collaboration among members of the teaching team?

ci: Technology transforms how we create and share ideas.
lo: How technology expands creative possibilities; The evolution of communication tools; The impact of technology on expression

s.d: Students record and arrange one short message as Morse-style rhythms, a radio jingle and a modern electronic soundscape. They hear how changing technology can reshape the same idea and influence how an audience responds. Each group gives another group only the audio and asks what message or mood they understood. Students then revise the least clear version after hearing that feedback. They finish with three contrasting recordings that show the evolution of audio communication. GarageBand's instruments, loops and audio tracks let students compose and record in one place.

Students draw and record a narrated timeline showing how one communication tool changed from an older form to a digital form. This makes the evolution of communication visible while students explain what each change made possible. Partners swap timelines and identify one benefit, one loss and one new responsibility created by the change. Students add these responses as a final annotated section. They finish with a short screencast that combines drawings, labels and spoken explanation. Explain Everything records the screen and voice while students draw and annotate.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short speech for an animated character explaining a cybersafe choice to younger learners. They explore how an on-screen speaker can make an important message clearer, friendlier or more persuasive. Each student tests two versions with different wording, then asks a younger peer which one is easiest to understand. Students revise the script so it avoids fear, blame and private information. They finish with a brief animated message ready to use in the student-led technology workshops. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students build an interactive 3D gallery showing how a single idea might be expressed through symbols, text, sound-related objects and virtual movement. This shows how digital spaces expand creative choices beyond a flat page. Groups exchange galleries and code one object to respond differently after visitors make a choice. Students test whether visitors can move through the scene and understand the intended message without spoken instructions. They finish with a coded virtual exhibition for classmates to explore. Delightex's CoBlocks let students program objects to move and respond inside the 3D scene.

Students build a survey asking how classmates create, communicate and decide what is safe to post online. The responses show how technology affects expression across their own school community. Students invite a younger class and an adult class to answer the same carefully worded questions. They compare the automatic charts and work out where age groups agree or differ. They finish with a survey and a set of evidence-based recommendations for their technology workshops. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and turns them into charts.

Students empathise with younger learners by watching where instructions become confusing, then define a need for a hands-on machine that communicates one clear step without spoken words. They ideate with sketches and prototype using LEGO, cardboard signs, paper engineering and recycled materials, adding a motor and either a distance, colour or force sensor. They test whether a younger student can trigger the model and understand its moving message without help. Teams rebuild weak mechanisms, adjust the code and simplify any unclear visual parts. At the workshop, each group demonstrates a reliable interactive model and explains how testing changed both its mechanism and message.

plannerText: The 'How We Express Ourselves' Year 4 unit explores how technology transforms creative expression and communication. Students investigate the evolution of communication tools, ethical and cybersafe digital practices, and how technology expands possibilities for sharing ideas. The unit blends inquiry, hands-on experimentation, and service learning, culminating in student-led technology workshops for younger peers. Learners reflect on their roles as principled, creative communicators and consider the impact of their digital choices on themselves and their community.

It is anticipated that students will explore how systems function through team-
based sports such as basketball, netball and European handball. These
activities are designed to mirror human systems by highlighting defined roles,
rules and interdependent actions. It is hoped that students will begin to see
how communication, cooperation and strategic planning support group goals,
reflecting the central idea that systems connect us. Through active
participation, they will be encouraged to consider how individual decisions
impact the whole group, and how adapting to change within a system can lead
to improved outcomes. Lessons will also aim to build understanding of the
importance of planning, as students experience firsthand how a clear plan of
action contributes to group success, connecting to both the conceptual
understanding of interactions and the movement concepts guiding their
physical development.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

PSPE
Students engaged in a range of team sports to explore how
systems operate, adapt and rely on connected parts working
together. While the goal was to highlight how structured systems,
like those in basketball and netball, support teamwork, leadership
and strategy, it became clear that social dynamics often played a
stronger role than anticipated.  Social issues such as
disagreements, group dynamics and peer relationships sometimes
disrupted the cohesion of the team ?systems.?

However, these challenges provided valuable opportunities for
authentic learning. Students were able to reflect on how
behaviour, communication and respect affect team function and
success, directly linking back to the idea that a plan of action is
necessary for a group to achieve its goal. In many cases, students
began to identify and correct breakdowns in their systems, gaining
a deeper understanding of both the structure and vulnerability of
collaborative environments.

Overall, while the execution of planned strategies was
inconsistent, the unit revealed rich opportunities for learning
about connection, leadership and the consequences of individual
actions within group systems, offering meaningful, if sometimes
messy, real-world parallels to the unit.

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to

What student-initiated inquiries arose and how did they inform the
process of inquiry?

What adjustments were made, and how did this enrich learning?

How are students supported in having voice, choice and ownership in
their unit of inquiry? (For example, through co-constructing learning
goals and success criteria, being engaged in student-initiated inquiries
and action, being involved in self-assessing and self-regulating, co-
designing learning spaces and so on).

How have these experiences impacted on how students feel about their
learning/ 9for example, through: developing and demonstrating
attributes of the learner profile and approaches to learning, developing
an understanding of the central idea, achieving learning goals, taking
action and so on).

 develop and evidence students? understanding of the central
idea?

Practical exploration and guided reflection were key strategies that
supported students in developing an understanding of the central idea,
?systems connect us.? Investigations into school-based systems helped
make the concept of systems tangible and relevant. The use of an
engaging provocation early in the unit captured curiosity and allowed
learners to connect global and community systems to those in their own
lives. Summative tasks, such as sustainability projects, provided authentic
opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding and
transfer knowledge to new contexts.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?

Learning experiences that required collaboration, inquiry, and problem-
solving particularly those linked to real-world systems encouraged
students to demonstrate attributes such as thinker, communicator, and
principled. Guided group discussions and student-led sustainability
initiatives promoted self-management and research skills, while reflective
journaling helped students to articulate their thinking and evaluate their
role in system interactions. The flexibility of the unit allowed students to
exercise agency by pursuing questions and actions that reflected their
personal interests and values.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understanding and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

Students demonstrated transfer of learning through their ability to apply
systems thinking across multiple contexts connecting scientific concepts
such as the water cycle and recycling systems with social and
organisational systems in the school. Written and oral presentations to
real audiences, such as the executive team, evidenced students? capacity
to use persuasive and expository writing to advocate for sustainability.
Their projects reflected an integrated understanding of how systems
influence one another and how human choices can impact environmental
outcomes.

 To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?

Collaboration among teaching staff was a notable strength of the unit,
particularly integrating literacy and science. Joint planning and shared
inquiry opportunities ensure conceptual coherence and meaningful
connections between disciplines. Mathematics integration was identified
as an area for further development, with opportunities to embed data
collection and analysis skills into sustainability inquiries in future
iterations. The shared focus on authentic, system-based learning
promoted consistent transdisciplinary understanding across the team.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?

The unit highlighted the value of systems thinking as a powerful lens for
deepening understanding across disciplines. Providing authentic, context-
driven learning experiences enhanced engagement and conceptual
transfer. The inquiry also reinforced the importance of allowing flexibility
for student agency and evolving lines of inquiry. Future learning will
benefit from greater integration of mathematical thinking and ongoing
opportunities for students to explore how systems connect beyond the
school environment, supporting sustained, meaningful inquiry.

Provide Focus:
As a class, discuss that many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander

It is important that students understand some of the key

 differences between an Acknowledgement of Country and
a Welcome to Country.

An Acknowledgement of Country is different from a
Welcome to Country, which is a formal welcome onto land
and can only be delivered by Traditional Owners or
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who have
been given permission from Traditional Owners to welcome
visitors to their Country. An Acknowledgement of Country
is a way of showing respect for the Traditional Owners and
can be given by both non-Indigenous people and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people who are connected to
another place.

?A Welcome to Country is like you're hosting a birthday: you do a
welcome and say thank you for coming to my birthday. And an
Acknowledgement of Country is like if you're a guest at the
birthday: you would say thank you for having me.?

SONGLINES
Focus: This activity introduces songlines and explains how they
connect land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander cultures. It lays the foundation for understanding
their significance in maintaining cultural continuity and identity.
Overarching question:
How do songlines help us understand the connection between
land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander cultures?

Engage:
Have students form pairs or groups of three, connect students
back to the overarching question from the previous activity. ?What
are the different ways we communicate, and why is
communication important??
You could break this into two sections:
What are the different ways we communicate? Let students chat
then regroup.
Why is communication important? Let students chat then regroup.
Remind students about the concepts of modes and
function/purpose and the discussion about maps/pathways.

Draw parallels between the use of maps and pathways as modes
of communication and introduce songlines as another form that
for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples connects
significant sites, conveys stories, holds cultural laws and
demonstrate how Indigenous Peoples moved across the nation
prior to colonisation.

 Provide Focus:
Watch: "What are songlines?" Colin Jones, a Kalkadoon and
Nunukul man, renowned artist, and scholar in Aboriginal culture,
art, and history, explains what songlines are in this clip.

Let students know you will pause at key moments for discussion
and note-taking.
Explain to students that they will be working together to build a
collective understanding of what songlines are. Highlight that this
understanding will grow and evolve as they learn more about
songlines, emphasising the collaborative and iterative nature of
learning.

After the initial viewing, facilitate a discussion, encouraging
students to share their thoughts and questions. Use these
discussions to start populating the anchor chart with keywords,
phrases, and students' illustrations that capture key concepts.

View the clip a second time, pausing at predetermined or
important moments to delve deeper into the content.
0:29 - What are songlines? Why are they called songlines? Create
a definition together and record on the anchor chart.
1:11- Why do you think Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people need songlines? What are they used for?
1:43- What information is often included in songlines? Discuss how
both landmarks like rivers and rocks as well as sacred areas and
events of the past are included in songlines.
End- Colin Jones refers to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people as ?natural ecologists? - what do you think he means by
this?

Encourage students to suggest when to pause based on their
curiosity or need for clarification.

As students contribute ideas and observations, collaboratively add
these to the anchor chart. Guide them to make connections
between their notes and the broader concepts of songlines, such
as how specific stories or symbols relate to navigation, trade, etc.

 Investigate and Connect:
Using the provided materials setup various stations around the
classroom, each dedicated to a different aspect of songlines.

Possible station ideas include:
Station 1: Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters Dreaming) National
Museum of Australia Digital Classroom Students engage with the
artwork and context statement

Station 2: Warakurna Community National Museum of Australia
Digital Classroom Students engage with the artwork and context
statement

Station 3: Explore the Walinynga rock art site and surroundings,
which includes the Seven Sisters artwork. Home - Walinynga rock
art (nma.gov.au)

Station 4: Using the book: ?Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters
(Margo Neale)? as visual stimulus to explore an artwork, and the
description and supporting text, students are asked to consider
how these relate to their existing learning of songlines.

Station 5: Clip Songlines explained: A 360 experience with Rhonda
Roberts

Station 6: The Seven Sisters by Reggie Sultan

Use the provided prompts and materials to guide students'
exploration and encourage them to consider how each station's
focus relates to the concept of songlines as a mode of
communication. Details around the resources and set up of
exploration stations are elaborated upon in the Teacher Support
Material. Questions to guide and extend students? thinking are
included for each station.

Celebrate and Evaluate:
This is an opportunity to spend time assessing students
understanding of the activity focus. Have students share their

 recordings from the exploration stations with a partner.

After the exploration stations, regroup and facilitate a reflective
discussion, prompting students to share how the station
explorations have influenced their understanding. Collaboratively
update the anchor chart, integrating new insights and making
connections between the initial concepts and the enriched
understanding gained from the stations.

You can reconnect students with the overarching question to
signpost to them how you are all building your understanding of
this question. "How do songlines help us understand the
connection between land, culture, and communication in
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures?"
