ci: Systems connect us.
lo: Human systems; The interconnections that exist within and across systems; The influence of systems on communities

s.d: Students photograph clean examples of paper, plastic and landfill items, then train an image model to sort them. This shows how a recycling system depends on clear inputs, rules and decisions. Groups swap unfamiliar items and find out where their models make mistakes or disagree. They improve the training examples, retest the model and decide which items still require a human choice. Students end with a working waste-sorting model and a record of its most revealing errors. It works like the camera-driven sorting systems used to direct materials inside recycling facilities.

Students map one school system, such as lunch orders, borrowing books or moving waste from classrooms to bins. They add each person, place, action and resource, then draw arrows to show how the parts connect. Groups swap boards and remove one important part to predict what would slow down, stop or affect another system. They then invite a staff member involved in the system to correct missing links and explain real constraints. Students end with a detailed system map showing normal operation, a breakdown and a possible improvement. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move ideas and redraw connections as their understanding changes.

Students collect daily counts of rubbish, recycling and compost produced by their class across one school week. They enter the numbers into a table and create graphs to spot patterns in the waste system. Each group chooses one practical change, such as moving a bin or improving a label, and gathers a second set of data after the change. Groups compare which change had the clearest effect rather than simply choosing the most popular idea. Students end with before-and-after graphs and an evidence-based recommendation for the school. Excel makes it easy to update charts when new measurements are added.

Students program Sphero BOLT to carry a small item through a model collection route linking a classroom, sorting point and reuse station. This makes the movement and timing inside a human system visible and testable. Another group changes one route condition, such as closing a path or moving a collection point, and the programmers must debug their solution. Students compare whether one long route or several short routes moves items more reliably. They end with a working program, a tested route and a short live demonstration of how the system responds to change. BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid can show both the route and the item's destination category.

Students record a 360-degree view of one school system in action, such as the library return area, compost station or busy bag-storage space. The full view helps them notice how people, signs, objects and pathways affect one another. They position the camera twice?once during a quiet period and once when the system is busy?while protecting people's privacy. Another class explores the recordings and identifies a bottleneck or missing instruction that Year 4 did not notice. Students end with two immersive views and a specific proposal for improving the space. The spherical recording keeps the whole surrounding system visible rather than showing only where a camera operator pointed.

Students empathise by observing a real recycling or composting problem at school, then define one action a small machine could improve. They sketch ideas and build a physical prototype from LEGO pieces, cardboard guides and clean recycled materials before adding SPIKE Prime motors and a colour, distance or force sensor. Teams code a working sorter, bin alert or moving collection system, then test it with repeated items and record where it jams, misses or gives the wrong response. They rebuild one part and adjust the code after feedback from another team. Students finish by demonstrating the improved machine and explaining how each physical and coded part helps the whole system work.

plannerText: The 'How We Organise Ourselves' Year 4 unit explores the central idea that 'systems connect us,' focusing on human-made and natural systems, their parts, and how they interact and influence communities. Students investigate systems in their school and environment, analyse how systems change or break down, and consider the impact of sustainability practices like recycling and composting. The unit emphasises collaboration, communication, and research skills through hands-on experiments, digital documentation, and creative projects, culminating in opportunities for students to take action and reflect on their learning.

It is anticipated that students will explore how systems function through team-
based sports such as basketball, netball and European handball. These
activities are designed to mirror human systems by highlighting defined roles,
rules and interdependent actions. It is hoped that students will begin to see
how communication, cooperation and strategic planning support group goals,
reflecting the central idea that systems connect us. Through active
participation, they will be encouraged to consider how individual decisions
impact the whole group, and how adapting to change within a system can lead
to improved outcomes. Lessons will also aim to build understanding of the
importance of planning, as students experience firsthand how a clear plan of
action contributes to group success, connecting to both the conceptual
understanding of interactions and the movement concepts guiding their
physical development.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

PSPE
Students engaged in a range of team sports to explore how
systems operate, adapt and rely on connected parts working
together. While the goal was to highlight how structured systems,
like those in basketball and netball, support teamwork, leadership
and strategy, it became clear that social dynamics often played a
stronger role than anticipated.  Social issues such as
disagreements, group dynamics and peer relationships sometimes
disrupted the cohesion of the team ?systems.?

However, these challenges provided valuable opportunities for
authentic learning. Students were able to reflect on how
behaviour, communication and respect affect team function and
success, directly linking back to the idea that a plan of action is
necessary for a group to achieve its goal. In many cases, students
began to identify and correct breakdowns in their systems, gaining
a deeper understanding of both the structure and vulnerability of
collaborative environments.

Overall, while the execution of planned strategies was
inconsistent, the unit revealed rich opportunities for learning
about connection, leadership and the consequences of individual
actions within group systems, offering meaningful, if sometimes
messy, real-world parallels to the unit.

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to

What student-initiated inquiries arose and how did they inform the
process of inquiry?

What adjustments were made, and how did this enrich learning?

How are students supported in having voice, choice and ownership in
their unit of inquiry? (For example, through co-constructing learning
goals and success criteria, being engaged in student-initiated inquiries
and action, being involved in self-assessing and self-regulating, co-
designing learning spaces and so on).

How have these experiences impacted on how students feel about their
learning/ 9for example, through: developing and demonstrating
attributes of the learner profile and approaches to learning, developing
an understanding of the central idea, achieving learning goals, taking
action and so on).

 develop and evidence students? understanding of the central
idea?

Practical exploration and guided reflection were key strategies that
supported students in developing an understanding of the central idea,
?systems connect us.? Investigations into school-based systems helped
make the concept of systems tangible and relevant. The use of an
engaging provocation early in the unit captured curiosity and allowed
learners to connect global and community systems to those in their own
lives. Summative tasks, such as sustainability projects, provided authentic
opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding and
transfer knowledge to new contexts.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?

Learning experiences that required collaboration, inquiry, and problem-
solving particularly those linked to real-world systems encouraged
students to demonstrate attributes such as thinker, communicator, and
principled. Guided group discussions and student-led sustainability
initiatives promoted self-management and research skills, while reflective
journaling helped students to articulate their thinking and evaluate their
role in system interactions. The flexibility of the unit allowed students to
exercise agency by pursuing questions and actions that reflected their
personal interests and values.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understanding and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

Students demonstrated transfer of learning through their ability to apply
systems thinking across multiple contexts connecting scientific concepts
such as the water cycle and recycling systems with social and
organisational systems in the school. Written and oral presentations to
real audiences, such as the executive team, evidenced students? capacity
to use persuasive and expository writing to advocate for sustainability.
Their projects reflected an integrated understanding of how systems
influence one another and how human choices can impact environmental
outcomes.

 To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?

Collaboration among teaching staff was a notable strength of the unit,
particularly integrating literacy and science. Joint planning and shared
inquiry opportunities ensure conceptual coherence and meaningful
connections between disciplines. Mathematics integration was identified
as an area for further development, with opportunities to embed data
collection and analysis skills into sustainability inquiries in future
iterations. The shared focus on authentic, system-based learning
promoted consistent transdisciplinary understanding across the team.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?

The unit highlighted the value of systems thinking as a powerful lens for
deepening understanding across disciplines. Providing authentic, context-
driven learning experiences enhanced engagement and conceptual
transfer. The inquiry also reinforced the importance of allowing flexibility
for student agency and evolving lines of inquiry. Future learning will
benefit from greater integration of mathematical thinking and ongoing
opportunities for students to explore how systems connect beyond the
school environment, supporting sustained, meaningful inquiry.

It is important that students understand some of the key

 differences between an Acknowledgement of Country and
a Welcome to Country.

An Acknowledgement of Country is different from a
Welcome to Country, which is a formal welcome onto land
and can only be delivered by Traditional Owners or
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who have
been given permission from Traditional Owners to welcome
visitors to their Country. An Acknowledgement of Country
is a way of showing respect for the Traditional Owners and
can be given by both non-Indigenous people and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people who are connected to
another place.

?A Welcome to Country is like you're hosting a birthday: you do a
welcome and say thank you for coming to my birthday. And an
Acknowledgement of Country is like if you're a guest at the
birthday: you would say thank you for having me.?

SONGLINES
Focus: This activity introduces songlines and explains how they
connect land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander cultures. It lays the foundation for understanding
their significance in maintaining cultural continuity and identity.
Overarching question:
How do songlines help us understand the connection between
land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander cultures?

Engage:
Have students form pairs or groups of three, connect students
back to the overarching question from the previous activity. ?What
are the different ways we communicate, and why is
communication important??
You could break this into two sections:
What are the different ways we communicate? Let students chat
then regroup.
Why is communication important? Let students chat then regroup.
Remind students about the concepts of modes and
function/purpose and the discussion about maps/pathways.

Draw parallels between the use of maps and pathways as modes
of communication and introduce songlines as another form that
for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples connects
significant sites, conveys stories, holds cultural laws and
demonstrate how Indigenous Peoples moved across the nation
prior to colonisation.

 Provide Focus:
Watch: "What are songlines?" Colin Jones, a Kalkadoon and
Nunukul man, renowned artist, and scholar in Aboriginal culture,
art, and history, explains what songlines are in this clip.

Let students know you will pause at key moments for discussion
and note-taking.
Explain to students that they will be working together to build a
collective understanding of what songlines are. Highlight that this
understanding will grow and evolve as they learn more about
songlines, emphasising the collaborative and iterative nature of
learning.

After the initial viewing, facilitate a discussion, encouraging
students to share their thoughts and questions. Use these
discussions to start populating the anchor chart with keywords,
phrases, and students' illustrations that capture key concepts.

View the clip a second time, pausing at predetermined or
important moments to delve deeper into the content.
0:29 - What are songlines? Why are they called songlines? Create
a definition together and record on the anchor chart.
1:11- Why do you think Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people need songlines? What are they used for?
1:43- What information is often included in songlines? Discuss how
both landmarks like rivers and rocks as well as sacred areas and
events of the past are included in songlines.
End- Colin Jones refers to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people as ?natural ecologists? - what do you think he means by
this?

Encourage students to suggest when to pause based on their
curiosity or need for clarification.

As students contribute ideas and observations, collaboratively add
these to the anchor chart. Guide them to make connections
between their notes and the broader concepts of songlines, such
as how specific stories or symbols relate to navigation, trade, etc.

 Investigate and Connect:
Using the provided materials setup various stations around the
classroom, each dedicated to a different aspect of songlines.

Possible station ideas include:
Station 1: Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters Dreaming) National
Museum of Australia Digital Classroom Students engage with the
artwork and context statement

Station 2: Warakurna Community National Museum of Australia
Digital Classroom Students engage with the artwork and context
statement

Station 3: Explore the Walinynga rock art site and surroundings,
which includes the Seven Sisters artwork. Home - Walinynga rock
art (nma.gov.au)

Station 4: Using the book: ?Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters
(Margo Neale)? as visual stimulus to explore an artwork, and the
description and supporting text, students are asked to consider
how these relate to their existing learning of songlines.

Station 5: Clip Songlines explained: A 360 experience with Rhonda
Roberts

Station 6: The Seven Sisters by Reggie Sultan

Use the provided prompts and materials to guide students'
exploration and encourage them to consider how each station's
focus relates to the concept of songlines as a mode of
communication. Details around the resources and set up of
exploration stations are elaborated upon in the Teacher Support
Material. Questions to guide and extend students? thinking are
included for each station.

Celebrate and Evaluate:
This is an opportunity to spend time assessing students
understanding of the activity focus. Have students share their

 recordings from the exploration stations with a partner.

After the exploration stations, regroup and facilitate a reflective
discussion, prompting students to share how the station
explorations have influenced their understanding. Collaboratively
update the anchor chart, integrating new insights and making
connections between the initial concepts and the enriched
understanding gained from the stations.

You can reconnect students with the overarching question to
signpost to them how you are all building your understanding of
this question. "How do songlines help us understand the
connection between land, culture, and communication in
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures?"

ci: Scientific investigations help us understand interactions within systems.
lo:
Interactions between objects, materials and living things
Gathering and analysing evidence
How scientific knowledge develops

s.d: Students program a conductivity tester, then test classroom objects and materials with crocodile clips. This shows how a controlled investigation can reveal interactions between electricity and different materials. Each group chooses one surprising object for another group to predict before testing it. Students finish with a working tester and a checked table of conductors and insulators. The micro:bit's pins provide the input, while its LED grid displays the result. Students repeat uncertain tests, change one condition at a time and debug their code when the evidence does not match.

Students measure how changing one part of a system affects another, such as ramp height and travel distance or water temperature and dissolving time. Entering repeated results into a table helps them gather enough evidence to spot patterns rather than trust one trial. Groups exchange data sets and check whether another team's conclusion is supported by the numbers. Students finish with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based conclusion. Excel turns the measurements into charts that make patterns and unusual results easier to see. Students add further trials when the graph shows gaps or results that do not fit.

Students build and record a frame-by-frame explanation of an interaction such as pollination, erosion, dissolving or a chain reaction. Moving one part at a time makes cause and effect within the system clear. Groups swap unfinished animations and predict the next change before the creators reveal it. Students finish with a short scientific animation that includes observations, evidence and a revised explanation. Stop Motion Studio combines the individual frames into a moving sequence. Students remake any section where the model suggests something that their investigation did not support.

Students photograph and sort material samples, then train an image model to recognise categories such as metal, plastic and paper. Comparing correct and incorrect classifications shows why scientific knowledge improves when more varied evidence is added. Each group challenges another group's model with crumpled, partly hidden or unusually coloured samples. Students finish with a tested classification model and a record of which examples confused it. This works like the camera-driven sorting systems used to direct materials along different paths in recycling facilities. Students retrain the model with better examples and check whether its decisions improve.

Students record a digital casebook showing how one scientific explanation changed after repeated investigations. They add written predictions, images, tables, recorded narration and corrected conclusions to show how evidence changes what we think. Another class reads the casebooks and leaves the authors with one question that the evidence should answer. Students finish with a multimodal book that compares their first explanation with their final one. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page. Students include one result that did not fit and explain whether it led to another test or a changed claim.

Students empathise with someone who needs to move a delicate object without touching it, then define clear success measures for a safe transfer system. They sketch ideas before building a physical prototype from LEGO beams, gears, motors and a force or distance sensor. Teams test one variable at a time, such as arm length, motor speed or sensor position, and record where the system fails. They rebuild and recode the model after each test instead of replacing the whole idea at once. At the end, students demonstrate the working transfer system and use test evidence to explain how its interacting parts were improved.

ci: Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people.
lo: The diversity of First Nations people; The importance of community, family and kinship; The importance of Country to First Nations people

s.d: Students build an interactive 3D exhibition showing how Country, language, family and community connect in one teacher-approved First Nations case study. Each part shows a relationship rather than treating culture as a collection of separate facts. Teams swap exhibitions and identify one connection that needs to be clearer. Students then revise their scene using feedback and check every detail against approved sources. The finished virtual exhibition gives visitors a path through linked places, people and ideas. CoBlocks can make labels or objects respond as visitors move through the scene.

Students map the diversity of First Nations peoples across several Australian regions using teacher-provided, authoritative information. They add careful annotations while recognising that cultural boundaries can overlap and are not the same as state borders. Students switch terrain, waterways and population layers on and off to work out how geography may shape connections to Country without claiming that geography determines culture. Partners compare maps and question any label that makes all First Nations communities seem the same. The finished map includes regions, language names, geographic evidence and a note about the limits of mapping living cultures. MapMaker's data layers let students test which geographic features help explain each place.

Students record a short podcast comparing two teacher-approved examples of First Nations language maintenance or renewal. They explain why language carries connections to Country, family, knowledge and identity. Each group plays a draft to another class and records one question that the first version did not answer clearly. Students edit their wording so they distinguish between the communities rather than speaking about one Indigenous culture. The finished episode includes an introduction, two specific examples, a comparison and a respectful closing reflection. Canva provides the recording and editing space needed to complete the episode on an iPad.

Students design a visual guide showing how to ask respectful questions when researching First Nations Country, language and community. They turn local protocols and teacher-approved guidance into clear actions such as checking sources, naming the specific community and avoiding copied cultural symbols. Groups exchange drafts and test whether a younger student could follow each instruction without extra explanation. Students choose which advice deserves the strongest visual emphasis and explain why. The finished guide can be displayed beside classroom research stations or sent to another Year 4 class. Adobe Express combines short text, images and graphic layout in one poster or infographic.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion that tests the claim that all First Nations peoples share one culture, language and experience. The chatbot asks open questions that prompt students to use specific examples of diversity, kinship and connection to Country. Students pause midway, reread their answers and replace any broad generalisation with more accurate wording. Partners compare transcripts and select the response that changed their thinking most. The finished transcript shows each student's first idea, supporting examples and revised conclusion. The teacher controls the chatbot's questions, timing and level of support, and students do not use it as a fact source.

Students empathise with visitors to a school display about caring for Country, then define how a physical model could prompt respectful behaviour without speaking on behalf of a First Nations community. Using LEGO, cardboard, recycled materials and teacher-approved messages, they ideate and build a model in which a force or distance sensor activates a motorised sign, gate or directional marker. Teams prototype the mechanism first, then code, test and debug its response with classmates acting as visitors. Feedback checks whether the message is clear, the movement works reliably and the design follows the approved guidance. Students finish by demonstrating the improved model and explaining how each design choice supports respectful action on Country.

plannerText: The Year 4 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores the significance of country, language, and community to First Nations peoples, focusing on diversity, tradition, and identity. Students inquire into Indigenous cultures locally and globally, examine the importance of language and connection to country, and reflect on perspectives through literature, research, and creative expression. The unit emphasizes respectful inquiry, collaborative learning, and action, with strong links to the Australian Curriculum and transdisciplinary skills. Activities include digital research, mapping, artistic responses, and sharing learning with the wider community.

It is anticipated that students will explore how systems function through team-
based sports such as basketball, netball and European handball. These
activities are designed to mirror human systems by highlighting defined roles,
rules and interdependent actions. It is hoped that students will begin to see
how communication, cooperation and strategic planning support group goals,
reflecting the central idea that systems connect us. Through active
participation, they will be encouraged to consider how individual decisions
impact the whole group, and how adapting to change within a system can lead
to improved outcomes. Lessons will also aim to build understanding of the
importance of planning, as students experience firsthand how a clear plan of
action contributes to group success, connecting to both the conceptual
understanding of interactions and the movement concepts guiding their
physical development.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

PSPE
Students engaged in a range of team sports to explore how
systems operate, adapt and rely on connected parts working
together. While the goal was to highlight how structured systems,
like those in basketball and netball, support teamwork, leadership
and strategy, it became clear that social dynamics often played a
stronger role than anticipated.  Social issues such as
disagreements, group dynamics and peer relationships sometimes
disrupted the cohesion of the team ?systems.?

However, these challenges provided valuable opportunities for
authentic learning. Students were able to reflect on how
behaviour, communication and respect affect team function and
success, directly linking back to the idea that a plan of action is
necessary for a group to achieve its goal. In many cases, students
began to identify and correct breakdowns in their systems, gaining
a deeper understanding of both the structure and vulnerability of
collaborative environments.

Overall, while the execution of planned strategies was
inconsistent, the unit revealed rich opportunities for learning
about connection, leadership and the consequences of individual
actions within group systems, offering meaningful, if sometimes
messy, real-world parallels to the unit.

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to

What student-initiated inquiries arose and how did they inform the
process of inquiry?

What adjustments were made, and how did this enrich learning?

How are students supported in having voice, choice and ownership in
their unit of inquiry? (For example, through co-constructing learning
goals and success criteria, being engaged in student-initiated inquiries
and action, being involved in self-assessing and self-regulating, co-
designing learning spaces and so on).

How have these experiences impacted on how students feel about their
learning/ 9for example, through: developing and demonstrating
attributes of the learner profile and approaches to learning, developing
an understanding of the central idea, achieving learning goals, taking
action and so on).

 develop and evidence students? understanding of the central
idea?

Practical exploration and guided reflection were key strategies that
supported students in developing an understanding of the central idea,
?systems connect us.? Investigations into school-based systems helped
make the concept of systems tangible and relevant. The use of an
engaging provocation early in the unit captured curiosity and allowed
learners to connect global and community systems to those in their own
lives. Summative tasks, such as sustainability projects, provided authentic
opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding and
transfer knowledge to new contexts.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?

Learning experiences that required collaboration, inquiry, and problem-
solving particularly those linked to real-world systems encouraged
students to demonstrate attributes such as thinker, communicator, and
principled. Guided group discussions and student-led sustainability
initiatives promoted self-management and research skills, while reflective
journaling helped students to articulate their thinking and evaluate their
role in system interactions. The flexibility of the unit allowed students to
exercise agency by pursuing questions and actions that reflected their
personal interests and values.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understanding and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

Students demonstrated transfer of learning through their ability to apply
systems thinking across multiple contexts connecting scientific concepts
such as the water cycle and recycling systems with social and
organisational systems in the school. Written and oral presentations to
real audiences, such as the executive team, evidenced students? capacity
to use persuasive and expository writing to advocate for sustainability.
Their projects reflected an integrated understanding of how systems
influence one another and how human choices can impact environmental
outcomes.

 To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?

Collaboration among teaching staff was a notable strength of the unit,
particularly integrating literacy and science. Joint planning and shared
inquiry opportunities ensure conceptual coherence and meaningful
connections between disciplines. Mathematics integration was identified
as an area for further development, with opportunities to embed data
collection and analysis skills into sustainability inquiries in future
iterations. The shared focus on authentic, system-based learning
promoted consistent transdisciplinary understanding across the team.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?

The unit highlighted the value of systems thinking as a powerful lens for
deepening understanding across disciplines. Providing authentic, context-
driven learning experiences enhanced engagement and conceptual
transfer. The inquiry also reinforced the importance of allowing flexibility
for student agency and evolving lines of inquiry. Future learning will
benefit from greater integration of mathematical thinking and ongoing
opportunities for students to explore how systems connect beyond the
school environment, supporting sustained, meaningful inquiry.

It is important that students understand some of the key

 differences between an Acknowledgement of Country and
a Welcome to Country.

An Acknowledgement of Country is different from a
Welcome to Country, which is a formal welcome onto land
and can only be delivered by Traditional Owners or
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who have
been given permission from Traditional Owners to welcome
visitors to their Country. An Acknowledgement of Country
is a way of showing respect for the Traditional Owners and
can be given by both non-Indigenous people and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people who are connected to
another place.

?A Welcome to Country is like you're hosting a birthday: you do a
welcome and say thank you for coming to my birthday. And an
Acknowledgement of Country is like if you're a guest at the
birthday: you would say thank you for having me.?

Focus: This activity introduces songlines and explains how they
connect land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander cultures. It lays the foundation for understanding
their significance in maintaining cultural continuity and identity.
Overarching question:
How do songlines help us understand the connection between
land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander cultures?

Engage:
Have students form pairs or groups of three, connect students
back to the overarching question from the previous activity. ?What
are the different ways we communicate, and why is
communication important??
You could break this into two sections:
What are the different ways we communicate? Let students chat
then regroup.
Why is communication important? Let students chat then regroup.
Remind students about the concepts of modes and
function/purpose and the discussion about maps/pathways.

Draw parallels between the use of maps and pathways as modes
of communication and introduce songlines as another form that
for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples connects
significant sites, conveys stories, holds cultural laws and
demonstrate how Indigenous Peoples moved across the nation
prior to colonisation.

 Provide Focus:
Watch: "What are songlines?" Colin Jones, a Kalkadoon and
Nunukul man, renowned artist, and scholar in Aboriginal culture,
art, and history, explains what songlines are in this clip.

Let students know you will pause at key moments for discussion
and note-taking.
Explain to students that they will be working together to build a
collective understanding of what songlines are. Highlight that this
understanding will grow and evolve as they learn more about
songlines, emphasising the collaborative and iterative nature of
learning.

After the initial viewing, facilitate a discussion, encouraging
students to share their thoughts and questions. Use these
discussions to start populating the anchor chart with keywords,
phrases, and students' illustrations that capture key concepts.

View the clip a second time, pausing at predetermined or
important moments to delve deeper into the content.
0:29 - What are songlines? Why are they called songlines? Create
a definition together and record on the anchor chart.
1:11- Why do you think Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people need songlines? What are they used for?
1:43- What information is often included in songlines? Discuss how
both landmarks like rivers and rocks as well as sacred areas and
events of the past are included in songlines.
End- Colin Jones refers to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people as ?natural ecologists? - what do you think he means by
this?

Encourage students to suggest when to pause based on their
curiosity or need for clarification.

As students contribute ideas and observations, collaboratively add
these to the anchor chart. Guide them to make connections
between their notes and the broader concepts of songlines, such
as how specific stories or symbols relate to navigation, trade, etc.

 Investigate and Connect:
Using the provided materials setup various stations around the
classroom, each dedicated to a different aspect of songlines.

Possible station ideas include:
Station 1: Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters Dreaming) National
Museum of Australia Digital Classroom Students engage with the
artwork and context statement

Station 2: Warakurna Community National Museum of Australia
Digital Classroom Students engage with the artwork and context
statement

Station 3: Explore the Walinynga rock art site and surroundings,
which includes the Seven Sisters artwork. Home - Walinynga rock
art (nma.gov.au)

Station 4: Using the book: ?Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters
(Margo Neale)? as visual stimulus to explore an artwork, and the
description and supporting text, students are asked to consider
how these relate to their existing learning of songlines.

Station 5: Clip Songlines explained: A 360 experience with Rhonda
Roberts

Station 6: The Seven Sisters by Reggie Sultan

Use the provided prompts and materials to guide students'
exploration and encourage them to consider how each station's
focus relates to the concept of songlines as a mode of
communication. Details around the resources and set up of
exploration stations are elaborated upon in the Teacher Support
Material. Questions to guide and extend students? thinking are
included for each station.

Celebrate and Evaluate:
This is an opportunity to spend time assessing students
understanding of the activity focus. Have students share their

 recordings from the exploration stations with a partner.

After the exploration stations, regroup and facilitate a reflective
discussion, prompting students to share how the station
explorations have influenced their understanding. Collaboratively
update the anchor chart, integrating new insights and making
connections between the initial concepts and the enriched
understanding gained from the stations.

sugs.d: Students become documentary filmmakers, capturing immersive 360? video field trips to local First Nations sites of cultural and environmental significance. By exploring the importance of Country to First Nations people, students step into the role of virtual guides, inviting classmates and families to experience sacred spaces through their eyes. The twist: students record interviews or voice narrations in language (where culturally appropriate), amplifying the voices and perspectives of First Nations knowledge holders. The final artefact is a narrated, interactive virtual tour that can be experienced by the school community at a showcase event or embedded in the campus website. Using the insta360's spatial audio and panoramic video capabilities, students create an experience that is more than just a flat video?viewers can look around and listen as if they are truly there. Students emerge as respectful storytellers, developing deep empathy and agency in advocating for cultural understanding and environmental stewardship.

Students conduct a digital biodiversity survey, using Field Guide to Victoria to identify plants and animals found at local First Nations sites and compare them with species described in traditional stories. This investigation deepens the line of inquiry into the diversity of First Nations people by connecting ecological richness with cultural narratives and language. The twist: student teams 'adopt' a species and research its cultural, ecological, and linguistic significance?then create a mini-field guide entry written from that species' perspective. The final product is a collaborative e-guide with audio pronunciations of species names in local First Nations languages, published as a resource for younger classes and families. Field Guide to Victoria's advanced species comparison tool allows students to filter and cross-reference detailed habitat data, uncovering how biodiversity and language are intertwined. Students become citizen scientists and cultural ambassadors, realising the power of Indigenous knowledge in caring for Country.

Students author digital storybooks inspired by First Nations oral traditions, weaving together their own narratives about community, family, and kinship. This creative writing project directly supports the exploration of the importance of community, family, and kinship to First Nations people by inviting students to celebrate diverse family structures and connections. The twist: students collaborate with an Elders' group or a local First Nations storyteller (in person or via video call), learning about protocols for sharing stories before crafting respectful retellings. The finished book is an interactive, multimodal publication featuring embedded audio of students reading in English, plus key words in a local language, published to the school library's digital shelf. Book Creator's built-in comic templates and audio hotspots enable students to create layered narratives that blend text, images, and voice for authentic engagement. Students become custodians of stories, developing intercultural understanding and a responsibility to honour and share community knowledge.

Students design and train an AI chatbot to role-play as different First Nations community members?Elders, youth, language custodians, and land carers?responding to questions about identity, tradition, and the significance of Country. This activity brings to life the line of inquiry about the diversity of First Nations people by immersing students in multiple perspectives and encouraging critical empathy. The twist: students hold 'community forum' sessions where the chatbot fields questions from parents and other classes, requiring students to research and input culturally accurate, respectful responses rooted in real sources. The final artefact is a living, conversation-ready chatbot accessible via the class website, supporting cross-age dialogue and reflection. Wise Discussion Chatbots' advanced branching scenarios and natural language processing allow nuanced, context-sensitive interactions that reflect the complexity of community voices. Students claim agency as digital custodians?curating respectful, informed conversations that challenge stereotypes and build bridges.

Students use Delightex to create immersive, interactive timelines that visualise the evolution of language, community, and Country across generations of First Nations people. This directly brings to life the unit's central idea by illustrating how language and culture are living, dynamic forces. The twist: students include both historical and contemporary milestones, highlighting local language revitalisation efforts and the ongoing contributions of Indigenous communities. The completed artefact is an interactive digital timeline embedded with audio clips, images, and external links, shared publicly in a school expo or parent night display. Delightex's 'Choose Your Own Path' branching timeline feature enables viewers to explore multiple narratives and see how diverse communities have shaped?and continue to shape?the story of this land. Students become digital historians, learning that the past is not fixed, but a living story they can honour and help continue.

In the makerspace, students prototype a 'Journey of Connection' gameboard using recycled cardboard, markers, and natural materials, where Sphero BOLT robots represent different clans or family groups travelling across Country. Working through the Design Cycle, students empathise by investigating traditional journeys and seasonal movement patterns, define the challenge as designing respectful pathways that acknowledge sacred sites, ideate varied terrains and obstacles, prototype physical routes with tactile elements, and test by coding Sphero BOLT to navigate these pathways. The wow factor: students embed QR codes along the journey, linking to digital stories or language snippets about each site, so the robot's path activates multimedia cultural insights. Iterating on their routes, students adjust coding and board design to ensure accessibility, accuracy, and respect for community protocols. The final demonstration is a hands-on, interactive learning exhibition where families and peers can drive the journey, experiencing the interconnectedness of Country, language, and kinship as a living, moving story.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human migration is a response to challenges and opportunities
lo: The reasons people migrate; Migration throughout history; Effects of migration on communities, cultures and individuals

s.d: Students map migration journeys caused by bushfires, floods, earthquakes or the search for work and safety. They add terrain, climate and population layers to work out why people left one place and chose another. Pairs swap maps and test whether the evidence supports each route and destination. Students then revise any route that ignores a mountain, river, hazard or settlement pattern. They finish with an annotated map showing causes, choices and effects on both communities. MapMaker's real geographic layers let students explore how several factors can shape one migration decision.

Students build two connected settlements, then change one with a flood, bushfire or earthquake that forces some residents to move. This shows how migration can begin with a challenge but lead towards new opportunities. Another group enters the world and chooses a safe migration route, a temporary shelter site and a place for a new community. The builders watch these choices and improve roads, services or warning systems that did not work as expected. Students finish with a world that shows the original community, the journey and the changed destination. Minecraft's shared building space makes the consequences of each planning choice visible.

Students watch curated clips about historical and recent migration, pausing to record reasons people moved and the challenges they faced. This helps them separate forced movement from migration shaped by work, family or other opportunities. Small groups compare answers and look for voices or viewpoints that the clips include or leave out. They then answer teacher-selected questions using evidence from exact moments in the videos. Students finish with a set of evidence-based responses comparing migration across time. ClickView's built-in questions keep viewing active and give the teacher a quick check of understanding.

Students draw and narrate a migration story from departure to arrival, using one researched historical example. They show the challenge or opportunity that prompted movement and the effects on individuals, cultures and communities. Partners exchange drafts and identify one point where the cause or consequence needs clearer evidence. Students revise the sequence while recording arrows, labels and spoken explanations on the screen. They finish with a narrated screencast that makes the journey and its effects easy to follow. Explain Everything records students' voices and on-screen drawing together.

Students program a portable decision device for a family preparing to leave a community threatened by a natural hazard. Button A displays an essential need, Button B displays a travel challenge, and shaking the board produces a changing event such as a blocked route or new shelter. This makes students weigh safety, limited choices and opportunity rather than treating migration as a simple trip. Groups swap devices, test each other's event sequences and suggest changes when a decision is too easy or unrealistic. Students finish with a working coded device and a short live demonstration of the choices it creates. The micro:bit's buttons, movement sensing and 5x5 LED grid make the decision process physical and repeatable.

Students empathise with people displaced by floods or earthquakes, then define one problem involved in moving essential supplies into a temporary settlement. Using LEGO beams, wheels, gears, motors and the distance or force sensor, they sketch ideas and build a physical transport or delivery prototype. They code it to move supplies, stop at a barrier or release a load, then test it on a cardboard route with damaged roads and narrow crossings. Teams measure where it fails, rebuild one part and debug the program before testing again. Each team demonstrates how its improved machine responds to a real challenge faced by communities during displacement.

plannerText: The Year 4 unit 'Where We Are in Place and Time' explores how changes to the Earth impact environments and communities, with a focus on natural disasters such as bushfires, floods, earthquakes, and their effects. Students investigate causes, processes, and community responses through research, hands-on experiments, mapping, and collaborative inquiry. The unit emphasises systems thinking, transdisciplinary connections (science, maths, English, digital skills), and authentic action, including student-led research projects and presentations. Learners develop research, communication, and self-management skills while reflecting on local and global challenges, culminating in creative and practical demonstrations of their understanding.

It is anticipated that students will explore how systems function through team-
based sports such as basketball, netball and European handball. These
activities are designed to mirror human systems by highlighting defined roles,
rules and interdependent actions. It is hoped that students will begin to see
how communication, cooperation and strategic planning support group goals,
reflecting the central idea that systems connect us. Through active
participation, they will be encouraged to consider how individual decisions
impact the whole group, and how adapting to change within a system can lead
to improved outcomes. Lessons will also aim to build understanding of the
importance of planning, as students experience firsthand how a clear plan of
action contributes to group success, connecting to both the conceptual
understanding of interactions and the movement concepts guiding their
physical development.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

PSPE
Students engaged in a range of team sports to explore how
systems operate, adapt and rely on connected parts working
together. While the goal was to highlight how structured systems,
like those in basketball and netball, support teamwork, leadership
and strategy, it became clear that social dynamics often played a
stronger role than anticipated.  Social issues such as
disagreements, group dynamics and peer relationships sometimes
disrupted the cohesion of the team ?systems.?

However, these challenges provided valuable opportunities for
authentic learning. Students were able to reflect on how
behaviour, communication and respect affect team function and
success, directly linking back to the idea that a plan of action is
necessary for a group to achieve its goal. In many cases, students
began to identify and correct breakdowns in their systems, gaining
a deeper understanding of both the structure and vulnerability of
collaborative environments.

Overall, while the execution of planned strategies was
inconsistent, the unit revealed rich opportunities for learning
about connection, leadership and the consequences of individual
actions within group systems, offering meaningful, if sometimes
messy, real-world parallels to the unit.

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to

What student-initiated inquiries arose and how did they inform the
process of inquiry?

What adjustments were made, and how did this enrich learning?

How are students supported in having voice, choice and ownership in
their unit of inquiry? (For example, through co-constructing learning
goals and success criteria, being engaged in student-initiated inquiries
and action, being involved in self-assessing and self-regulating, co-
designing learning spaces and so on).

How have these experiences impacted on how students feel about their
learning/ 9for example, through: developing and demonstrating
attributes of the learner profile and approaches to learning, developing
an understanding of the central idea, achieving learning goals, taking
action and so on).

 develop and evidence students? understanding of the central
idea?

Practical exploration and guided reflection were key strategies that
supported students in developing an understanding of the central idea,
?systems connect us.? Investigations into school-based systems helped
make the concept of systems tangible and relevant. The use of an
engaging provocation early in the unit captured curiosity and allowed
learners to connect global and community systems to those in their own
lives. Summative tasks, such as sustainability projects, provided authentic
opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding and
transfer knowledge to new contexts.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?

Learning experiences that required collaboration, inquiry, and problem-
solving particularly those linked to real-world systems encouraged
students to demonstrate attributes such as thinker, communicator, and
principled. Guided group discussions and student-led sustainability
initiatives promoted self-management and research skills, while reflective
journaling helped students to articulate their thinking and evaluate their
role in system interactions. The flexibility of the unit allowed students to
exercise agency by pursuing questions and actions that reflected their
personal interests and values.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understanding and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

Students demonstrated transfer of learning through their ability to apply
systems thinking across multiple contexts connecting scientific concepts
such as the water cycle and recycling systems with social and
organisational systems in the school. Written and oral presentations to
real audiences, such as the executive team, evidenced students? capacity
to use persuasive and expository writing to advocate for sustainability.
Their projects reflected an integrated understanding of how systems
influence one another and how human choices can impact environmental
outcomes.

 To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?

Collaboration among teaching staff was a notable strength of the unit,
particularly integrating literacy and science. Joint planning and shared
inquiry opportunities ensure conceptual coherence and meaningful
connections between disciplines. Mathematics integration was identified
as an area for further development, with opportunities to embed data
collection and analysis skills into sustainability inquiries in future
iterations. The shared focus on authentic, system-based learning
promoted consistent transdisciplinary understanding across the team.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?

The unit highlighted the value of systems thinking as a powerful lens for
deepening understanding across disciplines. Providing authentic, context-
driven learning experiences enhanced engagement and conceptual
transfer. The inquiry also reinforced the importance of allowing flexibility
for student agency and evolving lines of inquiry. Future learning will
benefit from greater integration of mathematical thinking and ongoing
opportunities for students to explore how systems connect beyond the
school environment, supporting sustained, meaningful inquiry.

It is important that students understand some of the key

 differences between an Acknowledgement of Country and
a Welcome to Country.

An Acknowledgement of Country is different from a
Welcome to Country, which is a formal welcome onto land
and can only be delivered by Traditional Owners or
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who have
been given permission from Traditional Owners to welcome
visitors to their Country. An Acknowledgement of Country
is a way of showing respect for the Traditional Owners and
can be given by both non-Indigenous people and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people who are connected to
another place.

?A Welcome to Country is like you're hosting a birthday: you do a
welcome and say thank you for coming to my birthday. And an
Acknowledgement of Country is like if you're a guest at the
birthday: you would say thank you for having me.?

Focus: This activity introduces songlines and explains how they
connect land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander cultures. It lays the foundation for understanding
their significance in maintaining cultural continuity and identity.
Overarching question:
How do songlines help us understand the connection between
land, culture, and communication in Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander cultures?

Engage:
Have students form pairs or groups of three, connect students
back to the overarching question from the previous activity. ?What
are the different ways we communicate, and why is
communication important??
You could break this into two sections:
What are the different ways we communicate? Let students chat
then regroup.
Why is communication important? Let students chat then regroup.
Remind students about the concepts of modes and
function/purpose and the discussion about maps/pathways.

Draw parallels between the use of maps and pathways as modes
of communication and introduce songlines as another form that
for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples connects
significant sites, conveys stories, holds cultural laws and
demonstrate how Indigenous Peoples moved across the nation
prior to colonisation.

 Provide Focus:
Watch: "What are songlines?" Colin Jones, a Kalkadoon and
Nunukul man, renowned artist, and scholar in Aboriginal culture,
art, and history, explains what songlines are in this clip.

Let students know you will pause at key moments for discussion
and note-taking.
Explain to students that they will be working together to build a
collective understanding of what songlines are. Highlight that this
understanding will grow and evolve as they learn more about
songlines, emphasising the collaborative and iterative nature of
learning.

After the initial viewing, facilitate a discussion, encouraging
students to share their thoughts and questions. Use these
discussions to start populating the anchor chart with keywords,
phrases, and students' illustrations that capture key concepts.

View the clip a second time, pausing at predetermined or
important moments to delve deeper into the content.
0:29 - What are songlines? Why are they called songlines? Create
a definition together and record on the anchor chart.
1:11- Why do you think Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people need songlines? What are they used for?
1:43- What information is often included in songlines? Discuss how
both landmarks like rivers and rocks as well as sacred areas and
events of the past are included in songlines.
End- Colin Jones refers to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people as ?natural ecologists? - what do you think he means by
this?

Encourage students to suggest when to pause based on their
curiosity or need for clarification.

As students contribute ideas and observations, collaboratively add
these to the anchor chart. Guide them to make connections
between their notes and the broader concepts of songlines, such
as how specific stories or symbols relate to navigation, trade, etc.

 Investigate and Connect:
Using the provided materials setup various stations around the
classroom, each dedicated to a different aspect of songlines.

Possible station ideas include:
Station 1: Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters Dreaming) National
Museum of Australia Digital Classroom Students engage with the
artwork and context statement

Station 2: Warakurna Community National Museum of Australia
Digital Classroom Students engage with the artwork and context
statement

Station 3: Explore the Walinynga rock art site and surroundings,

(Margo Neale)? as visual stimulus to explore an artwork, and the

Station 5: Clip Songlines explained: A 360 experience with Rhonda

Station 6: The Seven Sisters by Reggie Sultan

Use the provided prompts and materials to guide students'

 Embedding authentic Mathematics inquiry into

Year 4

?? 1. Mapping Natural Disasters

Focus: Mapping, Measurement, Data
Key maths skills: Scale, distance, direction,
reading coordinates
Activity:

? Provide students with a simple world map

and photos of recent earthquakes, cyclones,
or volcanoes.

? Learners plot locations using grid

coordinates.

? Measure how far the natural disaster

occurred from Australia (use string and
scale).

? Compare the number of disasters per

continent using a tally chart and bar graph.
Maths Challenge: ?How many centimetres on
the map is 1,000 km in real life??
Inquiry Question: How can we use maps and
measurement to understand the effects of
natural disasters?

? 2. Flooding and Water Runoff

 Focus: Volume, capacity, comparison
Key maths skills: Measuring in millilitres and
litres, estimating, comparing amounts
Activity:

? Create mini landscapes in trays using sand,

soil, grass, and plastic.

? Pour the same amount of water on each and
measure the runoff using measuring jugs.

? Predict which surface will flood quickest.

? Record the data in a simple table and

compare.
Extension: Graph the results to show which
surfaces absorb the most water.
Inquiry Question: What does maths tell us
about how water behaves during a flood?

? 3. Bushfire Area Estimation

Focus: Area, multiplication, data
Key maths skills: Counting squares, using arrays,
reading information
Activity:

? Use grid paper to draw and estimate the area
burned in a bushfire (e.g., ?each square = 10
hectares?).

? Compare the size of affected areas across

different bushfires using data cards.

 ? Multiply to estimate how many trees or

animals might be affected (e.g., ?3 animals
per hectare?).
Inquiry Question: How can we use area and
multiplication to understand the impact of a
bushfire?

?? 4. Erosion in Action

Focus: Measurement, prediction, change over
time
Key maths skills: Area, subtraction, comparison
Activity:

? Create a sand hill in a tray, then simulate

wind or water erosion using a spray bottle or
cup of water.

? Trace and measure the area before and after

(e.g., in square units or grid paper).

? Record changes over time using simple

charts.

? Predict how much land would be left after

more rain.
Inquiry Question: How can we measure and
track how the Earth is changing over time?

?? 5. Climate Data Detectives

 Focus: Graphing, data interpretation, number
patterns
Key maths skills: Reading tables, line/bar graphs,
calculating change
Activity:

? Provide simple climate charts showing

average rainfall or temperature over 10
years.

? Students look for patterns (e.g., Is it getting

hotter? Drier?).

? Ask questions like: ?What was the wettest

year??, ?How much did the temperature rise
between Year 1 and Year 10??
Extension: Create their own graphs using
weather data from your local area.
Inquiry Question: What can numbers and
graphs tell us about the way our
environment is changing?

? 6. Disaster Relief Budgeting

Focus: Money, budgeting, addition, multiplication
Key maths skills: Using dollars and cents,
calculating totals, comparing options
Activity:

? Present students with a list of items needed
after a natural disaster (e.g., food pack $12,
blanket $8, tent $50).

 ? Give them a budget (e.g., $300) and ask

them to choose how many of each item they
can buy to help a community.

? Record totals and justify their choices.

Extension: Create different budgets and
compare how decisions change.
Inquiry Question: How can we use maths to
make fair and helpful decisions after a

lo: Roles and responsibilities of effective leadership; The purpose of leadership in communities; Qualities of influential leaders

s.d: Students hold a written conversation with a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about a school leadership dilemma. They must decide what an effective leader should do, explain who is affected and respond to questions that challenge their choice. Each student receives the same dilemma but may reach a different decision. Students then compare their conversation with a partner and identify where listening, fairness or courage changed the outcome. They finish with a saved discussion showing how their thinking developed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support.

Students build a survey asking classmates which leadership qualities help a community most. This gathers real evidence about why people trust some leaders and not others. Small groups choose their own qualities to test, such as fairness, courage, listening and responsibility. They invite another Year 4 class to respond and look for surprising differences between the groups. Students finish with a survey and auto-generated charts that can guide leadership applications at school. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and displays the results automatically.

Students build a digital handbook showing how a student leader should respond to real school situations. Each page links a responsibility, a leadership quality and a practical action. Students ask a current school leader to choose one situation that needs the clearest advice, then revise that page for a younger audience. They add recorded explanations so younger students can hear why each choice matters. Students finish with a multimodal leadership handbook that can be read during class meetings. Book Creator combines text, images, audio and video within one book.

Students write scenario questions that ask players to choose the strongest response to a leadership challenge. This makes them apply leadership qualities rather than simply list them. Each group tests its questions on classmates and rewrites any item that causes confusion or has more than one reasonable answer. A buddy class then plays the finished quiz and discusses why the best answer would help the community. Students finish with a playable quiz that teaches responsible decision-making. Kahoot gives immediate responses after each short question.

Students post evidence showing how different leaders have shaped communities through decisions and actions. They connect each example to a quality such as persistence, empathy, fairness or clear communication. Classmates respond by adding a counterexample, a question or another leader who used the same quality differently. Students choose one post to revise after reading the responses rather than treating the first answer as final. The class finishes with a shared evidence wall that shows leadership can look different across communities. Padlet keeps notes, images, links and peer responses together on one wall.

Students empathise by watching a real class meeting and noticing problems such as interrupted speakers, unclear turns or decisions that exclude quieter voices. They define one problem, sketch several ideas and use LEGO pieces, a motor and the force, colour or distance sensor to build a working meeting aid, such as a turn indicator or voting mechanism. Teams prototype the physical mechanism first, then code it to move, light up or respond when a participant takes an action. They test it during a short meeting, collect spoken feedback and rebuild any part that is confusing or unreliable. Each team demonstrates the improved device and explains how its design helps a leader listen, organise or make fair decisions.

plannerText: The Year 4 'Who We Are' unit explores leadership through the central idea that 'Leaders shape communities.' Students investigate the roles and responsibilities of leaders, the purpose of leadership, and the strengths and qualities that make leaders effective. The unit emphasises personal reflection, collaborative inquiry, and real-world connections, with students researching famous leaders, reflecting on their own leadership qualities, and applying their learning through digital portfolios, creative projects, and leadership applications. The planner highlights opportunities for cross-curricular integration, student agency, and authentic action within the school community.

It is anticipated that students will explore how systems function through team-
based sports such as basketball, netball and European handball. These
activities are designed to mirror human systems by highlighting defined roles,
rules and interdependent actions. It is hoped that students will begin to see
how communication, cooperation and strategic planning support group goals,
reflecting the central idea that systems connect us. Through active
participation, they will be encouraged to consider how individual decisions
impact the whole group, and how adapting to change within a system can lead
to improved outcomes. Lessons will also aim to build understanding of the
importance of planning, as students experience firsthand how a clear plan of
action contributes to group success, connecting to both the conceptual
understanding of interactions and the movement concepts guiding their
physical development.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

PSPE
Students engaged in a range of team sports to explore how
systems operate, adapt and rely on connected parts working
together. While the goal was to highlight how structured systems,
like those in basketball and netball, support teamwork, leadership
and strategy, it became clear that social dynamics often played a
stronger role than anticipated.  Social issues such as
disagreements, group dynamics and peer relationships sometimes
disrupted the cohesion of the team ?systems.?

However, these challenges provided valuable opportunities for
authentic learning. Students were able to reflect on how
behaviour, communication and respect affect team function and
success, directly linking back to the idea that a plan of action is
necessary for a group to achieve its goal. In many cases, students
began to identify and correct breakdowns in their systems, gaining
a deeper understanding of both the structure and vulnerability of
collaborative environments.

Overall, while the execution of planned strategies was
inconsistent, the unit revealed rich opportunities for learning
about connection, leadership and the consequences of individual
actions within group systems, offering meaningful, if sometimes
messy, real-world parallels to the unit.

How did the strategies we used throughout the unit help to

What student-initiated inquiries arose and how did they inform the
process of inquiry?

What adjustments were made, and how did this enrich learning?

How are students supported in having voice, choice and ownership in
their unit of inquiry? (For example, through co-constructing learning
goals and success criteria, being engaged in student-initiated inquiries
and action, being involved in self-assessing and self-regulating, co-
designing learning spaces and so on).

How have these experiences impacted on how students feel about their
learning/ 9for example, through: developing and demonstrating
attributes of the learner profile and approaches to learning, developing
an understanding of the central idea, achieving learning goals, taking
action and so on).

 develop and evidence students? understanding of the central
idea?

Practical exploration and guided reflection were key strategies that
supported students in developing an understanding of the central idea,
?systems connect us.? Investigations into school-based systems helped
make the concept of systems tangible and relevant. The use of an
engaging provocation early in the unit captured curiosity and allowed
learners to connect global and community systems to those in their own
lives. Summative tasks, such as sustainability projects, provided authentic
opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding and
transfer knowledge to new contexts.

What learning experiences best supported students?
development and demonstration of the attributes of the learner
profile and approaches to learning?

Learning experiences that required collaboration, inquiry, and problem-
solving particularly those linked to real-world systems encouraged
students to demonstrate attributes such as thinker, communicator, and
principled. Guided group discussions and student-led sustainability
initiatives promoted self-management and research skills, while reflective
journaling helped students to articulate their thinking and evaluate their
role in system interactions. The flexibility of the unit allowed students to
exercise agency by pursuing questions and actions that reflected their
personal interests and values.

What evidence do we have that students are developing
knowledge, conceptual understanding and skills to support the
transfer of learning across, between and beyond subjects?

Students demonstrated transfer of learning through their ability to apply
systems thinking across multiple contexts connecting scientific concepts
such as the water cycle and recycling systems with social and
organisational systems in the school. Written and oral presentations to
real audiences, such as the executive team, evidenced students? capacity
to use persuasive and expository writing to advocate for sustainability.
Their projects reflected an integrated understanding of how systems
influence one another and how human choices can impact environmental
outcomes.

 To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary
connections through collaboration among members of the
teaching team?

Collaboration among teaching staff was a notable strength of the unit,
particularly integrating literacy and science. Joint planning and shared
inquiry opportunities ensure conceptual coherence and meaningful
connections between disciplines. Mathematics integration was identified
as an area for further development, with opportunities to embed data
collection and analysis skills into sustainability inquiries in future
iterations. The shared focus on authentic, system-based learning
promoted consistent transdisciplinary understanding across the team.

What did we discover about the process of learning that will
inform future learning and teaching?

The unit highlighted the value of systems thinking as a powerful lens for
deepening understanding across disciplines. Providing authentic, context-
driven learning experiences enhanced engagement and conceptual
transfer. The inquiry also reinforced the importance of allowing flexibility
for student agency and evolving lines of inquiry. Future learning will
benefit from greater integration of mathematical thinking and ongoing
opportunities for students to explore how systems connect beyond the
school environment, supporting sustained, meaningful inquiry.

It is important that students understand some of the key

 differences between an Acknowledgement of Country and
a Welcome to Country.

An Acknowledgement of Country is different from a
Welcome to Country, which is a formal welcome onto land
and can only be delivered by Traditional Owners or
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who have
been given permission from Traditional Owners to welcome
visitors to their Country. An Acknowledgement of Country
is a way of showing respect for the Traditional Owners and
can be given by both non-Indigenous people and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people who are connected to
another place.

?A Welcome to Country is like you're hosting a birthday: you do a
welcome and say thank you for coming to my birthday. And an
Acknowledgement of Country is like if you're a guest at the
birthday: you would say thank you for having me.?
