-

research and critical thinking skills through hands-on exploration.
Participating in meaningful action enabled students to connect
classroom learning with community needs, fostering a sense of
responsibility and empathy as principled individuals. This also
strengthened their social skills through collaboration with peers and
community members to address authentic challenges.

- Maintaining reflection journals encouraged students to engage in
regular self-assessment, enhancing their capacity to be reflective
learners. This practice also supported the development of self-
management skills by guiding them to set personal goals and monitor
their progress throughout their learning journey.

What evidence do we have that students are developing knowledge,
conceptual understandings and skills to support the transfer of
learning across, between and beyond subjects?

As part of the PYP Exhibition, students delivered a comprehensive presentation
that articulated their enduring understanding, demonstrating the depth of their
inquiry and the connections made throughout their learning journey.

Students demonstrated growth in transferable knowledge, conceptual
understanding, and skills through a range of evidence. Reflection journals
revealed their capacity to evaluate their own progress and establish purposeful
goals, highlighting metacognitive development. Media campaigns showcased
their ability to integrate research, analytical thinking, and creativity across
disciplines while engaging with authentic, real-world issues. Moreover, the
incorporation of transdisciplinary concepts such as media literacy and
persuasive techniques illustrated their skill in making meaningful connections
across learning areas and applying their understanding in broader contexts. This
development equipped students to extend their learning confidently beyond the
classroom.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary connections
through collaboration among members of the teaching team?
The collaboration among Y6 team significantly strengthened transdisciplinary
connections. Shared goals, resources, and feedback facilitated a richer
understanding of how different subjects interconnect, enabling students to
transfer knowledge seamlessly. Additionally, collaborative efforts ensured
alignment in teaching approaches, which reinforced consistent messaging about
the central idea and inquiry focus.

PSPE
The structure of our Term 1 PE lessons (particularly during
cooperative challenges and strategy-based games) provided
authentic opportunities for students to reflect on their decision-
making, self-perception and the role of social influence in physical
activity. Students were engaged in both the physical and reflective
aspects of the lessons, and many demonstrated growth in how
they viewed teamwork and personal responsibility. What worked
particularly well was the balance between movement and
conversation (giving space for students to unpack their choices
and behaviour). Next time, I would like to introduce more visible
thinking strategies to capture these reflections more consistently
and deepen the connection to unit learning.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: How community values shape the management of the natural environment; The need for sustainable practices; Taking action for environmental stewardship

s.d: Students layer population, climate and terrain data to compare how two communities manage nearby natural environments. This shows why the same environmental challenge can lead to different choices in different places. Each group chooses where it would protect land, allow development or restore habitat, then adds annotations explaining the trade-offs. Groups swap maps and challenge one decision using evidence from a different layer. Students finish with an annotated map that shows how community needs and environmental care can compete. MapMaker's geographic data layers let students test whether their first ideas still make sense when new evidence appears.

Students record 360-degree views of places around the campus where people affect soil, water, plants or wildlife. Seeing the whole setting helps them notice how paths, bins, gardens and buildings shape the environment. Each group asks another class to explore one recording and identify a stewardship problem the filmmakers missed. Students then record a second view that points out a practical improvement and explains who would need to support it. They finish with a pair of immersive recordings showing a place before and after a proposed community action. The camera captures the complete surroundings, so viewers can look beyond the feature the group first noticed.

Students interview a teacher, Camp Mallana staff member or invited community expert about a practice that protects the natural environment. Their questions explore how culture, experience and community values influence decisions about land, water and living things. Students place short recorded answers beside their own respectful commentary and checked background information. A partner group listens and adds one question that the book still needs to answer. Students finish with a narrated digital book containing interviews, images, text and practical stewardship ideas. Book Creator keeps recorded voice, video, images and writing together on each page.

Students program a Micro:bit to count different types of litter found during a marked schoolyard or Camp Mallana survey. They use the two buttons for separate categories and show running totals on the LED grid. This turns a general call to reduce waste into evidence that can guide a specific community response. Groups exchange devices, test the counting instructions and debug any program that records incorrect totals. Students finish with a portable litter-counting device and a tested plan for where it should be used. The buttons, LED grid and battery pack allow the device to collect counts away from a computer.

Students design an environmental campaign for one realistic change at Elsternwick, such as reducing lunch waste, protecting habitat or saving water. They select evidence, name the people whose support is needed and state one action the audience can take. Each campaign is tested with another class, whose response decides which wording or image the designers revise. The strongest campaigns can be shown to campus leaders or included in a real school sustainability drive. Students finish with a campaign poster, infographic or short promotional video. Canva's layouts support clear combinations of evidence, images and short calls to action.

Students empathise with cleaners, gardeners and local wildlife by examining where mixed waste creates problems, then define one item-sorting need. They sketch ideas and build a physical sorter from LEGO pieces, cardboard chutes and clean recycled packaging. Teams code a colour or distance sensor to trigger a motor that diverts model waste, then test it with repeated trials. They record failures by hand, adjust the chute, mechanism or code, and test again with another team's objects. Each team demonstrates a working prototype and explains how its design could support a community decision about waste.

plannerText: The Year 6 'Sharing the Planet' unit focuses on how communities interact with the environment in diverse ways, emphasizing stewardship, conservation, and the influence of community values. Students explore Indigenous practices, local and global case studies, and environmental challenges through inquiry-based learning, reflective tasks, and action projects. The unit integrates experiences from Camp Mallana, encourages advocacy and responsible action, and connects to curriculum areas such as science, social studies, and digital skills. Learning activities are designed to foster critical thinking, collaboration, and real-world application, culminating in student-led projects that promote environmental awareness and sustainable futures.

electromagnetic induction, a principle discovered by Michael Faraday. When a wire coil moves near a magnet, or a magnet
moves near a coil, an electric current is produced in the wire.

What William's Dynamo Was

A dynamo is a simple machine that converts mechanical energy (movement) into electrical energy. William built his using
parts he found in a scrapyard ? including a bicycle dynamo, wires, a fan blade, and an old bicycle frame.

The original dynamo was small ? the same kind used to power a bicycle headlight. William attached it to a windmill rotor he
designed himself.

How It Worked

1. The Wind Turns the Blades

When the wind blew, it spun the blades (which William made from melted PVC pipes and flattened pieces of plastic). The
blades were connected to a shaft.

2. The Shaft Spins the Dynamo

The shaft rotated the bicycle dynamo ? the key part that generates electricity. Inside the dynamo, a coil of wire spins
around magnets.

3. Mechanical Energy Becomes Electrical Energy

The spinning motion inside the dynamo created a flow of electric current (this is electromagnetic induction ? the same
principle used in large generators).

4. The Electricity Was Stored and Used

The dynamo produced direct current (DC) electricity, which William used to power a small light bulb. Later, he
improved his design with a larger generator and a battery, allowing him to store electricity and power lights, radios, and
even charge mobile phones.

For the How the World Works unit in 2026, it would be beneficial next year to
order DC motors, batteries, and wires so that students can engage in hands-on
construction tasks. Providing these materials would allow them to design and
build working models, deepening their understanding of energy transfer and
electrical circuits through practical exploration.

creating mind maps and investigating energy transformations), inquiry-driven
discussions, and reflective tasks like ?See Think Wonder,? allowed students to
actively engage with and unpack the central idea. These strategies encouraged
critical thinking and provided tangible opportunities for students to connect
theory with practice, enhancing their understanding of energy transformation
and sustainable practices. Evidence of understanding is visible in their ability to
explain concepts like the functionality of William's windmill or the energy
processes in coal-fired power stations, demonstrating their grasp of the central
idea: "Energy may be converted, transformed, and used to support human
progress

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals

Students achieved the learning goals for the unit. They

The unit fostered robust transdisciplinary connections by aligning science

PSPE
Our focus was on energy transfer and the function of movement, using striking
and fielding games as a platform for students to explore how their bodies
produce, use and manage physical energy.   They responded well to the
practical nature of the learning, especially during activities that required them to
consider how force, timing and positioning influenced their outcomes. The
language of ?energy transfer? became more familiar as we unpacked real-time
moments (like the swing of a bat or a burst of sprinting).  The concept of energy
use made sense to most students, and they began to reflect on how their bodies
produce and recover energy in game settings. The only thing I'd refine is to look
to build more focus around perspective and responsibility, by encouraging
students to think about the efficiency of their movement, and how pacing,
teamwork or positioning can help conserve energy and improve performance.

skills, social skills).
Each group has a large sheet of paper and markers.
Ask them to create a superhero character that embodies
their assigned approach to learning. They should include
the superpowers associated with that approach and how
they can use them to tackle learning challenges.
After 10 minutes, have each group present their superhero

?

to the class. Encourage creativity and enthusiasm!
Students can create their superhero and publish to their

Activity: Skill Stations

?

?

Set up stations around the classroom, each representing
one of the approaches to learning.
At each station, place an index card with a challenge or
activity related to that approach (e.g., at the
communication skills station, students might have to act
out a scene without speaking).

? Divide the class into smaller groups and have them rotate

?

?

through each station, spending about 5 minutes at each.
Encourage students to use the specific approach to tackle
the challenge at each station.
Keep track of how quickly each group completes the
challenges.

of each challenge based on speed and creativity.

Students Reflections
What are the students? perceptions of how the
learning experiences engaged them effectively?
Students found the learning experiences both engaging
and meaningful. They particularly valued the hands-on
elements, such as inquiry projects and collaborative
group tasks, which enabled them to investigate topics in
depth and learn through shared exploration with their
peers.

Did they feel they achieved the learning goals
outlined for the unit of inquiry?
Many students reported a strong sense of achievement in
meeting the learning goals established for the unit. They
expressed confidence in their understanding of their
chosen topics and took pride in the opportunity to design
and direct their own units of inquiry.

What are students? reflections on their
understanding of the central idea?
Students reflected positively on their understanding of
the central idea, noting that a range of activities
deepened their awareness of how media influences
opinions and enhanced their understanding of persuasive
techniques.

Do students feel they developed and demonstrated
the learner profile attributes that were identified
for this unit?
Students felt they had developed and demonstrated key
learner profile attributes, particularly those of being
inquirers and communicators. Through conducting
research and sharing their findings with peers, they
strengthened their curiosity, communication skills, and
confidence in expressing their ideas.

What did students feel challenged by?
Students were feeling challenged by synthesising
information from multiple sources during the inquiry
process. Others found it difficult to collaborate effectively
within diverse groups.

 What do students now know or understand that
they didn't before?
Students gained new knowledge about media literacy.
They learned about different media formats and their
impacts on public perception. They also learned about
how to create their own unit of inquiry.

What will students do with their new learning?
With their new learning, students expressed intentions to
follow through with the actions they were communicating
to their audience.

research and critical thinking skills through hands-on exploration.

- Maintaining reflection journals encouraged students to engage in

What evidence do we have that students are developing knowledge,
conceptual understandings and skills to support the transfer of
learning across, between and beyond subjects?

As part of the PYP Exhibition, students delivered a comprehensive presentation
that articulated their enduring understanding, demonstrating the depth of their
inquiry and the connections made throughout their learning journey.

Students demonstrated growth in transferable knowledge, conceptual
understanding, and skills through a range of evidence. Reflection journals
revealed their capacity to evaluate their own progress and establish purposeful
goals, highlighting metacognitive development. Media campaigns showcased
their ability to integrate research, analytical thinking, and creativity across
disciplines while engaging with authentic, real-world issues. Moreover, the
incorporation of transdisciplinary concepts such as media literacy and
persuasive techniques illustrated their skill in making meaningful connections
across learning areas and applying their understanding in broader contexts. This
development equipped students to extend their learning confidently beyond the
classroom.

To what extent have we strengthened transdisciplinary connections
through collaboration among members of the teaching team?
The collaboration among Y6 team significantly strengthened transdisciplinary
connections. Shared goals, resources, and feedback facilitated a richer
understanding of how different subjects interconnect, enabling students to
transfer knowledge seamlessly. Additionally, collaborative efforts ensured
alignment in teaching approaches, which reinforced consistent messaging about
the central idea and inquiry focus.

PSPE
The structure of our Term 1 PE lessons (particularly during
cooperative challenges and strategy-based games) provided
authentic opportunities for students to reflect on their decision-
making, self-perception and the role of social influence in physical
activity. Students were engaged in both the physical and reflective
aspects of the lessons, and many demonstrated growth in how
they viewed teamwork and personal responsibility. What worked
particularly well was the balance between movement and
conversation (giving space for students to unpack their choices
and behaviour). Next time, I would like to introduce more visible
thinking strategies to capture these reflections more consistently
and deepen the connection to unit learning.

future learning and teaching?

They ask why the person moved, what changed in the new place and whose experiences might be missing. This opens the central idea through one person's choices before students examine the wider event. Pairs compare the answers they received and write follow-up questions that challenge different points of view. Students finish with a saved written interview and three claims they will check against reliable historical sources. The teacher controls the character, discussion rules and level of support, so the chatbot guides thinking rather than acting as a research source.

Students map migration routes to Victoria and annotate the places where selected significant events began, unfolded and had lasting effects. They switch between population, terrain and climate layers to work out how geography may have influenced why people moved. Each group removes one layer before another group examines the map and identifies what evidence is now missing. Students finish with an annotated map that links routes, causes and changes to communities. They add short notes that clearly separate map evidence from questions needing further research. MapMaker's geographic data layers let students test different explanations rather than simply view a static map.

Students sort and compare Dollar Street photographs of homes, kitchens, bedrooms and valued objects from countries linked to migration stories they are researching. The visual evidence helps them consider what people may preserve, adapt or leave behind when events reshape a place. Students choose two households at similar income levels in different countries so culture is not confused with wealth. They exchange comparisons with another pair and check whether their first assumptions are supported by the photographs. Students finish with a captioned set of image observations and careful questions for further inquiry. Dollar Street arranges households by estimated monthly consumption, making fairer visual comparisons possible.

Students build a multimodal case study showing how one significant event changed a Victorian place before, during and after it occurred. They combine written explanations, primary-source images and recorded narration to show causes, different experiences and lasting impacts. A classmate listens without seeing the title and identifies which evidence makes the event seem significant. Students then revise any page where the link between evidence and change is unclear. They finish with a narrated digital book that can form part of the student-led exhibition. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together in one publishable book.

Students write a Kahoot quiz that asks classmates to judge whether events are significant rather than merely recall dates. Each question presents a short event summary and answer choices based on criteria such as scale, duration, change and different community perspectives. Groups swap quizzes and flag any question where more than one answer could be defended. The authors revise those questions or use them to start a class discussion about why historical significance can be contested. Students finish with a playable quiz that checks both historical knowledge and reasoning. Kahoot's immediate answer display gives the teacher a quick view of which significance criteria need more teaching.

Students empathise with migrants arriving at an unfamiliar transport hub, then define one physical navigation or luggage-moving problem that could make arrival safer and clearer. Using LEGO beams, wheels, motors, the distance, colour or force sensor, and cardboard signs, teams ideate and build a working model such as an automated barrier, guided trolley or alert point. They test it with classmates following a simple arrival scenario, record where the mechanism fails, and rebuild or debug it at least once. Each team demonstrates the improved prototype and explains how a significant wave of migration could change the services and design of a place. The final model must physically move or respond to an input, not simply represent the historical event.

plannerText: The Year 6 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit centers on the central idea that significant events shape a place, with a focus on migration, historical change, and the impact of events on communities. Students develop research, thinking, and communication skills as they investigate what makes an event significant, why events occur, and their lasting effects. The unit emphasizes inquiry-based learning, student agency, and transdisciplinary connections, culminating in student-led research projects and presentations about significant events. Activities include mapping family migration, analyzing primary sources, constructing timelines, and exploring the contributions of diverse groups, all aimed at fostering international mindedness and historical understanding.

electromagnetic induction, a principle discovered by Michael Faraday. When a wire coil moves near a magnet, or a magnet
moves near a coil, an electric current is produced in the wire.

What William's Dynamo Was

A dynamo is a simple machine that converts mechanical energy (movement) into electrical energy. William built his using
parts he found in a scrapyard ? including a bicycle dynamo, wires, a fan blade, and an old bicycle frame.

The original dynamo was small ? the same kind used to power a bicycle headlight. William attached it to a windmill rotor he
designed himself.

How It Worked

1. The Wind Turns the Blades

When the wind blew, it spun the blades (which William made from melted PVC pipes and flattened pieces of plastic). The
blades were connected to a shaft.

2. The Shaft Spins the Dynamo

The shaft rotated the bicycle dynamo ? the key part that generates electricity. Inside the dynamo, a coil of wire spins
around magnets.

3. Mechanical Energy Becomes Electrical Energy

The spinning motion inside the dynamo created a flow of electric current (this is electromagnetic induction ? the same
principle used in large generators).

4. The Electricity Was Stored and Used

The dynamo produced direct current (DC) electricity, which William used to power a small light bulb. Later, he
improved his design with a larger generator and a battery, allowing him to store electricity and power lights, radios, and
even charge mobile phones.

order DC motors, batteries, and wires so that students can engage in hands-on
construction tasks. Providing these materials would allow them to design and
build working models, deepening their understanding of energy transfer and

discussions, and reflective tasks like ?See Think Wonder,? allowed students to
actively engage with and unpack the central idea. These strategies encouraged
critical thinking and provided tangible opportunities for students to connect
theory with practice, enhancing their understanding of energy transformation
and sustainable practices. Evidence of understanding is visible in their ability to
explain concepts like the functionality of William's windmill or the energy
processes in coal-fired power stations, demonstrating their grasp of the central
idea: "Energy may be converted, transformed, and used to support human

The unit fostered robust transdisciplinary connections by aligning science

PSPE
Our focus was on energy transfer and the function of movement, using striking
and fielding games as a platform for students to explore how their bodies
produce, use and manage physical energy.   They responded well to the
practical nature of the learning, especially during activities that required them to
consider how force, timing and positioning influenced their outcomes. The
language of ?energy transfer? became more familiar as we unpacked real-time
moments (like the swing of a bat or a burst of sprinting).  The concept of energy
use made sense to most students, and they began to reflect on how their bodies
produce and recover energy in game settings. The only thing I'd refine is to look
to build more focus around perspective and responsibility, by encouraging
students to think about the efficiency of their movement, and how pacing,
teamwork or positioning can help conserve energy and improve performance.

PSPE
The structure of our Term 1 PE lessons (particularly during
cooperative challenges and strategy-based games) provided
authentic opportunities for students to reflect on their decision-
making, self-perception and the role of social influence in physical
activity. Students were engaged in both the physical and reflective
aspects of the lessons, and many demonstrated growth in how
they viewed teamwork and personal responsibility. What worked
particularly well was the balance between movement and
conversation (giving space for students to unpack their choices
and behaviour). Next time, I would like to introduce more visible
thinking strategies to capture these reflections more consistently
and deepen the connection to unit learning.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a future-self character describing how their identity, friendships, interests and strengths might change by secondary school. This helps them see that a sense of self keeps growing through new experiences and influences. Each student chooses one current influence that their future character will thank, question or leave behind. Partners watch the characters and suggest one thoughtful question for a second recording. Students finish with a short animated message from their imagined future self. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students paint a layered self-portrait showing physical features, emotions, interests and important influences. The portrait shows that identity has many parts and that some parts are easier to see than others. Students swap portraits without explaining them first, then hear what a partner noticed and decide whether to change one layer. They can hide and reveal layers while discussing how different settings bring out different sides of a person. Students finish with an original digital painting that combines visible and less visible parts of themselves. Brushes Redux layers let students revise one part without changing the whole portrait.

Students arrange six personal or teacher-approved images into a collage showing people, places, activities and ideas that have shaped them. This makes the influences on identity visible without asking students to rank one influence as the most important. Students add a short caption explaining whether each influence has stayed steady, grown stronger or changed over time. A partner identifies one connection between two images that the creator may not have noticed. Students finish with a captioned visual map of the influences around them. PicCollage's grid layouts make it easy to compare the six influences at a glance.

Students film and edit a two-minute interview with a trusted adult about one physical, social, emotional or intellectual change across life. The conversation helps students compare their own expectations of change with a real person's experience. Students choose one answer to place at the beginning as a question-provoking opening, rather than arranging every clip in recording order. Classmates watch selected films and note one similarity and one difference across generations. Students finish with a short interview film containing a title, carefully trimmed clips and a closing reflection. IMovie's editing tools let students reorder clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students design an infographic that traces one personal strength from an early memory to a goal for the next year. This shows how experiences, feedback and deliberate choices can change how someone sees themselves. Students ask a peer to check whether the steps between the memory and goal are clear, then revise the wording or layout. Each student chooses whether the finished piece is private, shared with one trusted person or displayed for the class. Students finish with a visual timeline containing evidence of growth and one realistic next action. Adobe Express templates support clear layouts with short text, icons and images.

Students empathise by gathering anonymous classroom examples of times when someone needs quiet, help or space to think, then define one need their desk device will support. Using LEGO pieces, cardboard labels and a paper pointer, they sketch ideas and build a prototype that uses a force, colour or distance sensor as an input and a motor as an output. They program the device so a user can deliberately signal a need without speaking, then classmates test whether the signal is easy to understand and control. Students improve the build, code or labels after observing confusion, accidental activation or mechanical problems. The final demonstration shows the user's need, the working sensor-and-motor response and the change made after testing.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' Year 6 unit focuses on the central idea that personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self. Students explore physical, social, emotional, and intellectual changes throughout life, investigate the influences around them, and examine how perceptions are shaped. The unit emphasizes inquiry into identity, belonging, and well-being, with strong links to literacy, visual art, PSPE, and digital skills. Learning experiences include digital collages, collaborative brainstorming, reflective storytelling, and personal goal setting, all designed to foster self-awareness, communication, and critical thinking. Student agency, peer feedback, and creative expression are central, with opportunities for both digital and hands-on learning.

electromagnetic induction, a principle discovered by Michael Faraday. When a wire coil moves near a magnet, or a magnet
moves near a coil, an electric current is produced in the wire.

What William's Dynamo Was

A dynamo is a simple machine that converts mechanical energy (movement) into electrical energy. William built his using
parts he found in a scrapyard ? including a bicycle dynamo, wires, a fan blade, and an old bicycle frame.

The original dynamo was small ? the same kind used to power a bicycle headlight. William attached it to a windmill rotor he
designed himself.

How It Worked

1. The Wind Turns the Blades

When the wind blew, it spun the blades (which William made from melted PVC pipes and flattened pieces of plastic). The
blades were connected to a shaft.

2. The Shaft Spins the Dynamo

The shaft rotated the bicycle dynamo ? the key part that generates electricity. Inside the dynamo, a coil of wire spins
around magnets.

3. Mechanical Energy Becomes Electrical Energy

The spinning motion inside the dynamo created a flow of electric current (this is electromagnetic induction ? the same
principle used in large generators).

4. The Electricity Was Stored and Used

The dynamo produced direct current (DC) electricity, which William used to power a small light bulb. Later, he
improved his design with a larger generator and a battery, allowing him to store electricity and power lights, radios, and
even charge mobile phones.

discussions, and reflective tasks like ?See Think Wonder,? allowed students to
actively engage with and unpack the central idea. These strategies encouraged
critical thinking and provided tangible opportunities for students to connect
theory with practice, enhancing their understanding of energy transformation
and sustainable practices. Evidence of understanding is visible in their ability to
explain concepts like the functionality of William's windmill or the energy
processes in coal-fired power stations, demonstrating their grasp of the central

Our focus was on energy transfer and the function of movement, using striking
and fielding games as a platform for students to explore how their bodies
produce, use and manage physical energy.   They responded well to the
practical nature of the learning, especially during activities that required them to
consider how force, timing and positioning influenced their outcomes. The
language of ?energy transfer? became more familiar as we unpacked real-time
moments (like the swing of a bat or a burst of sprinting).  The concept of energy

produce and recover energy in game settings. The only thing I'd refine is to look
to build more focus around perspective and responsibility, by encouraging
students to think about the efficiency of their movement, and how pacing,
teamwork or positioning can help conserve energy and improve performance.

PSPE
The structure of our Term 1 PE lessons (particularly during
cooperative challenges and strategy-based games) provided
authentic opportunities for students to reflect on their decision-
making, self-perception and the role of social influence in physical
activity. Students were engaged in both the physical and reflective
aspects of the lessons, and many demonstrated growth in how
they viewed teamwork and personal responsibility. What worked
particularly well was the balance between movement and
conversation (giving space for students to unpack their choices
and behaviour). Next time, I would like to introduce more visible
thinking strategies to capture these reflections more consistently
and deepen the connection to unit learning.

s.d: Students record short pieces of music that show calm, worry, anger or joy. This helps them hear how emotions can affect the way bodies and minds feel. Partners listen without being told the emotion, choose what they think it is and explain which sounds gave them clues. Students then change one sound to make their emotional message clearer or more open to interpretation. Each child finishes with a short emotional soundscape for a class listening gallery. GarageBand lets them combine and replay instrument sounds before recording their final piece.

Students program two characters to show what happens when one character feels left out during play. They explore how feelings can shape behaviour and change a relationship. Partners swap projects and choose a kind response for the second character to try. Students debug the sequence so the characters move, speak and respond in a clear order. Each pair finishes with a short animated story showing a problem and a caring choice. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young children sequence movement and speech without needing to read instructions.

Students sort teacher-prepared pictures of faces, body positions and everyday situations on a shared Freeform board. They discuss why the same picture might suggest different emotions to different people. Small groups move one picture between emotion groups and record their reasons with a drawing or short teacher-scribed note. The class adds simple calming choices beside situations that may affect wellbeing. Students finish with a connected visual board showing feelings, clues, situations and helpful responses. Freeform's open canvas makes it easy to move, group and connect ideas during discussion.

Students listen to a teacher-selected Epic audiobook in which a character experiences a strong emotion. They pause to name the feeling, point to clues in the words or pictures and copy the character's body position. Pairs choose one moment and act out two possible responses before listening to what happens next. The class compares the author's choice with the children's ideas for protecting wellbeing and relationships. Students finish with a spoken retelling that names the feeling, its cause and a caring response. Epic's read-aloud books allow children to listen while closely studying the illustrations.

Students record brief movements that show emotions such as excitement, disappointment, worry and calm. They replay each action slowly to notice changes in shoulders, hands, face, speed and personal space. Partners view a clip without hearing the emotion named and explain which movement clues shaped their interpretation. Students record the action again after changing one clue, then compare how the message changes. Each pair finishes with two short clips that show how behaviour can be read in different ways. Slow-motion replay makes small body movements visible enough for Prep children to discuss.

Students empathise with a class character who needs help moving from a busy play area to a calm space, then define what would make the journey feel safe and predictable. They ideate with paper emotion cards, cardboard scenery and Indi's coloured tiles, then prototype a floor pathway that includes places to pause, turn and continue. Pairs test the route by placing Indi on the tiles and watching whether it reaches the cardboard calm space as planned. They move tiles, shorten confusing sections and test again after feedback from another pair. At the end, students demonstrate the working pathway and explain where a person could use a calming or caring strategy along the journey.

plannerText: The Prep unit 'How We Express Ourselves' explores how emotions influence wellbeing, focusing on how feelings affect us, how we interpret emotions, and how our emotions and behavior impact relationships. Students learn to recognize, name, and express emotions through art, stories, and music, and reflect on strategies for self-regulation and caring for others. The unit is highly play-based and integrates communication, social, and self-management skills, with strong links to the Australian Curriculum in Health, English, and the Arts. Learning experiences are designed to be hands-on, creative, and inclusive, supporting students' understanding of themselves and others.

ci: The products people use go through a process of change.
lo: Where food comes from; How food can be changed for different purposes; An appreciation of food

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles on the carpet to show wheat changing from seed, to crop, to flour, to bread, then send Indi along the sequence. This makes each stage of food production visible, movable and easy to retell. Pairs swap pathways and work out whether the colour instructions take Indi through the stages in the correct order. Each pair chooses one stage where Indi must pause so they can explain who helped or what changed there. Students finish with a working floor pathway that another Prep group can follow and retell. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students arrange teacher-supplied photos of one food before, during and after it changes, such as apples becoming sauce. The image order helps children see that familiar products come from ingredients and a series of actions. Each pair removes one image before showing its collage to another pair, who must work out the missing stage. Students then restore the image and add short captions such as 'grown', 'washed', 'cut' and 'cooked'. They finish with a labelled visual sequence for a classroom food-process display. PicCollage's grid layouts keep the stages clear and easy to compare.

Students code a piece of fruit or grain to move through three scenes showing where it comes from and how people change it. The animation turns a food process into an ordered set of instructions that children can test and fix. Partners exchange projects and check whether the food changes in a sensible order from source to product. Students choose movements, speech and scene changes that make each stage clear without a teacher explaining it. They finish with a short coded story that younger buddies can tap through. ScratchJr's picture-based blocks let Prep students sequence movement and scene changes.

Students record real classroom sounds made while preparing a food, such as washing, chopping with safe utensils, mixing and crunching. Listening closely helps them notice that changing food involves a sequence of actions. Groups rearrange their recordings and ask classmates to identify the correct order using sound alone. They then choose one spoken sentence to add at the end explaining why they appreciate the finished food. Students finish with a short sound sequence that can accompany a class tasting display. GarageBand allows recorded sounds and voices to be arranged on separate tracks.

Students sort teacher-added food pictures into groups showing foods that grow on plants, come from animals or are made by people. This helps them work out where food begins before it reaches a shop or lunchbox. Pairs draw connecting lines from an ingredient to several possible products, such as milk to yoghurt, cheese and butter. Another pair follows the links and moves any picture they think needs more discussion. Students finish with a shared visual web of food origins and changes. Freeform's large canvas allows pictures, words and connecting lines to sit together.

Students empathise with a grower who needs to move soft strawberries from a field to a market without crushing or losing them. They define the problem, then sketch ideas and build a Bee-Bot route from cardboard, paper signs, recycled packaging and blocks, including a lightweight berry tray. Teams prototype the route, program Bee-Bot's directional buttons and test whether it reaches the market with all model berries still aboard. After each test, they change the tray, road or programmed sequence and run it again. Students finish by demonstrating their improved transport system and explaining which change protected the food best.

plannerText: The Prep 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores where food comes from, how it changes, and why we appreciate it. Students inquire into the origins of food, the processes foods undergo (such as growing, harvesting, and transforming into new products), and the importance of food in daily life. The unit emphasizes hands-on experiences, observation, sequencing, and reflection, with strong links to science, literacy, and the arts. Learning is supported by family engagement, class discussions, and creative projects that help students connect personal experiences to broader systems of food production and change.

Visual Art - In this unit of inquiry, Prep students will embark on a series of activities, where they will explore the dynamic interplay between forces
and paint. Using a variety of tools, including blower bulbs, straws, and string, students will embark on a playful journey of discovery. Through the
forces of pushing, pulling, blowing, and tipping paint, they will experiment with a multitude of techniques, each yielding unique and unexpected
results. Students will explore the scope for turning their experiments into characterful animals.

In library sessions, we will continue to nurture a love or reading while introducing basic research skills.  As part of the How the World Works unit on
materials and their properties, students will explore texts such as Pamla Allen's Mr Archimedes? Bath and the fairy tale The Three Little Pigs to
discover the properties of both solids and liquids.  These stories will help spark discussion about how different materials behave and how their
properties shape the world around us.

ci: The properties of materials influence how objects move and their use.
lo: Properties of materials; How objects move; How we use materials

s.d: Students record balls, blocks and toy wheels moving down ramps covered with foil, felt, cardboard and bubble wrap. They watch each movement slowly to see how the surface and object materials change rolling, sliding, bouncing and stopping. Before replaying each clip, partners predict which object will travel furthest and explain why. Students swap clips with another Prep class and ask them to spot one movement detail. They end with a set of short comparison recordings showing how materials influence movement. Slow-motion replay makes quick changes in speed and direction easier for young children to notice.

Students examine wood, metal, plastic, fabric, rubber and paper with Tablet Magnifiers before touching, bending and sorting the samples. Close observation helps them connect visible features such as fibres, bumps and holes with properties such as rough, smooth, flexible or rigid. Partners choose one mystery sample and give another pair three close-up clues to identify it. Students then sort the real samples by a property they can see and explain any item that could belong in two groups. They end with labelled sorting trays and a spoken bank of useful material words. Magnification reveals details that are difficult to see with the unaided eye.

Students build a small ramp scene and move real objects frame by frame to show rolling, sliding, bouncing and stopping. They use different classroom materials for the ramp and object so the animation shows how material choices can change movement. Pairs exchange unfinished films and suggest one change that would make the science clearer. Students reshoot frames after changing the surface, object or slope. They end with a short stop-motion comparison film that shows a clear before-and-after test. Stop Motion Studio joins individual frames so tiny changes appear as controlled movement.

Students photograph real classroom objects in Seesaw and record themselves naming each material and describing one property. They explain how that property helps the object do its job, such as rubber gripping or fabric bending. Families are invited to add one household example for children to discuss back at school. Students listen to a partner's entry and record a question or a different material choice. They end with a class collection of photographed objects, spoken explanations and responses. Seesaw keeps photos and voice recordings together in each child's portfolio entry.

Students draw two versions of a playground object in Sketchbook using different materials, such as a smooth metal slide and a soft fabric slide. They use arrows and colour to show where an object would slide, roll, bend or stop. Partners swap designs and choose which version would work better for its purpose, giving one reason aloud. Students revise one material choice after hearing the feedback. They end with a detailed digital design showing how material properties affect use and movement. Sketchbook's drawing tools let children change lines, shapes and colours without rebuilding the whole design.

Students empathise with a toy that needs to carry a small cardboard parcel safely across a floor route, then define the problem as keeping the parcel on the moving Bee-Bot. They ideate with paper sketches and prototype carriers from cardboard, recycled lids, fabric, foil, pipe cleaners and masking tape. Teams attach one carrier, program the Bee-Bot's directional buttons and test it over turns and different floor surfaces. They improve the carrier's shape or material after each dropped parcel, then repeat the same route for a fair test. At the end, students demonstrate a working carrier and explain which material property helped it hold, cushion or support the parcel.

plannerText: The Prep 'How the World Works' unit explores properties of materials, how objects move, and how materials are used. Students investigate materials through hands-on activities, observations, and playful experiments, connecting science concepts with everyday experiences. The unit emphasizes vocabulary development, sorting and comparing, and encourages students to design, test, and improve simple creations using a range of materials. Learning is supported by cross-curricular links to art, music, and literacy, with a focus on inquiry, communication, and early scientific thinking.

Student Reflections

retesting their design.

We found it hard, still in the early half of this term, to dedicate very
much time to our UOI as the children were needing so much time

received more time as the term moved on.

classroom.
The final activity of designing a floater was successful. Children
engaged with the task positively, embracing the idea of improving their

harder to judge
The Hands On incursion in week 6 was useful in consolidating mostly

done in school. The timing would not want to be any later.

Visual Art: Students will explore the themes of repetition, bold colours, and geometric shapes using oil pastels, inspired by Yayoi Kusama. They will
create dynamic compositions filled with dots, spirals, and linear patterns, mimicking Kusama's signature style.
Students will experiment with bright, contrasting colours such as vivid reds, yellows, and blacks while incorporating organic shapes and
repetitive motifs to evoke a sense of infinity and movement. The project will encourage students to express their creativity while paying homage to
Kusama's obsession with pattern and the transformative power of colour.

Language Acquisition: Students will learn how to identify and understand their emotions and how they help us to regulate our behaviour. Students
will learn to describe the emotions of people and talk about connections between feelings, body reactions and body language. They will also
identify and describe emotional responses people may experience in different situations.

Music: Students listen to a variety of musical examples, discussing how the music makes them feel. Students also show this through drawings and
moving to music. We look at how a composer can portray different feelings musically, by making changes in tempo, dynamics etc to create a
different mood. Class discussions were had about our favourite music. Music was played for relaxation and we talked about meditation music being
good for some people's well being.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students choose an on-screen character and record it explaining one way a family fairly shares food, space or time. This opens a child-friendly conversation about rights, responsibilities and limited resources inside everyday family life. Partners listen to each character and suggest one fair choice the speaker could add. Students then rerecord their message after hearing the new idea. They finish with a short talking-character explanation for a class gallery. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to each child's recorded voice.

Students lay coloured tiles on the carpet to guide Indi between cards showing family members, homes and celebrations. The pathways show that families connect in different ways and sometimes need to share the same spaces. Pairs swap pathways and work out how to reach every destination without removing another family's place. Students change the tile sequence when Indi takes an unexpected turn. They finish with a tested physical pathway that represents respectful family connections. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students build a short puppet conversation between two family members deciding how to share a special object, meal or celebration space. The conversation makes fairness, listening and responsibility visible through a familiar family situation. Another pair watches the first version and chooses a moment where one character could listen more carefully. Students revise the dialogue and record a fairer ending. They finish with a narrated puppet show that can be played to another Prep class. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one app.

Students paint a family symbol using colours, shapes and patterns connected to a tradition, value or celebration. This allows every child to show identity without needing to reveal private family details. Children exchange paintings and ask the artist what one chosen detail means. Students add a new layer that represents a connection their family shares with people, places or living things. They finish with an original layered painting and a short spoken explanation to the class. Brushes Redux lets students build and adjust separate layers while keeping their original artwork.

Students photograph a family-approved object or their own drawing and record why it matters to their family. This shows how objects and stories can carry culture, values and connections across generations. Families can contribute a short response from home, such as a corrected detail, remembered celebration or extra story. Students listen to the response and add a second recording explaining what they learned. They finish with a multimodal journal entry that brings a family voice into the classroom. Seesaw holds the image, voice recordings and family response together in one place.

Students empathise by listening to classmates describe what different families need at a shared celebration, then define the problem of giving everyone fair access to food, seating and a quiet space. Using cardboard, recycled boxes, paper signs and loose parts, groups ideate and prototype a floor plan on a large paper grid. They program a Bee-Bot with its directional buttons to travel from the entrance to each shared space, then test whether paths collide, exclude anyone or waste limited room. Groups move walls, widen routes and rewrite their button sequence after each test. They finish by demonstrating a revised physical model in which the Bee-Bot can reach every essential space fairly.

plannerText: The Prep 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores family histories, culture, and values, focusing on what makes a family, who is in it, and the connections between family members. Students investigate their own family backgrounds, traditions, and celebrations, using art, music, and storytelling to express their identities. The unit emphasizes communication, respect, and understanding of diversity, with activities such as creating family trees, mapping family origins, and sharing special objects or stories. Learning is hands-on and inquiry-based, supporting students to make connections between their personal histories and the wider world.

Students will experiment with bright, contrasting colours such as vivid reds, yellows, and blacks while incorporating organic shapes and

Kusama's obsession with pattern and the transformative power of colour.

ci: Family histories shape who we are and what we value
lo: What makes a family; The people in your family; Your family history; What is important to your family

s.d: Students build a short puppet show in which family characters tell how a tradition began or why an object matters. This shows how family stories can shape what children value today. Children choose which family members appear and may use imagined characters if they prefer privacy. Partners swap shows and notice one similarity and one difference between their families. Each child finishes with a narrated puppet story to play for classmates or families. Puppet Pals lets children move characters across backdrops while recording their voices.

Students photograph a meaningful family object and make it speak about where it came from and why it matters. This helps children connect family history with the things their families value. A family member can help the child choose the object's message before school, giving home voices a place in the classroom. Classmates listen without guessing whose family is better or more typical, then name connections they noticed. Each child finishes with a short talking-object recording for a class gallery. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and the child's recorded voice to the photograph.

Students paint a digital family portrait using colours, shapes and symbols to show people, pets, places or traditions that belong in their family story. This opens up the idea that families can look different while still offering love and belonging. Children choose a symbol that only someone who knows their family would understand, then explain it to a partner. The class places the finished paintings together as a varied picture of belonging at Wesley. Each child finishes with an original digital painting that can be revisited during reflection. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting in separate layers, so children can add or change details without starting again.

Students record one family story at a time in a digital book using drawings, photographs, short text and their own voices. This helps them place people, traditions and past events together as parts of family history. Families can contribute one spoken memory or greeting, while children decide what is safe and comfortable to include. Children read their books with a buddy and find one value that appears in both families. Each child finishes with a narrated family-history book that can grow across the inquiry. Book Creator keeps images, audio, video and text together on simple pages.

Students arrange toys, paper figures or family-object drawings to show how a tradition happens from beginning to end. This makes family customs easier to examine because children must decide which moments matter most. Small groups swap unfinished animations and work out whether the sequence makes sense without an explanation. They then move, add or remove frames so another class can understand the tradition. Each group finishes with a short stop-motion film showing a family practice such as preparing food, welcoming visitors or celebrating together. Stop Motion Studio captures the tiny frame-by-frame changes that make the objects appear to move.

Students empathise with a family member who needs to reach important people, places and traditions on a large floor map, then define where the journey must begin and end. They ideate several routes and prototype the map with cardboard homes, paper photographs, fabric, blocks and recycled materials. Children program the Bee-Bot's directional buttons, test whether it reaches each stop in the intended order, and adjust either the route or their command sequence. At the end, each group demonstrates a working journey and explains why every stop matters to that family story. The physical map can include many kinds of families without suggesting that every family follows the same path.

Learning experiences include creating family trees, mapping family origins, sharing family traditions, and connecting with cultural celebrations. Assessment is ongoing and includes creative tasks, discussions, and digital sharing. The unit emphasizes diversity, belonging, and making connections between home and school.

Visual Art: Students will explore the themes of repetition, bold colours, and geometric shapes using oil pastels, inspired by Yayoi Kusama. They will

Language Acquisition: Students will learn how to identify and understand their emotions and how they help us to regulate our behaviour. Students
will learn to describe the emotions of people and talk about connections between feelings, body reactions and body language. They will also
identify and describe emotional responses people may experience in different situations.

s.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a large floor map of the Junior School, stopping at places such as the classroom, toilets, library and playground. They match each route to a familiar routine, showing how school organisation helps everyone know where to go and what to do. Pairs swap destination cards and work out a new route without moving the Bee-Bot by hand. They test, debug and explain why their sequence is safe and efficient. The class ends with a set of tested route cards beside the floor map. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make each planned step visible and easy to change.

Students record a page about a family routine or tradition and a page about a school routine. They compare how routines at home and school help people care for one another, work together and become independent. Families can contribute a short story or greeting for children to add with teacher support. Each child chooses the images, words and voice recording that best represent their identity. The finished class book brings family stories and school routines together in one collection. Book Creator combines images, text and recorded narration on each page.

Students sort teacher-provided photos of Junior School people, places and routines into a PicCollage grid. This helps them see that classrooms, playgrounds and helpers each have a part in keeping school organised. Children compare collages with a partner and move one photo if their partner gives a clear reason. They add short labels such as 'helps us learn', 'keeps us safe' or 'helps us belong'. Each pair finishes with a labelled visual guide for a new Prep student. PicCollage's grid layout keeps the photo sorting clear for young learners.

Students photograph a familiar school object in ChatterPix Kids and record it explaining one helpful routine. A hat might explain sun safety, a drink bottle might explain healthy choices, or a school bag might explain morning organisation. Children play their talking images to another Prep class and listen for any instruction that needs to be clearer. They then re-record using a short sentence and a respectful voice. Each child finishes with a talking image that teaches one safe or independent habit. ChatterPix Kids adds a drawn mouth and a short voice recording to the photo.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a character welcoming a new child and explaining how one part of the Junior School works. Their messages show how routines and shared spaces help children learn, stay safe and work together. Each child chooses the routine they think a new Prep student most needs to know. Partners listen and suggest one missing detail before the message is recorded again. The class finishes with a collection of short animated welcome messages. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the character's mouth with the child's recorded voice.

Students empathise with a new Prep child, then define the need for a clear and safe route from the classroom door to a playground meeting place. Teams ideate with drawings, then prototype the route on the floor using Indi colour tiles, cardboard signs, recycled-material boundaries and paper arrows. They test whether Indi completes the planned path, move tiles when the sequence fails, and ask another team whether the route is easy to understand. After several changes, each team demonstrates a working route and explains how its signs, boundaries and sequence support safety and independence. Sphero Indi follows the colour-tile path without an app or screen, keeping the project physical and collaborative.

plannerText: The Prep 'Who We Are' unit explores family, culture, and identity through inquiry into family histories, traditions, and values. Students investigate what makes a family, who is in their family, and how their family history shapes who they are. The unit is play-based and teacher-guided, with activities such as creating family trees, sharing family photos, mapping family origins, and celebrating cultural traditions. The focus is on communication, respect, and understanding connections between people, supported by literacy, art, and music experiences.

ci: People use imagination and materials to express stories, ideas and culture through performance.
lo: Different materials to make puppets; Types and uses of puppets by different cultures; Features and purposes of puppet performances

s.d: Students photograph a puppet one frame at a time as it changes from loose materials into a character and begins a short performance. This shows how imagination can turn ordinary materials into a story. Pairs swap puppets halfway through and continue each other's story without changing the opening frames. They must use movement, position and expression to make the new part understandable without spoken words. Each pair finishes with a short animated puppet performance. Stop Motion Studio joins the individual frames to make the puppet appear to move by itself.

Students build a digital class book that compares puppets from different cultures and records what each puppet is used to express. This helps them notice how materials, movement and performance choices can carry cultural stories. Each pair adds one page, then records a question for the next pair to answer on a following page. Students include a drawing or photograph supplied by the teacher, a short label and their own spoken explanation. The class ends with a narrated puppet guide that families can read and listen to. Book Creator keeps text, images and recorded voices together on each page.

Students record and arrange short sounds for three puppet moments?an entrance, a problem and a celebration. This helps them work out how sound changes the mood and purpose of a performance. Groups exchange one sound sequence and invent a different puppet scene that matches what they hear. They then choose which sounds should be loud, soft, repeated or silent so the audience can follow the action. Each group finishes with a short soundtrack ready to accompany a live puppet show. GarageBand lets students record sounds and arrange them into a simple soundscape.

Students photograph and sort puppet-making items into material groups such as paper, fabric, wood and plastic, then train an image model to recognise the groups. This makes material choice something they can test rather than simply name. Groups challenge the model with crumpled, folded or partly hidden items and add better examples when it makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting systems in recycling facilities learn in a similar way by comparing new objects with many labelled examples. Students finish with a working classifier and a record of which materials were easiest or hardest for it to recognise. Teachable Machine trains a simple image-recognition model from student-provided examples.

Students draw several possible faces for the same puppet character, changing only the eyes, eyebrows and mouth. This helps them see how visual features can express feelings and make a performance easier to understand. Partners view the faces without being told the intended emotion and point to the one they can read most clearly. Students revise one face after hearing the partner's response, then design a matching backdrop for that moment in the story. Each student finishes with a clear puppet-face design sheet and one performance backdrop. Sketchbook's drawing tools let students test, erase and refine small expressive details.

Students follow Empathise?Define?Ideate?Prototype?Test to make a puppet that a Year 1 partner can operate easily and understand from the back of the room. They prototype with cardboard, paper fasteners, fabric scraps, craft sticks, string, straws and recycled packaging, focusing first on a reliable mouth, limb or rod mechanism. After each test performance, the audience names one movement they could read clearly and one part that was difficult to control. Students strengthen joins, change handle lengths or simplify moving parts, then use Seesaw photos and voice recordings to compare the first and final prototypes. They finish by demonstrating the improved mechanism in a short puppet performance and explaining why one design change worked.

plannerText: The 'How We Express Ourselves' Year 1 unit explores how people use imagination and materials to express stories, ideas, and culture through performance, with a focus on puppetry. Students investigate different types of puppets, their materials, and cultural uses, and learn about the features and purposes of puppet performances. The unit emphasizes creative thinking, communication, and collaboration, culminating in students designing and making their own puppets and performing short shows, supported by digital and hands-on learning experiences.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Students enjoyed:

This was a successful unit that engaged students through hands-on
experiences and authentic inquiry. The incursion where students built
wooden cars was the highlight, with high levels of enjoyment and

?

Incursion ? building the wooden cars and using tools (hammer,

?  Making ramps

engagement. Testing the cars back in the classroom on different
surfaces using push and pull effectively consolidated their
understanding of how materials and forces influence movement.
Parent helpers were essential and will continue to be needed for this
activity.

A mid-unit provocation video on push and pull was also highly
effective, helping to reaffirm key concepts and spark further
discussion. Non-fiction texts supported the exploration of vocabulary
and deepened students? understanding of force and motion.

One area for improvement is around simple machines (pulley, wheel
and axle, lever). Although students explored models with STEM
supplies, we did not spend enough time investigating these concepts
creatively. Next year, we could provide loose parts and invite children
to design or transform them into simple machines to solve problems.
This would allow for more open-ended exploration within the Year 1
level.

In the future, it would also be valuable to incorporate the school's
Generation Genius subscription, particularly their videos and
exercises, as these would strengthen concept reinforcement. While
past units have involved real-life problem-solving linked to simple
machines, this was determined to be beyond the Year 1 curriculum at
this stage. Instead, focusing on foundational concepts of causation,
form, and function gave students a strong grounding in understanding
how movement occurs and how designs can be adapted and
improved.

Overall, this was a good unit with a balance of hands-on learning,
conceptual understanding and student engagement.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.
