REFLECTING

?  The students have thoroughly enjoyed learning about invertebrates.
They engaged positively in all learning experiences and thoroughly
enjoyed the incursions and excursion.

?  They are now noticing them everywhere both in the classroom

and outdoors during play. They catch them in the bug catchers and
are eager to share their findings with their peers!

?  Many students have taken action by photographing invertebrates
they spot after school, bringing in pupa's they have found, and
sharing books or resources from home.

?  Students have been eager to discuss their discoveries and have

asked numerous thoughtful questions.

?  Even other JS students have joined in, excitedly sharing that they

found slaters reproducing in their playground.

?  The unit ran very well. Students were highly engaged, curious,

and developed a strong appreciation for invertebrates.

?  Having the full term and placing this unit at the end of the year
supported deeper thinking and the development of research
skills using non-fiction texts.

Learning Engagements:

?  The independent research task was very successful: students
used a template to collect information and produced a well-
structured information report.

?  Students enjoyed being ?experts? and sharing their findings

with Year 2 students and Year 1 peers.

?  Cross-class pairing supported collaboration while maintaining

individual accountability.

?  Labelled diagrams were excellent, and saving videos on

Seesaw will support future learning.

Incursion & Guest Speakers:

?  The incursion (Animals of Oz) was an effective provocation
that sparked student curiosity, even with more ?look at? than
?hands-on? opportunities.

?  Guest speakers (worms and waterbugs) added meaningful

depth, and student reflections captured key learning. It would
be great if Donna and Julie could visit again next year. We
should also look into inviting more ?experts? in to discuss
invertebrates.

 Excursion ? Melbourne Museum:

?  Bugs Alive strongly supported the unit; however, time was
limited due to the IMAX and teacher-led session. Focusing
solely on this exhibit (do not visit any others) and visiting IMAX
next year may be more effective.

?  The IMAX film was visually impressive but frightening for some

students due to the scale of the insects.

?  The staff-led session did not add new content and felt

repetitive. However, this may be due to when we visited (near
the end of the unit). This excursion should be mid-term if
possible.

inquiry. The structure, timing and sequence of learning engagements
supported both content understanding and ATL skill development.

Initial Reflection

PK:
Teachers establish the prior knowledge of the children in this cohort to establish focus and purpose for the unit. This is done by observing the
children at work and at play in the early days. Ascertain how they are able to notice, regulate and manage emotions. What strategies do they use to
manage conflict independently? What strategies do they use to manage their feelings?
IR:
Children would benefit from some focused time looking at the Colour Monsters. Our high EALD population means many of the children also
struggle to name emotions. More time spent sorting feelings words, using words in sentences and attaching them to different colour monsters
would be useful to support their emotional literacy.
Early Term 1, the children are very reluctant to try to resolve conflict at playtimes with any independence. Teaching them the Wheel of Choice and
the five-finger strategy have been done in early stages to support learning.

Transdisciplinary Connections

Visual Art: Students will use the visual elements of colour, line, shape, and form to create a paper sculpture that expresses a specific emotion or
feeling. By experimenting with bold lines, dynamic shapes, and expressive colours, students will explore how these elements can convey complex
emotional experiences. The sculptures will show their understanding of these foundational art concepts but also offer a personal and creative
interpretation of emotions, allowing each piece to resonate with individual meaning and artistic style.

supported students to name and recognise emotions in themselves and others ? a foundational skill explored through a follow-up Seesaw task. To
deepen their understanding of emotions, we also shared In My Heart by Jo Witek, using its vivid imagery to celebrate how recognising our feelings
helps us connect and relate to those around us.

listened to a range of music, considering how the music made them feel.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had
access to these historical toys otherwise. The pre- and post-incursion
resources were highly effective in frontloading student understanding and
supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of
the past compared to the present.

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students
frequently engaged with the texts during independent reading and inquiry
time, helping them make connections to key concepts in an age-appropriate
and accessible way.

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,
was a wonderful bridge between home and school. It helped ground the unit
in personal experience and gave students insight into family history in a
meaningful, relevant context.

For next year, it would be beneficial to begin with the HASS curriculum to
ensure clear alignment and deepen the focus on historical inquiry. Mapping
outcomes early on will help refine assessment and integrate the UOI more
closely with our required learning areas.

ci: Communities work together by creating systems to help people live and learn.
lo: The roles people play in a community; Systems and routines that help us stay organised; How communities work together to meet needs

s.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to carry messages, supplies and people between places on a floor map of a community. They see that communities need clear routes, ordered steps and different roles to meet people's needs. Groups swap maps and try to follow one another's systems without receiving extra instructions. When a route fails, students change the sequence and test it again. They finish with a working community map and a set of coded routes. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make each planned step visible and easy to debug.

Students answer a short picture-based survey about classroom jobs, routines and the people who help them learn. The responses show how a group can collect information before deciding what its community needs. The class chooses one routine to improve after reading the automatic charts together. Students then repeat the survey after trying the new routine for several days. They finish with before-and-after charts showing whether their decision helped. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and creates charts automatically.

Students photograph an everyday classroom object and record it explaining the job it does within a routine. This helps them notice that systems depend on people, objects and steps working together. A partner listens and asks what would happen if that object or step disappeared. Students revise their explanation so it includes the role, the routine and the need being met. They finish with a collection of short talking images for another Year 1 class. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and a recorded voice to each photograph.

Students build a shared picture map showing how a school need is met, such as borrowing a library book or getting help in the playground. They connect people, places, objects and steps to show that one action often depends on another. Groups remove one part of another group's map and ask them to work out what would stop working. Students reorganise the map until the pathway is clear to someone who has never followed it. They finish with a visual system map that can guide a new student. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes.

Students record themselves carrying out one classroom routine and explain each step as they go. This makes the purpose of routines visible instead of treating them as rules to memorise. Another class watches the entries and identifies any step that needs a clearer explanation. Students record an improved version that includes who is responsible and what need the routine meets. They finish with a student-made collection of practical routine guides. Seesaw keeps the videos, voice and reflections together in each student's journal.

Students empathise by watching how classmates move through a busy routine, then define one problem such as crowding at bag storage or confusion at a resource station. Teams ideate and build a physical system from cardboard, recycled containers, labels, paper arrows and cup-and-string signals. They prototype the layout, use the Insta360 camera to capture the whole space during a test, and review the spherical recording to spot queues or missed signs. Students move, rebuild or relabel parts and test the system again with a different group. They finish by demonstrating a working routine and explaining how their changes help the community meet a need.

plannerText: The 'How We Organise Ourselves' Year 1 unit focuses on understanding how communities function through systems, roles, and routines. Students explore the roles people play, the systems that help us stay organised, and how communities work together to meet needs. The unit integrates English, Maths, and Digital Technologies, with hands-on activities like mapping, poster creation, and collaborative builds. Emphasis is placed on inquiry, communication, and social skills, using both digital and physical tools to help students understand and represent community systems in age-appropriate, engaging ways.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Students enjoyed:

This was a successful unit that engaged students through hands-on
experiences and authentic inquiry. The incursion where students built
wooden cars was the highlight, with high levels of enjoyment and

?

Incursion ? building the wooden cars and using tools (hammer,
nails & pliers)
?  Making ramps

 ?  Building the simple machines

engagement. Testing the cars back in the classroom on different
surfaces using push and pull effectively consolidated their
understanding of how materials and forces influence movement.
Parent helpers were essential and will continue to be needed for this
activity.

A mid-unit provocation video on push and pull was also highly
effective, helping to reaffirm key concepts and spark further
discussion. Non-fiction texts supported the exploration of vocabulary
and deepened students? understanding of force and motion.

One area for improvement is around simple machines (pulley, wheel
and axle, lever). Although students explored models with STEM
supplies, we did not spend enough time investigating these concepts
creatively. Next year, we could provide loose parts and invite children
to design or transform them into simple machines to solve problems.
This would allow for more open-ended exploration within the Year 1
level.

In the future, it would also be valuable to incorporate the school's
Generation Genius subscription, particularly their videos and
exercises, as these would strengthen concept reinforcement. While
past units have involved real-life problem-solving linked to simple
machines, this was determined to be beyond the Year 1 curriculum at
this stage. Instead, focusing on foundational concepts of causation,
form, and function gave students a strong grounding in understanding
how movement occurs and how designs can be adapted and
improved.

Overall, this was a good unit with a balance of hands-on learning,
conceptual understanding and student engagement.

Also need to buy different materials to build ramps ? plastic, perspex,
materials and fabric, etc.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had
access to these historical toys otherwise. The pre- and post-incursion
resources were highly effective in frontloading student understanding and
supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of
the past compared to the present.

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students
frequently engaged with the texts during independent reading and inquiry
time, helping them make connections to key concepts in an age-appropriate
and accessible way.

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,
was a wonderful bridge between home and school. It helped ground the unit
in personal experience and gave students insight into family history in a
meaningful, relevant context.

For next year, it would be beneficial to begin with the HASS curriculum to
ensure clear alignment and deepen the focus on historical inquiry. Mapping
outcomes early on will help refine assessment and integrate the UOI more
closely with our required learning areas.

Assessment Reflections

The Venn diagram was a simple yet effective way to determine if students could distinguish between old and new toys. They had to consider the
materials of the toy when determining if it was old or new.

ci: Movement is dependent on different forces.
lo: Ways objects move; The influence different materials have on movement; How designs can be adapted and improved

s.d: Students record balls, toy cars and blocks moving down ramps, then replay each action in slow motion. They look closely for the moment a push begins, speed changes or friction slows an object. Groups swap ramp surfaces and challenge one another to explain why the same object moves differently. Students pause the footage at key moments and measure the distance travelled during repeated tests. They end with a set of slow-motion clips and spoken explanations comparing force, surface and movement. Slow-motion replay makes changes that happen too quickly for young eyes easy to see and discuss.

Students measure how far a toy car travels from the same ramp across carpet, cardboard, foil and fabric. They enter each distance into a teacher-prepared Excel table and repeat every test three times. Each group chooses one surface they predict would help a delivery vehicle travel safely rather than simply travel furthest. Students compare the results across the class and look for patterns or surprising measurements. They end with a table and column graph showing how materials influence movement. Excel turns repeated measurements into clear graphs that Year 1 students can read together.

Students photograph examples of rolling, sliding and spinning objects, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images into those three movement groups. This helps them test whether movement types can be recognised from visible clues. Groups exchange unusual examples, such as a rolling cylinder or spinning coin, to find out where the model becomes confused. Similar image recognition helps automated systems sort objects by what a camera can see, including camera-driven sorting machines in recycling facilities. Students end with a working image model and a list of examples it sorted correctly or incorrectly. Teachable Machine lets them add new training images and test whether those examples improve the model.

Students program an object to move after a character gives it a push or pull. They change the number and direction of movement blocks to show a gentle force and a stronger force. Partners swap projects and work out which force each animation represents before hearing the creator's explanation. Students then debug one sequence so the object stops, changes direction or travels a different distance. They end with a short coded animation that shows how changing a force changes movement. ScratchJr's movement blocks make direction and distance visible as a sequence young students can adjust.

Students record a puppet show in which two characters test a moving toy on different surfaces and disagree about which design works best. They explain pushes, pulls and friction through the characters' conversation using evidence from classroom ramp tests. Another pair watches the first version and suggests one design change for the characters to try. Students record a revised ending that explains whether larger wheels, a smoother surface or a changed ramp improved the movement. They end with a narrated puppet show containing a test, evidence and an improved design. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one simple scene-making tool.

Students use Sketchbook during an Empathise-Define-Ideate-Prototype-Test cycle to plan a moving toy for a younger child who needs it to travel slowly and stop safely. They sketch labelled ideas before building with cardboard, bottle tops, skewers, straws, rubber bands, masking tape and other recycled materials. Teams prototype a ramp, wheeled toy or pull mechanism, then test it on carpet, cardboard and fabric while changing only one feature at a time. After each test, they mark improvements directly on their design sketch and rebuild the physical model. Students finish by demonstrating how their final design uses push, pull or friction more successfully than their first prototype.

plannerText: The Year 1 'How the World Works' unit explores movement, forces, and simple machines through hands-on inquiry. Students investigate how objects move, the influence of different materials and surfaces, and how designs can be adapted and improved. Learning experiences include building and testing ramps, sorting objects by movement type, designing moving toys, and reflecting on the role of force in everyday life. The unit emphasizes science concepts (push, pull, friction), measurement, and design, with strong links to English and Maths. Students use a mix of physical materials and digital tools to record, reflect, and share their learning, fostering creative thinking, collaboration, and communication.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Students enjoyed:

This was a successful unit that engaged students through hands-on
experiences and authentic inquiry. The incursion where students built
wooden cars was the highlight, with high levels of enjoyment and

?

Incursion ? building the wooden cars and using tools (hammer,
nails & pliers)
?  Making ramps

 ?  Building the simple machines

engagement. Testing the cars back in the classroom on different
surfaces using push and pull effectively consolidated their
understanding of how materials and forces influence movement.
Parent helpers were essential and will continue to be needed for this
activity.

A mid-unit provocation video on push and pull was also highly
effective, helping to reaffirm key concepts and spark further
discussion. Non-fiction texts supported the exploration of vocabulary
and deepened students? understanding of force and motion.

One area for improvement is around simple machines (pulley, wheel
and axle, lever). Although students explored models with STEM
supplies, we did not spend enough time investigating these concepts
creatively. Next year, we could provide loose parts and invite children
to design or transform them into simple machines to solve problems.
This would allow for more open-ended exploration within the Year 1
level.

In the future, it would also be valuable to incorporate the school's
Generation Genius subscription, particularly their videos and
exercises, as these would strengthen concept reinforcement. While
past units have involved real-life problem-solving linked to simple
machines, this was determined to be beyond the Year 1 curriculum at
this stage. Instead, focusing on foundational concepts of causation,
form, and function gave students a strong grounding in understanding
how movement occurs and how designs can be adapted and
improved.

Overall, this was a good unit with a balance of hands-on learning,
conceptual understanding and student engagement.

Also need to buy different materials to build ramps ? plastic, perspex,
materials and fabric, etc.

viewpoints.

?  Curiosity About the World - Learning about global puppetry traditions builds interest in other

cultures.

?  Community Involvement - Inviting families to share cultural puppet experiences would foster

intercultural understanding.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

?  The students have thoroughly enjoyed learning about invertebrates.
They engaged positively in all learning experiences and thoroughly
enjoyed the incursions and excursion.

?  They are now noticing them everywhere both in the classroom

and outdoors during play. They catch them in the bug catchers and
are eager to share their findings with their peers!

?  Many students have taken action by photographing invertebrates
they spot after school, bringing in pupa's they have found, and
sharing books or resources from home.

?  Students have been eager to discuss their discoveries and have

asked numerous thoughtful questions.

?  Even other JS students have joined in, excitedly sharing that they

found slaters reproducing in their playground.

?  The unit ran very well. Students were highly engaged, curious,

and developed a strong appreciation for invertebrates.

?  Having the full term and placing this unit at the end of the year
supported deeper thinking and the development of research
skills using non-fiction texts.

Learning Engagements:

?  The independent research task was very successful: students
used a template to collect information and produced a well-
structured information report.

?  Students enjoyed being ?experts? and sharing their findings

with Year 2 students and Year 1 peers.

?  Cross-class pairing supported collaboration while maintaining

individual accountability.

?  Labelled diagrams were excellent, and saving videos on

Seesaw will support future learning.

Incursion & Guest Speakers:

?  The incursion (Animals of Oz) was an effective provocation
that sparked student curiosity, even with more ?look at? than
?hands-on? opportunities.

?  Guest speakers (worms and waterbugs) added meaningful

depth, and student reflections captured key learning. It would
be great if Donna and Julie could visit again next year. We
should also look into inviting more ?experts? in to discuss
invertebrates.

 Excursion ? Melbourne Museum:

?  Bugs Alive strongly supported the unit; however, time was
limited due to the IMAX and teacher-led session. Focusing
solely on this exhibit (do not visit any others) and visiting IMAX
next year may be more effective.

?  The IMAX film was visually impressive but frightening for some

students due to the scale of the insects.

?  The staff-led session did not add new content and felt

repetitive. However, this may be due to when we visited (near
the end of the unit). This excursion should be mid-term if
possible.

Overall: A successful unit with strong learning across all three lines of
inquiry. The structure, timing and sequence of learning engagements
supported both content understanding and ATL skill development.

Assessment Reflections:

?  Labelled diagrams were detailed and clearly presented, demonstrating a strong understanding of invertebrate features.
?  Research skills showed solid progress. Most students could independently respond to FORM-based questions, while many required support

?

to take notes connected to the CONNECTION and CHANGE lines of inquiry.
Information reports were well structured and informative. Explicit modelling of each section contributed significantly to the quality of the final
pieces.

?  Seesaw portfolio tasks were uploaded in real time and effectively captured students? learning focus at each stage of the unit.

Initial Reflection

PK:
Teachers establish the prior knowledge of the children in this cohort to establish focus and purpose for the unit. This is done by observing the
children at work and at play in the early days. Ascertain how they are able to notice, regulate and manage emotions. What strategies do they use to
manage conflict independently? What strategies do they use to manage their feelings?
IR:
Children would benefit from some focused time looking at the Colour Monsters. Our high EALD population means many of the children also
struggle to name emotions. More time spent sorting feelings words, using words in sentences and attaching them to different colour monsters
would be useful to support their emotional literacy.
Early Term 1, the children are very reluctant to try to resolve conflict at playtimes with any independence. Teaching them the Wheel of Choice and
the five-finger strategy have been done in early stages to support learning.

Transdisciplinary Connections

Visual Art: Students will use the visual elements of colour, line, shape, and form to create a paper sculpture that expresses a specific emotion or
feeling. By experimenting with bold lines, dynamic shapes, and expressive colours, students will explore how these elements can convey complex
emotional experiences. The sculptures will show their understanding of these foundational art concepts but also offer a personal and creative
interpretation of emotions, allowing each piece to resonate with individual meaning and artistic style.

Library ? In Library, students explored the theme of emotional wellbeing through stories about feelings, empathy, and friendship. Boy by Phil
Cummings sparked discussion about empathy and how understanding others? feelings can resolve conflicts, while The Way I Feel by Janan Cain
supported students to name and recognise emotions in themselves and others ? a foundational skill explored through a follow-up Seesaw task. To
deepen their understanding of emotions, we also shared In My Heart by Jo Witek, using its vivid imagery to celebrate how recognising our feelings
helps us connect and relate to those around us.

Music:: Behaviours necessary for ensemble playing ? taking turns, waiting, listening, musically linking with the group. Throughout the year, students also
listened to a range of music, considering how the music made them feel.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had

supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,

ci: Invertebrates are essential to living things and the environment.
lo: The characteristics of invertebrates; The interdependence of invertebrates and their environment; Life cycles of invertebrates

s.d: Students photograph invertebrates in the school grounds and use Seek by iNaturalist to suggest what each one might be. This helps them notice that many small animals support the environment around them. Pairs compare each suggestion with visible features such as wings, legs, body segments and shells before accepting it. Each pair chooses one identification that they can support with the clearest visual evidence. The class ends with a checked list of invertebrates living in different school microhabitats. Seek's camera-based identification gives students an immediate suggestion to question rather than simply accept.

Students sort close-up invertebrate photos into a PicCollage grid and add short labels for features such as six legs, no legs, wings or shell. This makes classification visible and helps children explain why animals belong in different groups. Partners swap collages and move one photograph they think has been placed incorrectly. The original creators then decide whether to keep or change their sorting and explain their choice. Students finish with a labelled visual classification chart for the classroom display. PicCollage's grids, images and captions keep the comparison clear for young readers.

Students watch a short ClickView clip about worms, bees or other invertebrates and pause whenever an animal helps another living thing. This shows how pollination, decomposition and food chains depend on small animals. Groups choose the most important moment and explain what might change if that invertebrate disappeared. Another group listens and checks whether the explanation includes both the animal and its environment. Students finish with a completed set of responses to key moments in the clip. ClickView's curated videos and built-in questions support focused viewing rather than passive watching.

Students enter class counts of invertebrates observed in places such as leaf litter, garden beds and open paths into Microsoft Excel. This helps them compare where different invertebrates are found and what those places provide. Pairs choose whether a column graph or picture-supported chart makes the pattern easiest for Year 1 students to read. They exchange charts and ask one question that can be answered from the data. Students finish with a graph showing which microhabitat held the most or fewest invertebrates. Excel turns the class counts into charts that make patterns easier to spot.

Students build the stages of a butterfly, beetle or snail life cycle from clay and photograph each small change in Stop Motion Studio. This makes growth and change visible instead of showing the stages as separate facts. Groups swap unfinished animations and ask another group to work out which stage should come next. Students revise any unclear movement, add the missing stage and check that the sequence repeats correctly. They finish with a short stop-motion life cycle film for a Prep buddy class. Stop Motion Studio joins frame-by-frame photographs so gradual changes appear to happen on screen.

Students empathise with a garden invertebrate by observing what it needs, then define the problem of reaching food and shelter without crossing hazards. They ideate and build a large floor habitat from cardboard, leaves, recycled packaging, paper flowers and bottle-cap water sources. Teams prototype a safe route by placing habitat features on the mat and programming a Bee-Bot with directional button presses. They test the route, notice wrong turns or missing resources, then move materials or change the programmed sequence. Each team demonstrates a revised habitat route and explains how its design supports the invertebrate's survival.

plannerText: The Year 1 'Sharing the Planet' unit focuses on invertebrates, exploring their characteristics, life cycles, and the ways they interact with and support the environment. Students investigate through hands-on inquiry, research, and creative expression, building understanding of classification, interdependence, and change. The unit emphasizes observation, data collection, and communication skills, with strong links to science, English, and mathematics. Learning experiences include incursions, excursions, digital research, drawing, and collaborative projects, all designed to foster curiosity, care for living things, and foundational research skills.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

?  The students have thoroughly enjoyed learning about invertebrates.
They engaged positively in all learning experiences and thoroughly
enjoyed the incursions and excursion.

?  They are now noticing them everywhere both in the classroom

and outdoors during play. They catch them in the bug catchers and
are eager to share their findings with their peers!

?  Many students have taken action by photographing invertebrates
they spot after school, bringing in pupa's they have found, and
sharing books or resources from home.

?  Students have been eager to discuss their discoveries and have

asked numerous thoughtful questions.

?  Even other JS students have joined in, excitedly sharing that they

found slaters reproducing in their playground.

?  The unit ran very well. Students were highly engaged, curious,

and developed a strong appreciation for invertebrates.

?  Having the full term and placing this unit at the end of the year
supported deeper thinking and the development of research
skills using non-fiction texts.

Learning Engagements:

?  The independent research task was very successful: students
used a template to collect information and produced a well-
structured information report.

?  Students enjoyed being ?experts? and sharing their findings

with Year 2 students and Year 1 peers.

?  Cross-class pairing supported collaboration while maintaining

individual accountability.

?  Labelled diagrams were excellent, and saving videos on

Seesaw will support future learning.

Incursion & Guest Speakers:

?  The incursion (Animals of Oz) was an effective provocation
that sparked student curiosity, even with more ?look at? than
?hands-on? opportunities.

?  Guest speakers (worms and waterbugs) added meaningful

depth, and student reflections captured key learning. It would
be great if Donna and Julie could visit again next year. We
should also look into inviting more ?experts? in to discuss
invertebrates.

 Excursion ? Melbourne Museum:

?  Bugs Alive strongly supported the unit; however, time was
limited due to the IMAX and teacher-led session. Focusing
solely on this exhibit (do not visit any others) and visiting IMAX
next year may be more effective.

?  The IMAX film was visually impressive but frightening for some

students due to the scale of the insects.

?  The staff-led session did not add new content and felt

repetitive. However, this may be due to when we visited (near
the end of the unit). This excursion should be mid-term if
possible.

Overall: A successful unit with strong learning across all three lines of
inquiry. The structure, timing and sequence of learning engagements
supported both content understanding and ATL skill development.

Assessment Reflections:

?  Labelled diagrams were detailed and clearly presented, demonstrating a strong understanding of invertebrate features.
?  Research skills showed solid progress. Most students could independently respond to FORM-based questions, while many required support

?

to take notes connected to the CONNECTION and CHANGE lines of inquiry.
Information reports were well structured and informative. Explicit modelling of each section contributed significantly to the quality of the final
pieces.

?  Seesaw portfolio tasks were uploaded in real time and effectively captured students? learning focus at each stage of the unit.

Initial Reflection

PK:
Teachers establish the prior knowledge of the children in this cohort to establish focus and purpose for the unit. This is done by observing the
children at work and at play in the early days. Ascertain how they are able to notice, regulate and manage emotions. What strategies do they use to
manage conflict independently? What strategies do they use to manage their feelings?
IR:
Children would benefit from some focused time looking at the Colour Monsters. Our high EALD population means many of the children also
struggle to name emotions. More time spent sorting feelings words, using words in sentences and attaching them to different colour monsters
would be useful to support their emotional literacy.
Early Term 1, the children are very reluctant to try to resolve conflict at playtimes with any independence. Teaching them the Wheel of Choice and
the five-finger strategy have been done in early stages to support learning.

Transdisciplinary Connections

Visual Art: Students will use the visual elements of colour, line, shape, and form to create a paper sculpture that expresses a specific emotion or
feeling. By experimenting with bold lines, dynamic shapes, and expressive colours, students will explore how these elements can convey complex
emotional experiences. The sculptures will show their understanding of these foundational art concepts but also offer a personal and creative
interpretation of emotions, allowing each piece to resonate with individual meaning and artistic style.

Library ? In Library, students explored the theme of emotional wellbeing through stories about feelings, empathy, and friendship. Boy by Phil
Cummings sparked discussion about empathy and how understanding others? feelings can resolve conflicts, while The Way I Feel by Janan Cain
supported students to name and recognise emotions in themselves and others ? a foundational skill explored through a follow-up Seesaw task. To
deepen their understanding of emotions, we also shared In My Heart by Jo Witek, using its vivid imagery to celebrate how recognising our feelings
helps us connect and relate to those around us.

Music:: Behaviours necessary for ensemble playing ? taking turns, waiting, listening, musically linking with the group. Throughout the year, students also
listened to a range of music, considering how the music made them feel.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had
access to these historical toys otherwise. The pre- and post-incursion
resources were highly effective in frontloading student understanding and
supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of
the past compared to the present.

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students
frequently engaged with the texts during independent reading and inquiry
time, helping them make connections to key concepts in an age-appropriate
and accessible way.

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,
was a wonderful bridge between home and school. It helped ground the unit
in personal experience and gave students insight into family history in a
meaningful, relevant context.

For next year, it would be beneficial to begin with the HASS curriculum to
ensure clear alignment and deepen the focus on historical inquiry. Mapping
outcomes early on will help refine assessment and integrate the UOI more
closely with our required learning areas.

 We could also look at this (possibly a line of inquiry):

how these have changed or remained the same over time

s.d: Students photograph an old toy or childhood object and record it explaining how children once used it. Hearing the object speak makes changes in play, materials and technology easy to understand. Students swap objects and check whether each recording includes a clear reason why life changed. They then play the talking objects to family members and ask what memory each one brings back. Each student ends with a short talking-object recording grounded in historical evidence. ChatterPix Kids makes this possible by adding a moving mouth and recorded voice to one photo.

Students help build a family survey about toys, school, chores and communication during childhood. Responses from parents and grandparents show how children's lives have changed and why some changes happened. Before viewing the results, students predict which experiences will show change and which will show continuity. They compare their predictions with the automatically collected class responses. The class ends with real charts showing patterns across several generations. Microsoft Forms gathers responses and turns them into automatic charts.

Students arrange coloured tiles to make Indi travel from an old childhood object to its modern version. Changing the tile sequence helps them see that inventions develop through a series of changes rather than one sudden leap. Partners swap routes, follow the visual story and explain why each object may have changed. Students revise any route where the historical sequence is unclear or Indi does not reach the correct object. Each pair ends with a working floor route that shows change over time. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen.

Students paint the same child's play space in the past and in a possible future. Their choices show how new materials, needs and technologies can change children's lives while some kinds of play continue. Students show their paintings to another class without revealing which details belong to each time and listen to what viewers notice. They then adjust one detail so the reason for change is clearer. Each student ends with a layered digital painting that can reveal past and future versions of the scene. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting on separate layers.

Students capture a 360-degree view of a classroom display arranged with old and new toys, school items and household objects. Looking in every direction helps them notice relationships between objects rather than studying each item alone. Students decide where each object should sit so viewers can move visually from past to present and then towards the future. Another class explores the image and identifies one change, one reason for change and one thing that has continued. The class ends with an immersive 360-degree view of children's lives across time. The Insta360 camera records the whole surrounding space in one spherical image.

Students empathise with Prep children who need a hands-on way to understand how toys have changed, then define what their teaching mat must show. They sketch several routes and build old, present and imagined future toy stations from cardboard, paper, fabric, recycled packaging and LEGO. Students place the stations on a large paper grid, program Bee-Bot's moves in advance and test whether it lands on them in historical order. They revise the spacing, route or sequence whenever Bee-Bot misses a station or the story is unclear. Each group demonstrates a tested physical prototype and explains why each toy changed before sending Bee-Bot to the next station.

plannerText: The Year 1 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit explores how understanding history helps us see how the past shapes the future. Students investigate ways children's lives have changed over time, reasons for these changes, and the role of technology, play, and artefacts. The unit emphasises concepts of causation, change, and continuity, using hands-on provocations (like artefacts and toys), interviews with family, and creative tasks to build historical thinking. Students compare old and new, sequence events, and reflect on how their own lives connect to broader historical changes.

engagement. Testing the cars back in the classroom on different
surfaces using push and pull effectively consolidated their
understanding of how materials and forces influence movement.
Parent helpers were essential and will continue to be needed for this
activity.

A mid-unit provocation video on push and pull was also highly
effective, helping to reaffirm key concepts and spark further
discussion. Non-fiction texts supported the exploration of vocabulary
and deepened students? understanding of force and motion.

One area for improvement is around simple machines (pulley, wheel
and axle, lever). Although students explored models with STEM
supplies, we did not spend enough time investigating these concepts
creatively. Next year, we could provide loose parts and invite children

past units have involved real-life problem-solving linked to simple
machines, this was determined to be beyond the Year 1 curriculum at
this stage. Instead, focusing on foundational concepts of causation,
form, and function gave students a strong grounding in understanding
how movement occurs and how designs can be adapted and
improved.

Overall, this was a good unit with a balance of hands-on learning,

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.

Student Reflections

REFLECTING

?  The students have thoroughly enjoyed learning about invertebrates.
They engaged positively in all learning experiences and thoroughly
enjoyed the incursions and excursion.

?  They are now noticing them everywhere both in the classroom

and outdoors during play. They catch them in the bug catchers and
are eager to share their findings with their peers!

?  Many students have taken action by photographing invertebrates
they spot after school, bringing in pupa's they have found, and
sharing books or resources from home.

?  Students have been eager to discuss their discoveries and have

asked numerous thoughtful questions.

?  Even other JS students have joined in, excitedly sharing that they

found slaters reproducing in their playground.

?  The unit ran very well. Students were highly engaged, curious,

and developed a strong appreciation for invertebrates.

?  Having the full term and placing this unit at the end of the year
supported deeper thinking and the development of research
skills using non-fiction texts.

Learning Engagements:

?  The independent research task was very successful: students
used a template to collect information and produced a well-
structured information report.

?  Students enjoyed being ?experts? and sharing their findings

with Year 2 students and Year 1 peers.

?  Cross-class pairing supported collaboration while maintaining

individual accountability.

?  Labelled diagrams were excellent, and saving videos on

Seesaw will support future learning.

Incursion & Guest Speakers:

?  The incursion (Animals of Oz) was an effective provocation
that sparked student curiosity, even with more ?look at? than
?hands-on? opportunities.

?  Guest speakers (worms and waterbugs) added meaningful

depth, and student reflections captured key learning. It would
be great if Donna and Julie could visit again next year. We
should also look into inviting more ?experts? in to discuss
invertebrates.

 Excursion ? Melbourne Museum:

?  Bugs Alive strongly supported the unit; however, time was
limited due to the IMAX and teacher-led session. Focusing
solely on this exhibit (do not visit any others) and visiting IMAX
next year may be more effective.

?  The IMAX film was visually impressive but frightening for some

students due to the scale of the insects.

?  The staff-led session did not add new content and felt

repetitive. However, this may be due to when we visited (near
the end of the unit). This excursion should be mid-term if
possible.

Overall: A successful unit with strong learning across all three lines of
inquiry. The structure, timing and sequence of learning engagements
supported both content understanding and ATL skill development.

?  Labelled diagrams were detailed and clearly presented, demonstrating a strong understanding of invertebrate features.

to take notes connected to the CONNECTION and CHANGE lines of inquiry.
Information reports were well structured and informative. Explicit modelling of each section contributed significantly to the quality of the final
pieces.

Initial Reflection

PK:
Teachers establish the prior knowledge of the children in this cohort to establish focus and purpose for the unit. This is done by observing the
children at work and at play in the early days. Ascertain how they are able to notice, regulate and manage emotions. What strategies do they use to
manage conflict independently? What strategies do they use to manage their feelings?
IR:
Children would benefit from some focused time looking at the Colour Monsters. Our high EALD population means many of the children also
struggle to name emotions. More time spent sorting feelings words, using words in sentences and attaching them to different colour monsters
would be useful to support their emotional literacy.
Early Term 1, the children are very reluctant to try to resolve conflict at playtimes with any independence. Teaching them the Wheel of Choice and
the five-finger strategy have been done in early stages to support learning.

Transdisciplinary Connections

Visual Art: Students will use the visual elements of colour, line, shape, and form to create a paper sculpture that expresses a specific emotion or
feeling. By experimenting with bold lines, dynamic shapes, and expressive colours, students will explore how these elements can convey complex
emotional experiences. The sculptures will show their understanding of these foundational art concepts but also offer a personal and creative
interpretation of emotions, allowing each piece to resonate with individual meaning and artistic style.

Library ? In Library, students explored the theme of emotional wellbeing through stories about feelings, empathy, and friendship. Boy by Phil
Cummings sparked discussion about empathy and how understanding others? feelings can resolve conflicts, while The Way I Feel by Janan Cain
supported students to name and recognise emotions in themselves and others ? a foundational skill explored through a follow-up Seesaw task. To
deepen their understanding of emotions, we also shared In My Heart by Jo Witek, using its vivid imagery to celebrate how recognising our feelings
helps us connect and relate to those around us.

Music:: Behaviours necessary for ensemble playing ? taking turns, waiting, listening, musically linking with the group. Throughout the year, students also
listened to a range of music, considering how the music made them feel.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had
access to these historical toys otherwise. The pre- and post-incursion
resources were highly effective in frontloading student understanding and
supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of
the past compared to the present.

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students
frequently engaged with the texts during independent reading and inquiry
time, helping them make connections to key concepts in an age-appropriate
and accessible way.

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,
was a wonderful bridge between home and school. It helped ground the unit
in personal experience and gave students insight into family history in a
meaningful, relevant context.

For next year, it would be beneficial to begin with the HASS curriculum to
ensure clear alignment and deepen the focus on historical inquiry. Mapping
outcomes early on will help refine assessment and integrate the UOI more
closely with our required learning areas.

 We could also look at this (possibly a line of inquiry):

how these have changed or remained the same over time
(AC9HS1K01)

materials of the toy when determining if it was old or new.
