ci: Emotions, values, and relationships guide how we connect and collaborate
lo: The function of different parts of the brain; Situations that cause pleasant and unpleasant feelings; Actions that support wellbeing

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a brain character explaining how one brain part helps with thoughts, feelings or actions. This shows that feelings and behaviour are guided by processes inside the brain. Partners swap characters and ask each other to add a helpful example from school life. Students choose the character, voice and situation that best explain their idea. They finish with a short talking character that can open a class discussion about emotions. The Animate from Audio feature automatically lip-syncs the character to each student's voice.

Students record short videos showing a pleasant or unpleasant feeling and one action that could help. This connects feelings with practical choices that support wellbeing. A partner watches each clip and suggests a second strategy the speaker could record. Students choose whether to explain breathing, asking for help, taking space or using kind words. They finish with a captioned collection of wellbeing reminders for the class. Apple Clips adds live captions, titles and stickers while students record.

Students film two versions of a playground disagreement?one where the problem grows and one where kind choices repair it. This makes the link between emotions, actions and relationships easy to see. Another pair watches the scenes and chooses which moment should be changed to improve the outcome. Students edit the strongest examples into a short film for a younger class. They finish with a clear before-and-after conflict-resolution film. iMovie lets them arrange clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students paint the same face twice to show how feelings can change before and after a wellbeing strategy. This helps them notice how colour, line and facial details can communicate pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Partners describe what they notice without guessing the story, then the artist adjusts any unclear details. Students choose a strategy such as movement, breathing, connection or quiet time to inspire the second image. They finish with a paired digital painting that shows an emotional change. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting on separate layers, so details can be refined without starting again.

Students build a personal book with pages for emotion words, body clues, common situations and helpful actions. This brings emotional literacy and self-management together in a resource they can revisit all year. Each student asks a classmate to contribute one kind sentence or calming idea to a page. Students decide which strategies genuinely work for them rather than copying one class answer. They finish with a narrated wellbeing book that can support reflection after real classroom challenges. Book Creator combines text, images, audio and video on each page.

Students empathise with a familiar friendship problem, then define one moment when a child needs help choosing what to do next. Using cardboard, paper, markers and recycled materials, they ideate and build floor tiles showing possible actions such as pause, breathe, speak kindly or ask for help. They prototype a pathway, program the Bee-Bot with directional buttons and test whether its sequence reaches a choice that supports wellbeing. Partners follow the route, explain how each action could affect the relationship and suggest one tile or step to change. Students revise the physical pathway and demonstrate a final programmed sequence that turns a difficult feeling into a safe, kind response.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' Year 1 unit is a yearlong inquiry into self, relationships, emotions, and wellbeing. Students explore how thoughts, feelings, and actions shape their relationships and overall health. The unit emphasises emotional literacy, self-management, empathy, and strategies for wellbeing through picture books, art, role play, and daily routines. Students learn to identify and name emotions, use strategies like the Wheel of Choice, and reflect on kindness and conflict resolution. The unit is highly play-based, with strong links to literacy, art, and social skills, and encourages student agency and reflection throughout the year.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Students enjoyed:

This was a successful unit that engaged students through hands-on
experiences and authentic inquiry. The incursion where students built
wooden cars was the highlight, with high levels of enjoyment and

?

Incursion ? building the wooden cars and using tools (hammer,
nails & pliers)
?  Making ramps

 ?  Building the simple machines

engagement. Testing the cars back in the classroom on different
surfaces using push and pull effectively consolidated their
understanding of how materials and forces influence movement.
Parent helpers were essential and will continue to be needed for this
activity.

A mid-unit provocation video on push and pull was also highly
effective, helping to reaffirm key concepts and spark further
discussion. Non-fiction texts supported the exploration of vocabulary
and deepened students? understanding of force and motion.

One area for improvement is around simple machines (pulley, wheel
and axle, lever). Although students explored models with STEM
supplies, we did not spend enough time investigating these concepts
creatively. Next year, we could provide loose parts and invite children
to design or transform them into simple machines to solve problems.
This would allow for more open-ended exploration within the Year 1
level.

In the future, it would also be valuable to incorporate the school's
Generation Genius subscription, particularly their videos and
exercises, as these would strengthen concept reinforcement. While
past units have involved real-life problem-solving linked to simple
machines, this was determined to be beyond the Year 1 curriculum at
this stage. Instead, focusing on foundational concepts of causation,
form, and function gave students a strong grounding in understanding
how movement occurs and how designs can be adapted and
improved.

Overall, this was a good unit with a balance of hands-on learning,
conceptual understanding and student engagement.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

Students were given voice and choice throughout the unit,
particularly in selecting their puppet characters, creating storylines
and designing how their performances would be presented. They
worked in collaborative groups, taking on roles and responsibilities
and made decisions together about dialogue, movement and
sound effects.

Opportunities to conference with the teacher, give and receive
peer feedback and reflect on their performance allowed students
to take ownership of their learning and identify areas for growth.

Students had the opportunity to conference with the teacher to discuss and
refine their puppet show ideas before rehearsing. They also performed a draft
version of their puppet performance for a peer group and received feedback
that was kind, helpful and-or specific to support improvement.

Following the final performance, students watched a recording of their puppet
show on SeeSaw and reflected on what they did well and what they could
improve next time.

REFLECTING

 Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

Students noted that they enjoyed:

?  The puppet show (incursion with Po Po)
?  Making the sock puppets
?  Free play with puppets
?  Creating and performing their puppet performance

This new unit has strong potential and offers rich opportunities for
storytelling, creativity and cultural exploration. Unfortunately, due
to a delayed start (ie. Because of book week), we missed some
time needed to fully develop key concepts particularly story
structure. Students made progress identifying characters, setting,
plot, and the beginning?middle?end format, but this needs further
reinforcement in future iterations.

The puppet-making incursion was a highlight well-pitched for the
students and ideally placed at the start of the unit. It served as
both a provocation and a hands-on learning experience. While we
could do puppet-making ourselves, having a facilitator elevated the
experience and takes the pressure of the teachers to source
materials and lead the lesson. Parent helpers were also essential
especially to man the hot glue guns!

Observing puppet shows (live and online) before creating their
own was critical. Students then used their handmade puppets in
group performances. Every group in 1CG included sound effects
or music, showing creativity and engagement. Performing in the
CMPS with microphones was effective and should be repeated.
Student puppet shows were shown to parents at the SLC ? this
was a great idea and parents enjoyed the show!

Next time, we should dedicate more time to exploring puppets
from different cultures and how they are used to share stories and
traditions. Inviting parents to share cultural perspectives could
enrich this line of inquiry and strengthen the concept of
connection. It would be also beneficial to spend some time looking
at shadow puppets ? students could make them and perform a
short puppet performance with them.

Looking ahead, integrating music, dance and drama specialist
sessions would further enhance the unit and support student

 expression through performance. Perhaps this could be done in
non-musical years.

It would be valuable for the school to invest in a wider range of
puppets to support this unit. While Michelle provided her own
collection of hand and finger puppets, it would greatly benefit
students if Wesley had access to a variety of puppet types such
as marionettes, rod puppets, shadow puppets, and others for
hands-on exploration and play.

Future idea ? building our own puppet theatre in the STEM room!

Assessment Reflections

 The puppet performance was an effective summative assessment that allowed students to demonstrate their understanding of story structure,
collaboration and performance. Using the story map template helped students organise their ideas clearly identifying characters, setting, problem,
and resolution. This scaffold supported their planning well, though next time, students could take it a step further to further develop the problem and
solution and or by writing a simple script to improve dialogue and sequencing.

During performances, students showed growth in voice projection and manipulating puppets, especially when using microphones in the CMPS.
These performance skills are developing well and should continue to be a focus.

Working in small groups also supported the development of collaboration skills, including turn-taking, idea sharing and compromise an essential
part of the learning process in this unit.

Teacher Reflections

During the community helpers partner research task, students were
given the opportunity to select both their partners and the community
helper they wished to explore. This supported the development of
student agencies. While research skills are still emerging, many
students require support to locate and interpret relevant information.
Further guided experiences using non-fiction texts to extract key facts
would be beneficial to strengthen their skills as inquirers. This could be
supported in library sessions alongside the UOIs. The social skills self-
reflection on SeeSaw was successful and allowed students to reflect
on being kind, listen to the ideas of their partner, take turns and share
the workload with their partner. A similar reflection could be used
again in Term 4.

Students are also developing their presentation skills, particularly by
creating informative posters. A model layout was demonstrated by
MCY, which many students used as a guide. While this scaffold
supported their success, additional opportunities to practise creating
and publishing posters independently would support the development
of confident communicators. Next time, students could complete a
self-reflection

Our integration of BeeBots provided a meaningful link between
Mathematics (directions and spatial awareness) and the UOI. Although
time constraints limited us from designing custom maps of a
community, students responded enthusiastically to the activity. Some
students demonstrated an ability to give and follow directions, but this
remains an area for continued development. The BeeBots are a highly
engaging and hands-on learning tool, supporting open-minded thinking

 and collaborative problem solving.

A highlight for this unit was constructing a paper model of a
community. This hands-on task engaged students deeply and required
them to collaborate and negotiate as they considered the placement of
different buildings and community spaces. The activity encouraged
social and self-management skills and allowed students to practise
being reflective and open-minded when working with others. It was
wonderful to see how thoughtfully and respectfully students worked
together to represent a functioning community.

and outdoors during play. They catch them in the bug catchers and
are eager to share their findings with their peers!

?  Many students have taken action by photographing invertebrates
they spot after school, bringing in pupa's they have found, and
sharing books or resources from home.

?  Students have been eager to discuss their discoveries and have

asked numerous thoughtful questions.

?  Even other JS students have joined in, excitedly sharing that they

found slaters reproducing in their playground.

?  The unit ran very well. Students were highly engaged, curious,

and developed a strong appreciation for invertebrates.

?  Having the full term and placing this unit at the end of the year
supported deeper thinking and the development of research
skills using non-fiction texts.

Learning Engagements:

?  The independent research task was very successful: students
used a template to collect information and produced a well-
structured information report.

?  Students enjoyed being ?experts? and sharing their findings

with Year 2 students and Year 1 peers.

?  Cross-class pairing supported collaboration while maintaining

individual accountability.

?  Labelled diagrams were excellent, and saving videos on

Seesaw will support future learning.

Incursion & Guest Speakers:

?  The incursion (Animals of Oz) was an effective provocation
that sparked student curiosity, even with more ?look at? than
?hands-on? opportunities.

?  Guest speakers (worms and waterbugs) added meaningful

depth, and student reflections captured key learning. It would
be great if Donna and Julie could visit again next year. We
should also look into inviting more ?experts? in to discuss
invertebrates.

 Excursion ? Melbourne Museum:

?  Bugs Alive strongly supported the unit; however, time was
limited due to the IMAX and teacher-led session. Focusing
solely on this exhibit (do not visit any others) and visiting IMAX
next year may be more effective.

?  The IMAX film was visually impressive but frightening for some

students due to the scale of the insects.

?  The staff-led session did not add new content and felt

repetitive. However, this may be due to when we visited (near
the end of the unit). This excursion should be mid-term if
possible.

Overall: A successful unit with strong learning across all three lines of
inquiry. The structure, timing and sequence of learning engagements
supported both content understanding and ATL skill development.

Teacher Reflections

This Unit of Inquiry was an enjoyable and engaging experience for both
students and teachers. One of the highlights was the incursion, which
provided an authentic and hands-on opportunity for students to explore toys
from the past. The incursion was essential? students would not have had
access to these historical toys otherwise. The pre- and post-incursion
resources were highly effective in frontloading student understanding and
supporting meaningful reflection afterward. This incursion is a definite must-
do again next year.

Students particularly loved the chance to play with and investigate a wide
variety of old-fashioned toys. Their curiosity and enthusiasm during this part
of the unit were evident, and it significantly deepened their understanding of
the past compared to the present.

The Epic collection of books was another popular resource. Students
frequently engaged with the texts during independent reading and inquiry
time, helping them make connections to key concepts in an age-appropriate
and accessible way.

The interview task, where students connected with parents or grandparents,
was a wonderful bridge between home and school. It helped ground the unit
in personal experience and gave students insight into family history in a
meaningful, relevant context.

For next year, it would be beneficial to begin with the HASS curriculum to
ensure clear alignment and deepen the focus on historical inquiry. Mapping
outcomes early on will help refine assessment and integrate the UOI more
closely with our required learning areas.

Assessment Reflections

The Venn diagram was a simple yet effective way to determine if students could distinguish between old and new toys. They had to consider the
materials of the toy when determining if it was old or new.

ci: Storytellers use different methods to convey meaning.
lo: Mediums and techniques artists use; Connections between story and illustrations; How ideas and information are communicated

s.d: Students build a frame-by-frame story showing the Moon changing shape across several nights. This shows how movement, sequence and viewpoint can communicate a sky pattern without a narrator. Pairs swap unfinished animations and work out whether the images alone make the meaning clear. They then adjust the timing, camera angle or placement of their paper Moon pieces after hearing the feedback. Each pair finishes with a short stop-motion film that turns scientific observations into a visual story. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame capture makes small changes appear as smooth movement.

Students draw the same night-sky event twice?once as a scientific diagram and once as an imaginative story illustration. Comparing the pictures helps them notice how colour, scale, labels and composition change the meaning. A partner views both images without an explanation and describes the message received from each one. Students revise one detail that caused confusion or made an important idea easy to miss. They finish with two polished digital illustrations and a clear visual connection between science and storytelling. Sketchbook's drawing tools support detailed lines, colour and original illustration.

Students record a short audio story about watching a sunrise, a changing Moon or a seasonal night sky. This lets them explore how voice, word choice, pauses and sound can convey meaning without illustrations. Each student records two different openings, and classmates choose which one makes them want to keep listening. They edit the chosen version so the science is clear and the mood matches the sky event. The class finishes with a collection of short sky stories for another Year 2 class to hear. Podcasting using Canva allows students to record and edit the complete audio story on an iPad.

Students record one daily sky observation in a class spreadsheet, such as daylight, cloud cover or whether the Moon was visible. This helps them see that tables and graphs can tell a true story about patterns over time. Small groups choose whether a column chart or line graph makes their pattern easiest for another class to understand. They compare choices and change any graph that gives a confusing message. The result is a set of graphs that show how the sky changed across the observation period. Excel turns the class data into charts that students can read, compare and discuss.

Students train an image model to sort their physical sky drawings into day, night and changing-Moon groups. This tests whether visual features such as colour, shape and position communicate the intended meaning clearly. Groups exchange drawings and test which images the model sorts correctly, then redraw examples that confuse it. Astronomers use related image-recognition systems to sort large collections of telescope images, although people still check the results. Students finish with a working classifier and a set of revised illustrations with clearer visual clues. Teachable Machine learns from the image examples students show through the camera.

Students empathise with younger children who need a clear way to follow a story about day, night and Moon phases, then define what each picture and movement must explain. Using cardboard, paper illustrations, recycled materials and a large floor grid, teams ideate and prototype a physical story path before placing the Bee-Bot on it. They program the directional buttons so the Bee-Bot visits each sky scene in the intended order, then test the route with classmates who identify any confusing step. Teams move pictures, shorten routes and debug the programmed sequence until movement and illustrations tell the same story. Each team demonstrates a tested physical story mat in which the Bee-Bot travels through an observable sky pattern.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

The Wonder Walk unit effectively engaged the students with the
history and identity of Wesley Glen Waverley. Through photographing
plaques, statues, and artefacts, students practiced observing evidence
and connecting it to the past.

 Our guest speakers, Erin added personal perspectives, helping
students see how school life and learning have changed over time.

The excursion to Como House was amazing and one to repeat, very
engaging and appropriate at introducing our lines of inquiry and central
idea.

Activities such as comparing historical and current images,
investigating artefacts, and completing the plaque timeline encouraged
students to think critically, ask questions, and make connections
between personal and school history. The visit to Campbell place also
gave students the opportunity to speak to older people to hear stories
from the past.

The culminating artefact project allowed students to express their
understanding creatively, with agency, while developing their reflection
and communication skills.

Overall, the unit successfully fostered curiosity, observation, and
historical thinking, while helping students appreciate the significance of
the school's heritage.

ci: A sequence of processes enables a system to function.
lo: The systems in our lives; The purpose of various systems; How systems are made of many interdependent parts

s.d: Students program a Beebot to travel through the steps of a familiar school system, such as borrowing a library book or ordering lunch. Each square on the floor mat represents one part that must happen in the correct order. Groups swap mats, run each other's programs and work out where a missing or misplaced step causes the system to fail. They then change one step and predict what the Beebot will do before pressing go. Students end with a tested floor map and a working sequence of commands. The directional buttons let them enter, clear and debug the route directly on the robot.

Students photograph or draw the parts of a classroom system and arrange them in order on a shared Freeform board. They connect the parts with arrows to show how people, objects and actions depend on one another. Another group removes or moves one part, then the original group explains what would stop working and repairs the sequence. Students can choose systems such as morning arrival, packing a school bag or returning sports equipment. They end with a visual map showing the system working, failing and being fixed. Freeform's open canvas makes it easy to move, group and connect each part.

Students record a sound for every step in a daily system, such as washing hands, preparing for lunch or packing up the classroom. They place the sounds in sequence so a listener can work out the process without seeing it. Pairs exchange recordings, identify any unclear or missing step and suggest one change. Students then reorder or rerecord sounds until another pair can follow the whole process correctly. They end with a short sound sequence that has a clear beginning, middle and end. GarageBand lets them record and arrange each sound on a timeline.

Students build a short class survey about how people complete a familiar process, such as getting ready for school. They ask which step happens first, which parts are sometimes missed and what happens when the order changes. Another Year 2 class completes the survey, giving students real examples that may differ from their own routines. Students read the automatic charts and work out which steps are common and which vary between families. They end with a survey and a set of charts that show how one purpose can be reached through different sequences. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and displays simple response charts.

Students build a tabletop model of a system and photograph one small movement at a time to show its process. They might animate a note travelling through the school office, a book moving through the library system or rubbish reaching the correct bin. Groups deliberately make a second version with one part missing, then ask classmates to spot where the system breaks down. After receiving feedback, they add or reorder frames to repair the process. Students end with two short animations showing a system failing and functioning. Stop Motion Studio joins the individual frames into a clear moving sequence.

Students empathise by watching where classroom deliveries, such as notes or returned books, become slow or confusing, then define one route that needs improvement. Using cardboard buildings, recycled containers, paper signs and Indi's coloured tiles, groups sketch ideas and build a physical delivery system with clear stops. They prototype a route by placing the tiles, then test whether Indi travels to each stop in the intended order. When Indi turns too early, misses a destination or takes an inefficient path, students move tiles or rebuild parts and test again. Each group demonstrates its improved system and explains how every tile, pathway and stop helps the whole route function.

plannerText: The 'How We Organise Ourselves' Year 2 unit explores the concept of systems in daily life, focusing on how processes are made up of interdependent steps that work together to achieve a purpose. Students investigate familiar systems at home and school, learn to sequence and represent processes, and reflect on what happens when parts of a system are missing or out of order. The unit emphasizes hands-on inquiry, visual mapping, and student agency, with opportunities for creative expression, digital documentation, and collaborative projects. Through real-world examples and cross-curricular links, students build foundational understanding of systems thinking, process, and interconnection.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.
They plan to share their learning from this unit of inquiry at the SLC.

Assessment Reflections

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key
characteristics such as texture, strength, flexibility, and absorbency. Through hands-on activities and guided discussions, many pupils were able to
identify why specific materials are chosen for particular purposes in products they use.

While exploring the reuse and recycling of materials through physical change, the children enjoyed engaging in a variety of practical
experiments. They developed a clearer understanding of how materials can be changed without altering their chemical composition. For example,
during a recycling project based activity, the children successfully sorted materials and reused them to create a different product. We observed the
children really grasping the importance of sustainably managing materials. They showed increasing awareness of environmental issues such as
waste, pollution, and resource depletion. Through class discussions, group projects, and eco-friendly challenges (like creating new products from
old materials), many pupils expressed thoughtful ideas about reducing waste and making more sustainable choices in their daily lives.
Next steps and further action will be to continue integrating sustainability themes across the curriculum wherever possible. Students voiced their
desire to have more opportunities for project-based learning involving upcycling and community involvement. Some children took this as home
action. We feel including more reflective activities next year where children can evaluate the impact of their material choices would be a great idea.
Inviting a local artist to share their experiences would be beneficial to see first hand products and the process involved.

ci: Changes to materials affect how we use and reuse them in daily life.
lo: Understanding material properties; Reuse and recycling through physical change; Sustainably managing materials

s.d: Students photograph clean samples of paper, foil, plastic and fabric, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images by material. This makes them look closely at properties such as texture, shine, stiffness and transparency before deciding how an item could be reused or recycled. Groups swap unfamiliar objects and test whether each other's model can classify them correctly. They retrain the model when it makes mistakes, showing why a wide range of examples matters. This mirrors the camera-driven sorting arms used in recycling facilities to separate materials moving along conveyor belts. Students finish with a working image classifier and a short demonstration of what it gets right and wrong.

Students record bending, stretching, tearing and crushing tests on everyday materials, then edit the clips into a short comparison film. Seeing each change side by side helps them explain that a material can change shape without becoming a different material. Each group chooses one changed object that could now have a useful second life and adds a spoken explanation. Another class watches the films and votes for the reuse idea they would genuinely try. Students finish with a titled science film showing the tests, observations and reuse choice. iMovie's trimming, titles, transitions and voice recording keep the evidence clear and easy to follow.

Students watch a teacher-selected ClickView clip showing what happens to recyclable materials after they leave a household bin. This helps them connect crushing, shredding and reshaping with the new uses made possible by physical change. Pause at key moments and ask pairs to predict the next machine action before the video continues. Students then answer built-in questions that separate what they observed from what they first expected. The class ends with a completed response set showing where ideas changed. ClickView's curated videos and built-in questions make an unfamiliar industrial process visible and manageable for Year 2.

Students photograph a clean discarded object in ChatterPix Kids and record it explaining its material properties and possible next use. Giving the object a voice makes students justify why bending, cutting, folding or crushing would help rather than simply calling it rubbish. Classmates listen without seeing the original label and decide whether the proposed reuse matches the material's properties. Students revise their spoken message if the audience cannot work out why the choice is suitable. They finish with a short talking-image collection for a classroom recycling display. ChatterPix Kids lets them draw a mouth on the photograph and add a brief voice recording in the same app.

Students record the sounds made when safe materials are tapped, scrunched, torn or shaken, then arrange the recordings into a short composition. Comparing the sounds draws attention to properties such as hardness, thickness and flexibility while keeping the materials themselves at the centre. Groups exchange compositions and try to identify each material from sound alone before hearing the explanation. Students choose whether to repeat, layer or leave space around each sound so the material remains recognisable. They finish with a recorded piece and a spoken ending that names the materials and suggests how each could be reused. GarageBand's audio recorder and track arrangement tools let students capture and organise the sounds in one place.

Students empathise with school cleaners by examining why mixed materials placed in the wrong bins make recycling harder, then define the problem as getting each item to the correct collection point. They ideate and build a floor-sized sorting route from reused cardboard, paper signs, bottle tops and clean packaging, with Bee-Bot starting spaces and labelled destinations. Teams prototype directional sequences, run the Bee-Bot, and check whether it reaches the correct bin without relying on sensors. They test one another's layouts, then move signs or change the programmed steps when a route fails. At the end, students demonstrate a reliable sorting journey and explain how the material's properties affected its reuse or recycling destination.

plannerText: The Year 2 'How the World Works (Materials)' unit explores how materials can be changed physically (bending, stretching, tearing, crushing) without altering their composition, and how these changes enable reuse and recycling. Students investigate material properties, conduct hands-on experiments, and learn about sustainable practices. The unit connects science with art, music, and cultural perspectives, encouraging students to think about how materials are used in daily life and how responsible choices can help the environment. Assessment includes reflective writing, visual representations, and creative projects using recycled materials.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.
They plan to share their learning from this unit of inquiry at the SLC.

discussions and real-world phenomena like noticing the moon's

sparked meaningful conversations about diverse worldviews and
helped students connect scientific concepts with human history and
culture, further enriching their understanding of space.

Their growing curiosity and confidence in using scientific language was
evident in both group discussions and individual reflections. Interest in
reading material continues.

Assessment Reflections

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key
characteristics such as texture, strength, flexibility, and absorbency. Through hands-on activities and guided discussions, many pupils were able to
identify why specific materials are chosen for particular purposes in products they use.

The Wonder Walk unit effectively engaged the students with the

 Our guest speakers, Erin added personal perspectives, helping

idea.

Activities such as comparing historical and current images,
investigating artefacts, and completing the plaque timeline encouraged
students to think critically, ask questions, and make connections
between personal and school history. The visit to Campbell place also
gave students the opportunity to speak to older people to hear stories
from the past.

The culminating artefact project allowed students to express their
understanding creatively, with agency, while developing their reflection
and communication skills.

Overall, the unit successfully fostered curiosity, observation, and
historical thinking, while helping students appreciate the significance of
the school's heritage.

ci: Patterns in the sky help us understand our place in the universe.
lo: Earth's place in the solar system; Observable patterns in the sky; Tools and methods we use to observe the sky

s.d: Students build a 3D model showing Earth, the Sun and the Moon, then program each object to move in a repeating path. This helps them see how movement in space creates patterns such as day, night and changing Moon views. Pairs swap models and check whether the movement matches the explanation. They revise any confusing sizes, paths or labels after the test. Each pair finishes with an interactive solar system scene that classmates can explore. Delightex's block coding lets students make objects move and repeat actions.

Students record the Moon's visible shape or the position of a playground shadow in a simple Excel table across several observations. The growing table helps them work out that changes in the sky follow patterns rather than happening randomly. Groups compare charts and suggest what might happen at the next observation. They add the next result to see whether their prediction was close. Each group finishes with a labelled chart and a short statement describing the pattern. Excel turns the entered observations into a graph that makes change over time easy to see.

Students program an animation in which Earth turns while the Sun stays in one place, changing one side of Earth from day to night. This makes the repeating day-and-night pattern visible and links it to Earth's movement. Students exchange projects and follow each other's code to find any movement that does not make scientific sense. They debug the sequence and add a character who explains what the sky would look like from Earth. Each student finishes with a working animated explanation of one complete day. ScratchJr's motion and repeat blocks make the cycle run again and again.

Students record regular sky observations in a digital book using drawings, short text and spoken explanations. This brings together evidence about Moon phases, daylight and the tools people use to observe the sky. Each student chooses one page to rewrite for a younger class, replacing difficult space words with a clear comparison. Partners listen to the narration and point out any claim that needs stronger evidence. Students finish with a narrated sky-pattern book that can be read across the term. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page.

Students stretch virtual bands between pegs to recreate familiar star patterns and invent a constellation that can be recognised when rotated. This shows that people notice, name and communicate patterns in the night sky even though the stars are far apart in space. Students swap designs and test whether a partner can rebuild the constellation from spoken directions alone. They revise the pattern or directions when the result does not match. Each student finishes with a clear constellation design made from points and connecting lines. Geoboard lets students move the bands quickly while exploring position, shape and symmetry.

Students empathise with someone trying to explain Earth's place in the solar system, then define the need for a clear floor model that shows order and movement. Teams ideate and build a large mat from cardboard, paper, recycled lids and labelled planet markers, with squares forming a route from the Sun to Earth and beyond. They prototype a Bee-Bot program that stops at selected planets, test it with another team and revise the mat or sequence when the robot reaches the wrong place. Students must measure each square carefully because Bee-Bot moves in fixed steps and follows only the directions entered in advance. Each team demonstrates its improved model by programming Bee-Bot from the Sun to Earth and explaining why Earth occupies that position.

Students engage in hands-on investigations, creative projects, and digital documentation to build understanding of cycles, systems, and patterns. The unit emphasizes inquiry, observation, and communication, connecting science with cultural perspectives and encouraging students to share their learning through models, presentations, and reflective activities.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.
They plan to share their learning from this unit of inquiry at the SLC.

Assessment Reflections

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key
characteristics such as texture, strength, flexibility, and absorbency. Through hands-on activities and guided discussions, many pupils were able to
identify why specific materials are chosen for particular purposes in products they use.

experiments. They developed a clearer understanding of how materials can be changed without altering their chemical composition. For example,
during a recycling project based activity, the children successfully sorted materials and reused them to create a different product. We observed the
children really grasping the importance of sustainably managing materials. They showed increasing awareness of environmental issues such as
waste, pollution, and resource depletion. Through class discussions, group projects, and eco-friendly challenges (like creating new products from
old materials), many pupils expressed thoughtful ideas about reducing waste and making more sustainable choices in their daily lives.
Next steps and further action will be to continue integrating sustainability themes across the curriculum wherever possible. Students voiced their
desire to have more opportunities for project-based learning involving upcycling and community involvement. Some children took this as home
action. We feel including more reflective activities next year where children can evaluate the impact of their material choices would be a great idea.

Teacher Reflections

Student Reflections

The Wonder Walk unit effectively engaged the students with the
history and identity of Wesley Glen Waverley. Through photographing
plaques, statues, and artefacts, students practiced observing evidence
and connecting it to the past.

 Our guest speakers, Erin added personal perspectives, helping
students see how school life and learning have changed over time.

The excursion to Como House was amazing and one to repeat, very
engaging and appropriate at introducing our lines of inquiry and central
idea.

Activities such as comparing historical and current images,
investigating artefacts, and completing the plaque timeline encouraged
students to think critically, ask questions, and make connections
between personal and school history. The visit to Campbell place also
gave students the opportunity to speak to older people to hear stories
from the past.

The culminating artefact project allowed students to express their
understanding creatively, with agency, while developing their reflection
and communication skills.

Overall, the unit successfully fostered curiosity, observation, and
historical thinking, while helping students appreciate the significance of
the school's heritage.

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles to make a route that carries water from a reservoir to homes, farms and a hospital. They work out how distance, blocked paths and limited supply can affect who receives water. Each group chooses whether its route is fastest, shortest or fairest, then another group tests that choice. Students change the tiles when Indi stops, turns the wrong way or misses a community. They finish with a working floor model of water moving from source to use. Indi's coloured tiles let students change the route without using a screen.

Students build a digital book comparing two children's daily access to water using teacher-provided case information. This shows how the same essential resource can be safe and nearby for one community but scarce or distant for another. Students record questions for a partner class, which adds spoken answers or suggestions to the book. Each pair decides on one realistic water-saving action to include on the final page. They finish with an illustrated, narrated book about water access and responsibility. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration on each page.

Students photograph and identify plants, insects and animals found near the school garden or a local waterway. They discuss what each living thing might need from water and what could happen during drought or pollution. Pairs compare identifications and check uncertain matches against visible features before accepting them. Students choose one species whose water needs they want the class to protect. They finish with a set of local species records and a specific watering or habitat-care suggestion. Seek uses the camera to suggest an identification, so each result should be treated as a guide to check.

Students record a puppet-show meeting in which families, farmers and wildlife must share a limited water supply. This makes unequal access and competing community needs easier for young learners to discuss. Another group watches the scene, pauses before the decision and suggests a fair solution. The creators then record a revised ending that shows the consequences of that choice. Students finish with a short narrated story showing a water problem and a possible response. Puppet Pals lets them move characters across backdrops while recording their voices.

Students draw and connect the stages that move water from a catchment through storage and treatment to a household tap. This helps them see that clean water depends on many connected places and processes. Groups exchange boards and place a warning beside one stage where water could be wasted, polluted or delayed. The original group adds a practical change that could protect the supply at that point. Students finish with a clear flow diagram showing the water system, a risk and a response. Freeform's large canvas allows drawings, labels and arrows to remain connected on one board.

Students empathise with a community carrying water a long distance, then define the need to move blue paper droplets without losing them. They ideate and prototype a transport route using cardboard, straws, recycled cups, foil and bottle caps, with a small carrier fitted around a Bee-Bot. Teams program the Bee-Bot in advance, test whether it reaches each collection point and count any droplets that fall or destinations it misses. They improve the carrier, route or command sequence after every test while keeping the Bee-Bot's directional buttons accessible. Each team demonstrates a reliable physical model and explains how its changes made water transfer safer, shorter or fairer.

plannerText: The Year 2 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores water as a limited and essential resource, focusing on themes of access, sustainability, and global responsibility. Students investigate the water cycle, how water is transferred from source to use, and the impact of unequal access on communities. Through inquiry, hands-on activities, and creative projects, learners develop empathy, scientific understanding, and practical strategies for water conservation. The unit emphasizes systems thinking, cultural perspectives, and student agency, encouraging children to take meaningful action for a fairer and more sustainable world.

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploring the past helps us to understand the present.
lo: Evidence and its significance in a place; Connections between the past and present within a place; Personal history shapes the present

s.d: Students capture 360-degree views of several Wesley College spaces where old photographs show clear changes. This helps them look closely at evidence and work out how the past still shapes the campus today. Pairs choose the camera position that best matches each historical photograph, then invite another class to search the view for what has stayed and what has changed. They produce an immersive virtual tour of the campus in the present. The spherical view lets viewers turn around and inspect the whole setting rather than seeing one carefully framed angle. Students finish by naming which visible detail gives the strongest evidence of change.

Students sort teacher-provided photographs of Wesley College buildings, clothing, classrooms and objects into past-and-present pairs. They see that photographs can provide evidence about how a place and its people have changed. Each pair removes one caption and asks classmates to work out which clues reveal the older image. They produce a clear comparison grid with short captions naming what changed, what stayed and why it matters. PicCollage makes it easy to arrange images side by side and add brief labels. Students revise any caption that states a guess without pointing to visible evidence.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short explanation spoken by an on-screen character representing a carefully studied object from Wesley College's past. Giving the object a voice helps them explain what it can tell us about school life at the time. Students swap recordings and check whether each explanation separates visible evidence from an imagined detail. They produce a short lip-synced character video for a class history display. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically matches the character's mouth to the recorded voice. Students end with the sentence, 'This matters today because...', linking the object to present-day school life.

Students interview a family or Wesley community member about one object, place or routine they remember from childhood. Personal stories show how earlier experiences can shape choices, traditions and routines today. Students choose one follow-up question after hearing an unexpected detail rather than reading every question from a fixed list. They produce a short, clearly recorded oral-history interview that can be played for families or another Year 2 class. The physical microphones and recorders help capture the speaker's voice clearly in a quiet space. Students introduce the speaker and explain which part of the recording counts as historical evidence.

Students build a simple 3D scene showing one Wesley College space in the past and another version of it in the present. Rebuilding the same place twice makes changes in buildings, objects and daily routines easy to compare. Partners exchange scenes and suggest one missing detail that could be added only if evidence supports it. They produce an interactive virtual comparison with objects that respond when selected. Delightex lets students build 3D worlds and use CoBlocks to control how objects move or respond. Students include one unchanged feature so the scene shows continuity as well as change.

Students empathise with younger visitors who need an easy way to find important historical places around Wesley College, then define which locations and clues the route must include. Using cardboard, printed photographs, recycled materials and paper labels, they ideate and build a large floor map before programming a Bee-Bot through the sequence. They prototype direction cards, test whether the robot reaches each place, and change the map or instructions whenever the route fails. Another group tests the route without help and explains which historical clue was clear or confusing. Students finish by demonstrating a reliable heritage route and explaining how each stop connects the college's past with its present.

plannerText: The 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit for Year 2 explores how investigating the past helps us understand the present, with a focus on evidence, connections between past and present, and personal histories. Students inquire into the significance of artefacts, buildings, and stories at Wesley College, compare changes over time, and reflect on how personal and community history shapes today. The unit emphasizes observation, documentation, and communication through excursions, interviews, artefact analysis, and creative projects, fostering curiosity, reflection, and historical thinking.

Supporting student agency

Student self-assessment and peer feedback

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.
They plan to share their learning from this unit of inquiry at the SLC.

Assessment Reflections

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key
characteristics such as texture, strength, flexibility, and absorbency. Through hands-on activities and guided discussions, many pupils were able to
identify why specific materials are chosen for particular purposes in products they use.

While exploring the reuse and recycling of materials through physical change, the children enjoyed engaging in a variety of practical
experiments. They developed a clearer understanding of how materials can be changed without altering their chemical composition. For example,
during a recycling project based activity, the children successfully sorted materials and reused them to create a different product. We observed the
children really grasping the importance of sustainably managing materials. They showed increasing awareness of environmental issues such as
waste, pollution, and resource depletion. Through class discussions, group projects, and eco-friendly challenges (like creating new products from
old materials), many pupils expressed thoughtful ideas about reducing waste and making more sustainable choices in their daily lives.
Next steps and further action will be to continue integrating sustainability themes across the curriculum wherever possible. Students voiced their
desire to have more opportunities for project-based learning involving upcycling and community involvement. Some children took this as home
action. We feel including more reflective activities next year where children can evaluate the impact of their material choices would be a great idea.
Inviting a local artist to share their experiences would be beneficial to see first hand products and the process involved.

ci: Humans have a responsibility in their relationships to value the rights of others
lo: The difference between needs and wants; Everybody has rights and responsibilities; What is a respectful relationship

s.d: Students photograph classroom places where a right is being valued, then record a short voice explanation. They show how everyday actions such as taking turns, listening and including others carry responsibilities. Partners compare entries and suggest one small change that would make each place fairer. Students revise their explanation after trying the change in the classroom. They end with a class collection of photographed rights and responsibilities. Seesaw keeps the photos, voice recordings and reflections together in each student's journal.

Students paint a digital quilt square showing what respect looks like between two people. They include colours, shapes and small details that show listening, fairness or inclusion. Each student first asks a partner which respectful action matters most to them, then uses that answer in the painting. The finished squares can be displayed together as a digital kindness quilt. Students explain which part of their image represents a right and which part represents a responsibility. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with layers.

Students build a short class survey that asks whether familiar items are needs, wants or sometimes both. They include examples such as water, a home, friendship, toys and internet access. Another Year 2 class completes the survey, giving students an audience beyond their own discussion group. Students read the automatic charts and discuss why people may answer some questions differently. They end with real class data and a list of examples that need further discussion. Microsoft Forms collects responses and turns them into charts automatically.

Students record a puppet scene in which two characters disagree over space, belongings or joining a game. They show the characters naming their rights, accepting responsibilities and working towards a respectful solution. Groups swap planned scenarios so they must solve a problem written by someone else. Students replay the shows and check whether both characters were heard and treated fairly. They end with a short narrated puppet show that can prompt a class discussion. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students code an animated story where a character must choose how to respond when someone is excluded or treated unfairly. They create two possible responses and show what happens after each choice. A partner tests the story without being told which response is respectful, then explains what the code helped them notice. Students debug the sequence so actions and speech happen in a clear order. They end with an interactive story that shows how choices affect relationships. ScratchJr uses simple blocks to control characters, movement and speech.

Students empathise with a child who needs a calm, safe and welcoming route through a busy classroom, then define what could block that child's right to take part. Using cardboard, paper, recycled boxes and signs, teams build a floor mat with shared spaces, obstacles and helpful stopping points. They ideate several routes, program the Bee-Bot's directional buttons, and test whether it can reach each space without crossing an unfair barrier. Teams move or rebuild parts of the mat and debug the movement sequence after feedback from classmates. Each team demonstrates its improved route and explains how the physical design values another person's rights.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' Year 2 unit explores identity, respectful relationships, and the importance of valuing the rights of others. Students inquire into the difference between needs and wants, the meaning of rights and responsibilities, and what makes a respectful relationship. Learning experiences include role-play, collaborative art (like a kindness quilt), scenario-based discussions, and reflection activities. The unit emphasizes empathy, fairness, and inclusion, with strong links to social skills, communication, and student agency. Students are encouraged to express their understanding through creative projects, digital storytelling, and peer feedback, building a classroom culture of respect and care.

At the conclusion of our space unit, students engaged in self-assessment
and peer feedback to reflect on their learning and growth. Using success
criteria co-created during the unit, students thoughtfully evaluated their
understanding of key concepts such as Earth's place in the solar
system and observable patterns in the sky. They considered how
effectively they had communicated their learning through their informative
planet texts and papier-m?ch? solar system models.
Through peer feedback sessions, students had the opportunity to share
their work, celebrate each other's efforts, and offer constructive
suggestions for improvement. This process helped them develop
important skills in giving and receiving feedback, active listening, and
reflective thinking. It also reinforced a sense of collaboration and
ownership of their learning journey.

Student agency was meaningfully developed throughout this unit as
learners took ownership of their understanding of LI 1 Earth's place
in the solar system and LI 2 observable patterns in the sky such
as day/night, moon phases, and seasons.
By engaging in open-ended investigations, students were
empowered to ask questions, seek answers, and explore concepts
that genuinely interested them such as the reasons behind moon
phases or why different planets have different lengths of years. This
encouraged curiosity, self-direction, and critical thinking.
In the STEM lab experience, students demonstrated agency through
choice and voice selecting a planet of interest, researching it
independently or in small groups, and creating an informative text
that reflected both their understanding and their personal connection
to the topic. The papier-m?ch? solar system project allowed them to
express their learning through hands-on creation, collaboration, and
problem-solving, building confidence and a sense of ownership over
the final product.
Throughout the unit, students were active participants in their learning,
setting goals, making decisions about how to present their
understanding, and reflecting on what they had learned. These
experiences not only supported the development of content knowledge
but also nurtured key aspects of student agency: voice, choice,
responsibility, and independence.
They plan to share their learning from this unit of inquiry at the SLC.

The children demonstrated a growing understanding of material properties, including the ability to describe and compare materials based on key
characteristics such as texture, strength, flexibility, and absorbency. Through hands-on activities and guided discussions, many pupils were able to
identify why specific materials are chosen for particular purposes in products they use.

The Wonder Walk unit effectively engaged the students with the
history and identity of Wesley Glen Waverley. Through photographing
plaques, statues, and artefacts, students practiced observing evidence

 Our guest speakers, Erin added personal perspectives, helping
students see how school life and learning have changed over time.

engaging and appropriate at introducing our lines of inquiry and central
idea.

Activities such as comparing historical and current images,
investigating artefacts, and completing the plaque timeline encouraged
students to think critically, ask questions, and make connections
between personal and school history. The visit to Campbell place also
gave students the opportunity to speak to older people to hear stories
from the past.

The culminating artefact project allowed students to express their
understanding creatively, with agency, while developing their reflection
and communication skills.

Overall, the unit successfully fostered curiosity, observation, and
historical thinking, while helping students appreciate the significance of
the school's heritage.
