ci: People's beliefs contribute to the diversity of human life.
lo: Spiritual or religious beliefs; Similarities and differences of spiritual beliefs; Contributions of different religions to human diversity

s.d: Students post one carefully sourced image, fact or question about a spiritual or religious belief to a shared Padlet wall. This shows how beliefs shape identity, traditions and communities while making room for similarities and differences. Students respond to two classmates by naming a connection and asking a respectful question rather than judging the belief. The class invites another Year 4 group to add what they notice and what they still wonder. Students finish with a collaborative gallery of evidence, questions and connections that can grow across the inquiry. Padlet keeps notes, images, links and peer responses together on one shared wall.

Students design an infographic comparing how two spiritual or religious traditions express one shared idea, such as gratitude, belonging, care or remembrance. This keeps the comparison focused on a human idea rather than ranking entire belief systems. Each student chooses the traditions and checks that images, symbols and words are used respectfully. Partners swap drafts and identify one similarity that is easy to miss at first glance. Students finish with a clear exhibition panel for a classroom gallery walk. Adobe Express combines short text, images and graphic layout in one place.

Students write respectful survey questions about everyday values, belonging and practices that are safe for classmates to answer. The responses show that people can share values while expressing them through different beliefs, traditions or personal choices. Students include a 'prefer not to say' option and decide which questions should remain anonymous. They study the automatic charts and discuss what the data does not tell them about a person's identity. Students finish with a class survey and a set of charts showing patterns without naming individuals. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and displays summary charts.

Students record a short interview with a willing family or community member about a tradition, value or belief that contributes to their sense of belonging. This gives students a real voice to listen to instead of treating religions and spiritual beliefs as lists of facts. Students send questions in advance and let the guest choose anything they do not wish to discuss. Pairs listen back and select a respectful section that challenges a stereotype or reveals a shared value. Students finish with a collection of short recorded interviews for a supervised listening station. The physical microphones and recorders capture clear voices during face-to-face conversations.

Students build an interactive 3D gallery showing how several belief communities contribute to human diversity through celebrations, service, art, architecture or care for others. This helps them show both distinct practices and ideas that communities may share. Each group gives another group a virtual space to check for missing context, stereotypes or unclear labels. Students then code selected objects to reveal a short explanation or question when a visitor interacts with them. Students finish with a virtual gallery that classmates can explore and discuss. Delightex supports 3D scene building and block coding for object responses.

Students empathise with visitors who may feel unsure or excluded, then define how a welcoming display could communicate respect across different beliefs without favouring one. They sketch ideas and build a physical first prototype from cardboard, paper, recycled materials and LEGO, such as a doorway that reveals messages of welcome when someone approaches. They rebuild the strongest idea with LEGO SPIKE Prime, coding a distance or force sensor to trigger a motorised panel or moving greeting. Visitors test whether the model feels clear, welcoming and respectful, and students adjust the wording, movement and timing after feedback. Each team demonstrates a working model and explains how its design supports belonging within a diverse community.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' unit for Year 4 explores identity as individuals and as part of a collective, focusing on physical, emotional, and spiritual health and well-being, relationships, and belonging. Students investigate how people's beliefs contribute to human diversity, examining similarities and differences among world religions and spiritual beliefs. The unit emphasises open-mindedness, knowledge, and communication, with learning experiences including gallery walks, research, virtual and real-world visits to places of worship, and the creation of information reports and cultural posters. Students engage in inquiry, reflection, and action to deepen their understanding of diversity, identity, and the role of beliefs in shaping communities.

s.d: Students design a small 3D classroom aid for a person who finds an everyday task difficult, such as holding cards, organising pencils or turning book pages. They work from a short user brief so every choice has a clear purpose. Students swap models and check whether the size, shape and openings would suit the intended user. They revise one feature after receiving specific feedback. Each student ends with a measured 3D model ready for a plastic test print. Tinkercad lets students reshape and resize solid objects as their ideas improve.

Students collect and connect notes about small problems experienced by people around the school. They sort the needs by user, place and purpose before choosing one worth solving. Another class adds questions and marks the ideas that would make the greatest difference. Students then map several possible solutions and show why one best matches the need. Each group ends with a clear design brief and a visual trail from problem to chosen idea. Freeform's shared infinite canvas keeps notes, sketches and feedback together.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a designed character delivering a 30-second message that asks the school community to support a useful change. They choose the character, words and tone to suit a specific audience such as younger students, families or teachers. Partners listen without seeing the planning notes and explain what action they think the message requests. Students rewrite and record the message until the purpose is immediately clear. Each student ends with a short animated appeal that can be played to its intended audience. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the on-screen character to the student's recorded voice.

Students explore and build in Revamp Melbourne to create a solution for the city's future needs: https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/revamp-melbourne. They make design choices that respond to what people need now and may need later. Teams exchange builds and test whether visitors can work out each solution's purpose without an explanation. Students revise confusing spaces, signs or structures after the visit. Each team ends with a working Minecraft model of a purposeful Melbourne improvement. Minecraft's shared building world allows students to walk through and experience one another's designs at human scale.

Students build a short Kahoot that teaches an audience how to use a newly designed school service, space or object. They write questions that reveal whether their instructions and visual choices are clear. A different group plays the quiz without receiving any extra explanation. Students study the incorrect responses and rewrite the questions or information that caused confusion. Each group ends with a tested interactive quiz that teaches its intended audience. Kahoot displays player responses immediately, giving designers quick evidence about what worked.

Students empathise with a school user and define one repetitive task that a moving LEGO model could make easier, such as sorting coloured tokens or opening a model barrier. They ideate with paper sketches, then prototype with LEGO elements, motors and only the colour, distance or force sensor needed for the task. Another group tests the model using agreed success criteria while the designers observe failures, rebuild parts and debug the code. Students finish by demonstrating the improved working model and explaining how testing changed its movement, structure or controls.

ci: Economic systems are an integral part of human society.
lo: Wealth is more than money; Responsibilities when managing income; Income is earned and managed in many ways

s.d: Students compare photos of beds, kitchens, toys and transport across different income levels on Dollar Street. They look for signs of wealth that money alone cannot explain, such as safety, time, health, skills and family support. Each pair chooses one everyday object and swaps its photo trail with another pair to check whether their conclusions are fair. Students discuss why two homes with similar incomes may still offer very different choices and opportunities. They finish with a paper evidence board showing the photos they examined, what they noticed and one question they still have. Dollar Street's homes are arranged by purchasing-power-adjusted consumption, making visual comparison across countries possible.

Students build a survey that asks classmates how they would manage a fixed weekly income across needs, wants, saving, giving and unexpected costs. This makes the responsibilities of managing income visible through real choices rather than a single correct budget. Another Year 5 class completes the survey, then the creators compare the responses with their own predictions. Students revise one question if its wording pushed people towards a particular answer. They finish with an auto-generated chart and a short written conclusion about the choices people valued most. Microsoft Forms collects responses and creates charts automatically.

Students draw and record a narrated money-flow diagram showing how income moves through a household, business or community organisation. They explain where money is earned, spent, saved, taxed or donated and what happens when one part changes. Partners exchange diagrams and ask the creator to add one unexpected event, such as a broken appliance, fewer customers or a rise in costs. Students then update their explanation to show how the whole economic system responds. They finish with a narrated screencast that makes each decision and consequence easy to follow. Explain Everything records students' voices while they draw, move and annotate items on the whiteboard.

Students layer population and terrain data, then annotate places where people might earn income through farming, manufacturing, tourism, trade or services. This shows that income is earned in different ways because places have different resources, environments and connections. Small groups exchange maps and challenge one claim that does not yet have enough geographic evidence. Students adjust their annotations and add a possible responsibility, such as protecting land or paying workers fairly. They finish with an annotated map showing how geography can shape economic choices and opportunities. MapMaker's data layers let students compare patterns rather than simply view a static map.

Students design a short campaign video arguing that a community should measure wealth with more than money. They choose three indicators, such as health, education, clean spaces, free time, belonging or access to services, and explain why each matters. The videos are shown to another class, whose students choose the indicators they would use when judging whether a community is doing well. Creators revise one scene after hearing which message was least clear. They finish with a polished video that proposes a broader way to describe community wealth. Adobe Express provides simple layouts, text, images and short-video editing in one app.

Students empathise with a school canteen worker and customers, then define a problem involving fair, quick and accurate distribution of limited items. Using LEGO pieces, cardboard signs and reusable tokens, they ideate and build a physical dispenser that uses a motor and either the force, colour or distance sensor to release or sort one item at a time. Teams test it with different customers, record jams or unfair outcomes on paper, and rebuild the mechanism or debug the code. The final demonstration shows the working dispenser, explains how it manages scarce resources and identifies who is responsible when the system makes a mistake. This follows the Empathise-Define-Ideate-Prototype-Test cycle while keeping the mechanism physical and testable.

ci: The interactions between living things, materials, and light enable us to make decisions about the world
lo: How structural features and adaptations help living things survive; How weathering and erosion cause change to Earth's surface; How light is used in science and technology

s.d: Students program a micro:bit to measure light levels in sunny, shaded and covered places around the classroom or school grounds. They test how leaves, feathers, paper, plastic and other materials change the reading when placed between the board and a light source. This shows how living things and technologies can use or respond to different amounts of light. Groups swap their mystery materials and use only the readings to work out which ones block, scatter or let through the most light. Each group ends with a coded light meter, a table of readings and a decision about the best material for shade. The micro:bit's built-in light sensing and 5x5 LED grid make the testing visible straight away.

Students build three versions of the same coastline to show its shape before erosion, after gentle weathering and after a major storm. They change blocks in measured layers so viewers can see how moving water and loosened material reshape Earth's surface. Another group inspects the sequence and suggests where plants, rocks or barriers might reduce further erosion. Students then revise the final coastline and add signs explaining which evidence guided their decisions. Each group ends with a walk-through model that shows change over time and a tested protection idea. Minecraft's block-based world makes removed, moved and deposited material easy to compare.

Students photograph and sort examples of leaves into visible feature groups such as broad, narrow, waxy, hairy or spiny, then train an image model to recognise the groups. This helps them test whether structural features can be identified reliably and how those features may support survival. Groups exchange unfamiliar leaf images and check when the model makes a strong match, a weak match or a mistake. Wildlife-monitoring cameras and identification apps use a similar process, learning patterns from many labelled images before classifying a new one. Students end with a working classifier and a record of the extra examples they added to improve it. Teachable Machine displays confidence scores that make uncertain classifications easy to discuss.

Students move sand, pebbles and paper landforms one small step at a time to record weathering, erosion, transport and deposition. The animation makes slow changes to Earth's surface visible within a short viewing time. Groups swap films without titles and check whether viewers can identify each process from the movement of material alone. Students reshoot unclear sections so the cause and effect can be seen rather than merely stated. Each group ends with a short stop-motion sequence showing where material starts, how it moves and where it settles. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame capture lets students control each stage precisely.

Students collect repeated measurements of how far light travels through clear, translucent and opaque materials, then enter the results in Microsoft Excel. They use tables and graphs to compare how material type and thickness affect the amount of light that passes through. Each group receives another group's graph without its material labels and uses the pattern to predict which sample was tested. The original group reveals the samples and checks which conclusions were supported by the data. Students end with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based recommendation for a window, shade cover or scientific instrument. Excel's chart tools turn repeated measurements into patterns that are easier to compare.

Students empathise with people monitoring a fragile sand coastline, then define the need for a device that can detect when part of the model has eroded. They ideate with sketches and prototype a physical shoreline from sand, cardboard, recycled plastic and LEGO, using a SPIKE Prime distance, colour or force sensor only where it can measure a real change. Teams test their model with poured water, observe failures, and rebuild the barrier or sensor position after each trial. They code the model to move or display an alert when the chosen change is detected. At the end, students demonstrate the improved physical prototype and explain how test evidence changed both its structure and its code.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: The need for conservation; Community values inform management of the natural environment; Ways environmental stewardship can drive change

s.d: Students photograph a local creek, reserve or school habitat in 360 degrees, making sure the whole environment can be seen. This shows how paths, bins, plants, water and buildings reveal what a community values and protects. Groups choose one place where better management could help wildlife or reduce human impact, then capture a second view from that decision point. Another class explores the images and identifies evidence of conservation, neglect or competing needs. Students end with an immersive before-action tour that can open discussion about environmental stewardship. The spherical view lets viewers look in every direction rather than seeing only what the photographer framed.

Students collect counts of litter, native plants, introduced plants, shade, foot traffic or visible wildlife across several school locations and enter them into Microsoft Excel. Comparing the results helps them work out where conservation action is most needed. Each group must use its data to recommend one realistic change, then swap spreadsheets with another group to see whether the evidence supports the same decision. Students end with organised tables, charts and a short evidence-based recommendation written in the spreadsheet. The class can combine its results to compare how different uses of the grounds affect environmental health. Excel's chart tools make patterns and differences easier to see.

Students hold a structured written discussion about whether a local natural area should prioritise habitat protection, recreation, cultural care or new community facilities. This helps them examine how different community values can shape management of the same environment. The teacher sets the chatbot as a Socratic Tutor that asks students to explain trade-offs, question assumptions and improve weak reasoning without supplying research facts. Students then revisit one answer after reading a class case study and show how stronger evidence changed their view. They end with a discussion transcript and a carefully justified management decision. The teacher-controlled prompts and support level keep the conversation focused and suitable for Year 5.

Students program a Micro:bit to record light-level readings at several points around a garden, habitat corridor or proposed planting area. This gives them real evidence for deciding where shade-loving or sun-loving plants might be placed as part of a conservation plan. Groups exchange devices and test whether another group's instructions produce consistent readings in the same locations. They then debug their code or measurement method when results vary unexpectedly. Students end with a working light data logger and a site recommendation based on repeated measurements. The built-in light sensing and battery pack allow the Micro:bit to gather readings away from the computer.

Students design a public campaign that asks the Wesley community to support one achievable conservation action, such as protecting habitat, reducing litter or planting local species. This turns environmental stewardship into a clear request for change rather than a general message to care for nature. Each group creates two versions for different audiences, such as students and the local council, changing the evidence, wording and images to match what each audience values. Peers compare both versions and identify which choices make the action more convincing. Students end with a pair of campaign posters or exhibition panels ready for a sustainability pitch. Canva's layout and infographic tools help students combine short persuasive text, evidence and visuals.

Students empathise with people and wildlife affected by litter near a creek or reserve, then define one small item their machine should move without disturbing the surrounding habitat. Using LEGO beams, wheels, gears, motors and either the distance, colour or force sensor, they ideate and build a physical working prototype that lifts, pushes or sorts model litter. Teams test it on a cardboard habitat containing paper, foil and clean recycled packaging, record failures, and rebuild the mechanism rather than changing the challenge. They compare speed, accuracy and habitat disturbance across repeated trials. At the end, each team demonstrates its improved machine and explains which test result caused its most important design change.

plannerText: The Year 5 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores how communities interact with the environment, focusing on conservation, stewardship, and the influence of community values on environmental management. Students investigate local and global conservation efforts, analyze the role of councils and First Nations perspectives, and engage in design thinking to propose and pitch sustainability initiatives. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, communication, and collaborative problem-solving, integrating cross-curricular links with science, geography, and the arts. Learning experiences include text analysis, field observations, mapping, persuasive presentations, and hands-on prototyping, all aimed at fostering responsible action and environmental awareness.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: The discovery of resources has impacted the growth and development of nations.
lo: Significance of resource discovery in development of societies; Impact of migration on cultural, social and economic growth; Exploration and settlement effects on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students map gold discoveries, shipping routes and migration paths that changed Australia during the Gold Rush. They add terrain and population layers to work out why some settlements grew while others did not. Groups swap maps and challenge each other to explain one pattern using geographic and historical evidence. They also mark areas where mining and settlement disrupted Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Country. Each group ends with an annotated map showing links between resources, movement, settlement and change. MapMaker's data layers let students test different explanations rather than simply viewing a finished map.

Students build a multimodal book that follows one Victorian goldfields location before, during and after the Gold Rush. They combine short historical accounts with maps, images and recorded narration to show how resource discovery changed people and places. Each group includes contrasting pages voiced from colonial, migrant and Indigenous perspectives, while clearly separating evidence from imagined details. Groups exchange books and identify whose perspective is strongest, missing or supported by the best evidence. Students finish with a narrated digital history that shows change over time rather than listing disconnected facts. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together in one readable book.

Students compose a short soundscape tracing a journey from an overseas port to the crowded Victorian goldfields. They arrange sounds to show migration, difficult travel, mining work, rapid settlement and environmental change. Another group listens without an explanation and places markers where they think the journey, mood or setting changes. The composers then revise any section that did not communicate their intended historical moment clearly. Students finish with an original audio timeline that can open a class exhibition. GarageBand's tracks and sound library allow sounds to overlap, repeat and change in volume.

Students post evidence cards showing one social, cultural, economic or environmental change caused by the Gold Rush. They sort posts around questions such as who benefited, who was harmed, what changed quickly and what effects remain. Students must respond to a classmate by adding supporting evidence, a respectful challenge or a missing perspective. A partner class reads the wall and votes for the three links between resources and national growth that are most convincingly explained. The class ends with a collaborative evidence wall containing sources, claims and peer responses. Padlet's shared wall keeps the discussion visible so students can trace how an explanation improves.

Students record and edit a short interview that compares two perspectives on migration, mining or settlement during the Australian Gold Rush. Their questions explore why people moved, what opportunities they expected and how rapid development affected different communities. Partners listen for claims that need stronger evidence and record a revised section after receiving feedback. Selected episodes are played to families beside a question inviting listeners to decide whether the Gold Rush brought progress, harm or both. Students finish with a polished podcast episode containing an introduction, interview and evidence-based conclusion. Podcasting using Canva lets students record and edit the whole episode on an iPad.

Students empathise with people moving food, water and mining supplies across a crowded goldfield, then define one transport problem that caused delay, danger or waste. Using LEGO beams, wheels, gears, motors and recycled cardboard, they ideate and build a working model that moves a small supply load between two points. They code the model to stop at a delivery point using the distance, colour or force sensor, then test it on an uneven route with fixed limits on time and materials. Teams measure successful deliveries, identify failures and rebuild or debug one part after each test. Their final demonstration explains how access to resources and transport could help a settlement grow while also changing land and communities.

plannerText: The 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit for Year 5 explores how the discovery of resources and migration have shaped Australia's development, with a focus on historical events like the Gold Rush, the impact on Indigenous and colonial populations, and the interconnectedness of people, resources, and environments. Students engage in inquiry-based learning, research, mapping, and creative projects to understand causation, change, and perspective. The unit emphasizes design thinking, empathy, and multimodal communication, integrating history, geography, and the arts to deepen students' understanding of Australia's past and its ongoing story.

REFLECTING

Assessment Reflections

ci: Managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies.
lo: Establishing, managing and maintaining relationships; Managing behaviours in digital situations; Managing changes associated with puberty

s.d: Students paint a three-layer self-portrait showing who they were, who they are now and who they hope to become as they manage change. This makes identity and puberty visible without asking anyone to reveal private details. Students choose colours, symbols and brush marks that show strategies, trusted relationships and growing confidence. They swap portraits with a partner, who responds only to the strengths and changes they notice. Each student finishes with an original digital portrait that can anchor a private reflection or class gallery. Separate painting layers let students reveal each stage one at a time.

Students hold a teacher-guided written conversation about a realistic digital dilemma, such as being excluded from a group chat or receiving an unkind message. They work out how acceptance, knowledge and practical strategies can change what happens next. The teacher sets the chatbot as a Socratic Tutor so it asks questions rather than supplying answers. Students compare two possible responses and choose the one most likely to protect both safety and relationships. Each student ends with a written conversation and a short personal action plan. Teacher controls for rules, timing and support keep the discussion focused and age-appropriate.

Students record and edit two versions of a short scene about friendship, disagreement or respectful online communication. One version shows a rushed reaction, while the other shows a strategy such as pausing, checking meaning, setting a boundary or asking for help. Another class watches both endings and explains which choices helped the relationship recover. Students revise unclear dialogue after hearing that feedback. Each group produces a short comparison film with titles naming the strategies used. IMovie's editing tools let students trim scenes and arrange the two outcomes clearly.

Students build an anonymous class survey about helpful ways to manage friendship changes, strong emotions and difficult digital situations. This gives them real evidence about which strategies peers understand and which need more teaching. They avoid questions about bodies, personal experiences or named people and test every question for safety before publishing it. Groups study the automatic charts and choose one class strategy that deserves more attention. Each group finishes with a survey, a set of response charts and an evidence-based recommendation. Microsoft Forms collects responses automatically without requiring students to sort answers by hand.

Students build a 3D scene showing a digital situation where a character must decide how to respond to pressure, exclusion or an unwanted message. They code two choices so objects move or respond and each decision leads to a different outcome. Classmates explore the scene and explain which response protects wellbeing and relationships most effectively. The creator then changes one choice or consequence after listening to that feedback. Each student finishes with an interactive 3D decision scene that can be explored on an iPad. CoBlocks make it possible to code how objects respond inside the virtual world.

Students empathise with classmates who may find it hard to say whether they need help, quiet time or company, then define one communication problem their design should solve. Using LEGO beams, gears, cardboard labels and the force, colour or distance sensor, they first build a physical tabletop device with three clear choices. They add a motor-driven pointer or movement, code the selected sensor to activate it, and test whether another group can understand the message without spoken instructions. Feedback leads them to rebuild unclear labels, strengthen the mechanism and debug the code. At the end, students demonstrate a working prototype and explain how it could support respectful relationships during times of change.

plannerText: The 'Who We Are' unit for Year 5 explores identity, relationships, change, and responsibility. Students inquire into managing change (including puberty and digital citizenship), building and maintaining relationships, and strategies for wellbeing. The unit emphasizes reflection, empathy, and self-management, with strong links to digital safety, emotional intelligence, and respectful communication. Visual Art and digital portraiture are integrated, and students engage in journaling, collaborative projects, and presentations to deepen their understanding of self and others.

Assessment Reflections

ci: The media engages its audience and invites a response
lo: How media targets audiences; Techniques used to engage and persuade; Critical evaluation of media messages

s.d: Students question a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about how a tempting advertisement targets a Year 6 audience. This helps them notice how colour, popularity, urgency and selective facts invite a response. The chatbot keeps asking for evidence when a student makes a claim too quickly. Students then swap advertisements and test whether a partner reaches the same conclusion. Each student ends with a written conversation showing how their thinking changed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support in Schoolbox.

Students watch and pause selected advertising clips to record the exact moment each one tries to influence its audience. This makes persuasive techniques easier to spot than discussing advertising in general. Groups compare whether the same clip influences them differently and explain why. Students then answer built-in questions that separate facts, feelings, assumptions and missing information. Each group ends with an evidence-based evaluation of one media message. Clickview's curated clips and built-in questions keep the viewing focused and manageable.

Students build a survey that asks peers what influences their choices between similar products. This shows whether price, packaging, friends, social media, sustainability claims or brand names have the strongest pull. Each group predicts the result before sending its survey to another Year 6 class. Students compare their prediction with the automatically collected responses and look for surprising differences between groups. They end with a survey and a set of charts that reveal real audience patterns. Microsoft Forms automatically gathers responses and displays clear summary charts.

Students compose two short jingles for the same product?one designed to create excitement and one designed to build trust. This lets them test how sound can engage an audience before any factual claim is made. Another class listens without seeing the product and records which version makes it seem more appealing. Students revise the less effective jingle after hearing the audience's reasons. Each group ends with two contrasting recordings and a refined final jingle. GarageBand provides instruments, loops and recording tools in one music-making space.

Students photograph and sort clean packaging into recyclable and non-recyclable groups, then train an image model to recognise the two categories. This opens a sharp discussion about whether green colours and nature images persuade people even when the packaging itself is difficult to recycle. Groups test each other's models with misleading packages and record where the computer makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, using images to direct materials into different streams. Students end with a working classifier and a test record showing which visual clues helped or confused it. Teachable Machine trains a simple image-recognition model from student-provided examples.

Students empathise with shoppers who want quick, honest product information, then define what a fair supermarket display should reveal before a purchase. Using recycled cardboard, paper packaging and LEGO SPIKE Prime pieces, they ideate and build a shelf display where pressing a product activates a motor that reveals a hidden environmental or ethical consequence card. Teams prototype the mechanism, code the force sensor and motor, and test whether classmates understand the message without an explanation. They refine the wording, movement and timing after watching where users hesitate or choose only from the attractive front labels. Each team demonstrates a working physical display that changes a consumer's decision by making missing information visible.

plannerText: The Year 6 'How We Express Ourselves' unit explores the influences on consumer choices, the consequences of those decisions, and alternative models of consumerism that support a fair and sustainable future. Students investigate advertising strategies, peer and social influences, and the environmental and ethical impacts of products. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, and multimodal communication, with students working collaboratively to analyze products, collect data, and present findings through creative formats such as videos, infographics, and performances. The learning experiences are designed to foster agency, reflection, and action, empowering students to make informed, responsible choices as consumers.

Student Reflections

Teacher Reflections
From 2024: This unit has gone well.  The documentaries we use to
support the concepts we are introducing worked well and are still
relevant.  Both excursions were great.  This year we did a tour of
Parliament and it worked just as well as the role play.  Perhaps Drama
could incorporate this role play into their curriculum in future. The
personal migration narrative stills very well for this unit.  Perhaps we
could do some deeper case studies of migration that would be helpful
to unpack the concept and expose the students to different migration
stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

LINK TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCE

Assessment Reflections

The pre-assessment ?What it means to be Australian?? is a great way to access their understanding of this concept. It allows us to see if some are
aware of the pull factors in migration, and connection to the culture of Australia. We also get to see the student's awareness of some the rights and

 freedoms available to Australian citizens and the personal identity associated with this.

The persuasive piece ?Should we change the date of Australia Day?? gives us access to their thinking around the debate from different
perspectives. They can draw on their learning and experiences throughout the unit to connect to their own ideas and thinking around this.

The summative assessment on Seesaw ? allows us to see what three key concepts/ideas they take away from the unit. We can see if these align
to the overriding conceptual understandings from the unit. When asked about what they can do as a citizen they were able to draw this knowledge
down to being kind, inclusive, speaking about indigenous issues etc. When students weren't able to do this, we could see that this understanding
was missed and perhaps this is something we can explicitly teach next year.

s.d: Students collect advertising examples and build a shared map showing how price, packaging, influencers, friends and values shape consumer choices. This shows how organisations connect people, messages and purchasing systems. Groups draw arrows between examples and label who benefits, who pays and what happens after the product is discarded. Another class adds comments showing which messages would influence them and why. Students then reorganise the board to separate strong evidence from assumptions. They finish with a visual map of the forces behind everyday purchases.

Students enter class ratings for several product advertisements and graph which messages most affect willingness to buy. This makes peer pressure, price, sustainability claims and emotional appeals visible in real data. Groups compare results by changing one advertising feature at a time and recording any shift in ratings. They use the patterns to advise a fictional company which strategy is persuasive and which could mislead buyers. Students finish with a spreadsheet containing organised data, charts and evidence-based recommendations. Excel's tables and charts make patterns easier to spot and question.

Students hold a structured written discussion about whether a company should sell a cheap product when its production harms workers or the environment. This helps them examine how business decisions affect consumers, communities and a sustainable future. The teacher sets up a Socratic Tutor that asks students to explain evidence, consider another viewpoint and revise weak claims. Students swap one key argument with a partner, then return to the discussion and test whether their position still holds. They finish with a written conversation showing how their thinking changed. The teacher-controlled prompts keep the discussion focused without treating the chatbot as a research source.

Students build a virtual shop where each product choice leads to a different social, financial or environmental consequence. This makes the links between advertising, purchasing, organisations and waste easier to see. Groups exchange shops and test whether the clues provided are enough to support a fair choice. They then revise prices, signs and consequences so the choice is difficult rather than obviously right or wrong. Students finish with an interactive 3D scene that invites visitors to make and explain a consumer decision. CoBlocks let students code how objects respond when a visitor selects them.

Students design a short advertisement for a familiar product, then remake it as an honest version that includes its environmental and ethical costs. This shows how organisations can frame information to influence what people notice and buy. Groups show both versions to another class and ask which words, images and omissions changed their response. They revise the honest advertisement so it stays persuasive without hiding important information. Students finish with a matched pair of social-style graphics or short promotional videos. Adobe Express provides quick layouts for combining clear text, images and simple video.

Students empathise with shoppers confused by sustainability labels, then define the need for a clear packaging-return station. Using LEGO parts, cardboard and cleaned recycled packages with coloured category labels, they build and code a working model that uses the colour sensor and motors to direct items into different return bins. Teams sketch several ideas, prototype one, and test it with users who deliberately insert items quickly, backwards or into the wrong opening. They improve the structure, instructions and code after recording where the system fails. Each team demonstrates a working physical model and explains how its design could help a school community make more responsible consumer choices.

plannerText: The Year 6 'How We Organise Ourselves' unit explores how influences shape consumer choices and impact the world's sustainable future. Students investigate advertising strategies, peer and social influences, and the ethical and environmental consequences of consumer decisions. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, and communication skills through collaborative inquiry, data analysis, and creative multimodal presentations. Students are encouraged to reflect on alternative, fair, and sustainable models of consumerism, culminating in group projects and action-oriented tasks that connect learning to real-world contexts.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Teacher Reflections
From 2024: This unit has gone well.  The documentaries we use to
support the concepts we are introducing worked well and are still
relevant.  Both excursions were great.  This year we did a tour of
Parliament and it worked just as well as the role play.  Perhaps Drama
could incorporate this role play into their curriculum in future. The
personal migration narrative stills very well for this unit.  Perhaps we
could do some deeper case studies of migration that would be helpful
to unpack the concept and expose the students to different migration
stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

LINK TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCE

Assessment Reflections

The pre-assessment ?What it means to be Australian?? is a great way to access their understanding of this concept. It allows us to see if some are
aware of the pull factors in migration, and connection to the culture of Australia. We also get to see the student's awareness of some the rights and

 freedoms available to Australian citizens and the personal identity associated with this.

The persuasive piece ?Should we change the date of Australia Day?? gives us access to their thinking around the debate from different
perspectives. They can draw on their learning and experiences throughout the unit to connect to their own ideas and thinking around this.

The summative assessment on Seesaw ? allows us to see what three key concepts/ideas they take away from the unit. We can see if these align
to the overriding conceptual understandings from the unit. When asked about what they can do as a citizen they were able to draw this knowledge
down to being kind, inclusive, speaking about indigenous issues etc. When students weren't able to do this, we could see that this understanding
was missed and perhaps this is something we can explicitly teach next year.

ci: Scientists undertake experimentation to confirm, contest and create new theories.
lo: The scientific method; How experiments lead to new understandings; The relationship between planets and the Sun; Energy transfer and transformation in circuits

s.d: Students wire foil switches to a Micro:bit and program its LED grid to show when a test circuit is open or closed. They change one variable at a time, such as the number of connected components, and record whether their prediction holds. Each group swaps its device with another group, which must work out the tested variable from the program's response. Students then debug any test that gives inconsistent results and repeat it. They end with a working circuit-testing device and a short set of evidence-based conclusions. The pins, crocodile clips and programmable LED grid make the circuit's input and output easy to see.

Students build a Minecraft experiment that tests how changing one condition affects a clear result, while keeping all other conditions the same. This makes the scientific method visible and shows why repeated trials can confirm or contest an idea. Groups exchange worlds and run each other's experiments without being told the expected outcome. They then revise any setup that does not produce fair or repeatable evidence. Students end with a working experiment, recorded trial results and a conclusion displayed inside the world. Minecraft's blocks make variables easy to isolate, rebuild and test.

Students enter results from repeated circuit or energy-transfer experiments into an Excel table. They calculate averages and create graphs to check whether the evidence supports their first prediction. Groups receive the same data with one unusual result included and decide whether it is an error, an exception or a reason to repeat the test. They compare graph choices and select the one that communicates the pattern most honestly. Students end with a labelled graph and a written claim supported by specific data. Excel's formulas and charts allow results to be checked and viewed in several ways.

Students photograph examples of recyclable and non-recyclable packaging in Teachable Machine and train an image model to sort them. They test whether changing the number, angle and background of the training images improves the model's reliability. Another group challenges the model with difficult items, such as crushed boxes or partly hidden containers, before suggesting better training data. This mirrors camera-driven sorting systems that guide robotic arms in recycling facilities. Students end with a tested classification model and a record of examples it still sorts incorrectly. Teachable Machine shows confidence levels, helping students decide whether the evidence is strong enough to trust.

Students draw a Sun, planets and orbital paths in Explain Everything, then record themselves explaining how distance and movement shape the planetary system. They use arrows, scale notes and moving objects to distinguish a useful scientific model from the real system it represents. Partners pause the recording at one questionable claim and add a challenge that must be answered with clearer reasoning. Students revise the explanation when the challenge exposes missing evidence or an inaccurate assumption. They end with a narrated screencast that shows both the model and how their explanation changed. Explain Everything records the screen and voice while students move and annotate their diagrams.

Students empathise with school staff who sort mixed classroom waste, then define one packaging item their machine should move into the correct container. They ideate with sketches before building a physical prototype from LEGO parts, motors, cardboard chutes and clean recycled packaging. They code the model to use a colour or distance sensor, then test it repeatedly with different item positions and adjust the mechanism. Teams record failed trials on paper and change one feature at a time so each improvement is based on evidence. At the end, each machine demonstrates a complete sensing, movement and sorting cycle while students explain the energy transfers and experimental evidence behind its final design.

plannerText: The Year 6 'How the World Works' unit explores the interdependence of human and natural worlds, focusing on consumer choices, their consequences, and alternative models for a sustainable future. Students investigate advertising strategies, peer influences, and environmental impacts through research, surveys, and analysis. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, collaboration, and communication, with learning experiences ranging from scientific inquiry and data analysis to creative multimodal presentations and hands-on STEM projects. Assessment tasks require students to synthesize their findings and propose actionable solutions for responsible consumerism.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Teacher Reflections
From 2024: This unit has gone well.  The documentaries we use to
support the concepts we are introducing worked well and are still
relevant.  Both excursions were great.  This year we did a tour of
Parliament and it worked just as well as the role play.  Perhaps Drama
could incorporate this role play into their curriculum in future. The
personal migration narrative stills very well for this unit.  Perhaps we
could do some deeper case studies of migration that would be helpful
to unpack the concept and expose the students to different migration
stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

LINK TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCE

Assessment Reflections

The pre-assessment ?What it means to be Australian?? is a great way to access their understanding of this concept. It allows us to see if some are
aware of the pull factors in migration, and connection to the culture of Australia. We also get to see the student's awareness of some the rights and

 freedoms available to Australian citizens and the personal identity associated with this.

The persuasive piece ?Should we change the date of Australia Day?? gives us access to their thinking around the debate from different
perspectives. They can draw on their learning and experiences throughout the unit to connect to their own ideas and thinking around this.

The summative assessment on Seesaw ? allows us to see what three key concepts/ideas they take away from the unit. We can see if these align
to the overriding conceptual understandings from the unit. When asked about what they can do as a citizen they were able to draw this knowledge
down to being kind, inclusive, speaking about indigenous issues etc. When students weren't able to do this, we could see that this understanding
was missed and perhaps this is something we can explicitly teach next year.

ci: The influences on our consumer choices reveal the interdependence between human and natural systems and call for responsible action toward just and sustainable futures.
lo: Influences on consumer choices (function); How consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats (causation); Alternative models of consumerism that honour a fair and sustainable future (perspective)

s.d: Students design two advertisements for the same everyday product, with one selling status or convenience and the other selling fairness and sustainability. This helps them see how images, slogans and selected facts can steer consumer choices. Students swap the advertisements with another class, which votes on the more convincing message and explains why. They then revise the less convincing advertisement using the audience feedback. Each student finishes with a paired set of campaign posters that exposes how advertising changes what people value. Canva's poster templates and Remove Background feature make it easy to control which product details attract attention.

Students map the possible journey of a familiar product such as chocolate, a cotton shirt or a mobile phone. They add and compare layers for climate, population and terrain to work out where natural and human systems meet along the supply chain. Groups exchange maps and question any route or claim that lacks clear evidence. They then annotate places where workers, wildlife, habitats or consumers may carry the hidden cost of the product. Each group finishes with a labelled supply-chain map showing where a fairer choice could change the journey. MapMaker's data layers let students test ideas against real geographic patterns rather than relying on a static map.

Students record a short podcast interview that compares the views of a consumer, producer, worker and environmental advocate on one product. This shows why a decision that feels simple at the checkout can affect people and habitats far away. Pairs exchange unfinished episodes and identify whose voice or evidence is still missing. Students then edit their questions and ending so listeners must choose between realistic alternatives rather than an obvious right answer. Each pair finishes with a focused podcast episode that recommends a fairer model of buying, borrowing, repairing or sharing. Canva supports recording and editing the whole audio episode on an iPad.

Students photograph and sort examples of packaging into clear visual groups such as reusable, recyclable and difficult to recycle, then train an image model to recognise them. This helps them question how packaging design influences what consumers buy and what later enters habitats. Teams test one another's models with unfamiliar items and record which shapes, colours or labels cause mistakes. They adjust their training examples so the model relies less on misleading features such as brand colour. Each team finishes with a working classifier and a short demonstration of its successes and limits. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, using trained image systems to direct different materials into separate streams.

Students program a Micro:bit to tally choices during a rapid series of shopping dilemmas, using button A for the cheaper option and button B for the fairer or lower-impact option. This makes the pull between price, convenience and responsibility visible as decisions accumulate. Groups change one piece of information in each dilemma, such as adding a habitat warning or fair-work label, and repeat the test. They compare how strongly each new message changes the pattern of button presses. Each group finishes with a portable choice counter that displays totals on the LED grid. The two buttons, variables and LED display allow the whole decision test to run on one small device.

Students empathise with shoppers and store workers by discussing the spills, effort and confusion that can make package-free buying difficult, then define one problem a refill station must solve. They ideate with sketches and build a physical prototype from cardboard, reused containers and LEGO pieces, using a SPIKE Prime motor with a force or distance sensor to control a measured release. Teams test the dispenser with dry reusable items such as counters, revise the chute or code when it jams or releases too much, and test again. They compare how well each design reduces packaging while remaining safe, fair and easy to use. Each team demonstrates a working refill-station prototype and explains which test led to its most important improvement.

plannerText: The Year 6 'Sharing the Planet' unit explores how influences shape consumer choices and their impact on the world's sustainable future. Students investigate advertising strategies, peer and social influences, and the environmental and ethical consequences of consumer decisions. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, and communication skills through collaborative inquiry, data analysis, and creative multimodal presentations. Learners are challenged to propose and advocate for alternative, fairer models of consumerism, connecting their actions to global sustainability and responsible citizenship.

REFLECTING

Student Reflections

Teacher Reflections
From 2024: This unit has gone well.  The documentaries we use to
support the concepts we are introducing worked well and are still
relevant.  Both excursions were great.  This year we did a tour of
Parliament and it worked just as well as the role play.  Perhaps Drama
could incorporate this role play into their curriculum in future. The
personal migration narrative stills very well for this unit.  Perhaps we
could do some deeper case studies of migration that would be helpful
to unpack the concept and expose the students to different migration
stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

LINK TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCE

Assessment Reflections

The pre-assessment ?What it means to be Australian?? is a great way to access their understanding of this concept. It allows us to see if some are
aware of the pull factors in migration, and connection to the culture of Australia. We also get to see the student's awareness of some the rights and

 freedoms available to Australian citizens and the personal identity associated with this.

The persuasive piece ?Should we change the date of Australia Day?? gives us access to their thinking around the debate from different
perspectives. They can draw on their learning and experiences throughout the unit to connect to their own ideas and thinking around this.

The summative assessment on Seesaw ? allows us to see what three key concepts/ideas they take away from the unit. We can see if these align
to the overriding conceptual understandings from the unit. When asked about what they can do as a citizen they were able to draw this knowledge
down to being kind, inclusive, speaking about indigenous issues etc. When students weren't able to do this, we could see that this understanding
was missed and perhaps this is something we can explicitly teach next year.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human needs drive the development of nations.
lo: How human needs drive national development; Role of migration in nation building; Impacts of development on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students map Australian migration routes and layer them with population, terrain and climate data. This helps them work out how needs such as safety, work, water and transport shaped where communities grew. Groups compare one migration route with the Country it crossed and add notes about effects on First Nations peoples. They swap maps and challenge another group to explain which need had the greatest influence on development. Each group ends with an annotated evidence map showing routes, needs, settlement patterns and impacts. MapMaker's data layers let students test whether their first explanation still holds when new information appears.

Students compare photographs of homes, food, transport and everyday objects from families in countries linked to Australian migration. The comparisons show how access to safety, income, education and services can influence decisions to move. Each group chooses one family they must describe without stereotypes, using only details visible on Dollar Street. Groups then compare how the same human need can look different across places and income levels. Students end with a carefully selected set of visual evidence and short written observations. Dollar Street's income-ordered photographs make everyday differences easier to see and question.

Students edit a short documentary that connects one personal or community migration story with a wider event in Australian history. This shows how individual needs and national policies can shape one another over time. They ask a family or community member to check whether the story is accurate and respectfully represented before the final edit. Classmates then watch the films and identify repeated patterns such as seeking safety, work, family or opportunity. Each student ends with a titled documentary containing narration, evidence and a clear historical explanation. iMovie's editing, titles and transitions let students join several pieces of evidence into one coherent film.

Students build a multimodal book that places an Indigenous account, a colonial account and a migrant account beside the same Australian place. This helps them examine how development can benefit one population while disrupting another. Students exchange drafts and flag any page where one voice is missing, simplified or treated as less important. They then record a final reflection explaining whose needs shaped decisions and whose needs were ignored. Each group ends with a digital book containing text, images and recorded narration. Book Creator keeps these different forms of evidence together in one page-by-page publication.

Students build an interactive 3D scene showing one Australian place before colonisation, during colonial development and after later migration. This makes changes to land, movement, services and cultural life visible across time. Another group explores the scene and chooses objects to question, prompting the builders to strengthen weak or one-sided explanations. Students code selected objects to reveal short information points or move when a visitor interacts with them. Each group ends with a virtual historical scene that visitors can explore rather than simply watch. Delightex's 3D building tools and CoBlocks make the changes and interactions part of the explanation.

Students empathise by reading migration accounts and identify one practical barrier faced on arrival, such as moving belongings, finding services or accessing transport. They define one need, sketch several ideas, and build a physical prototype from LEGO, cardboard, paper signs and recycled materials before adding any code. Teams then use SPIKE Prime motors and a colour, distance or force sensor to make the model perform a useful action, such as routing a supply cart or opening an accessible service point. Another team tests it with a clear task, while the designers measure failures, rebuild weak parts and debug the program. Students finish by demonstrating the improved working model and explaining how infrastructure can respond to human needs without ignoring the people already connected to a place.

plannerText: The Year 6 'Where We Are in Place and Time' unit explores how migration, colonization, and evolving systems have shaped Australian identity, citizenship, and cultural heritage. Students investigate pre- and post-colonized Australia, the relationship between migration and needs, and the influence of systems on citizens. The unit emphasizes critical thinking, research, and multimodal communication, with learning experiences including documentary analysis, museum excursions, map art, personal migration narratives, and group presentations. Students are encouraged to connect personal and community stories to broader historical patterns, analyze the impact of systems, and reflect on how place and time shape identity and society.

stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

LINK TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCE

Assessment Reflections

The pre-assessment ?What it means to be Australian?? is a great way to access their understanding of this concept. It allows us to see if some are
aware of the pull factors in migration, and connection to the culture of Australia. We also get to see the student's awareness of some the rights and

 freedoms available to Australian citizens and the personal identity associated with this.

The persuasive piece ?Should we change the date of Australia Day?? gives us access to their thinking around the debate from different
perspectives. They can draw on their learning and experiences throughout the unit to connect to their own ideas and thinking around this.

The summative assessment on Seesaw ? allows us to see what three key concepts/ideas they take away from the unit. We can see if these align
to the overriding conceptual understandings from the unit. When asked about what they can do as a citizen they were able to draw this knowledge
down to being kind, inclusive, speaking about indigenous issues etc. When students weren't able to do this, we could see that this understanding
was missed and perhaps this is something we can explicitly teach next year.

s.d: Students paint a layered self-portrait showing influences on identity, wellbeing and learning. Each layer represents something different, such as relationships, values, experiences, emotions or brain function. Students choose which parts remain clear, overlap or sit beneath the surface, so they control what the portrait reveals. Partners view the paintings and describe the connections they notice before the artist explains their choices. Students finish with an original digital painting that shows identity as complex and changing. The app's layers let students build, hide and reorder parts of the portrait.

Students animate a short brain response to a challenging learning moment using paper shapes, clay or labelled cards. They show how a trigger, emotion, body response, thought and regulation strategy can form a sequence. Groups swap animations and check whether the brain process and chosen strategy are easy to follow. Students then adjust unclear frames or timing after receiving this feedback. Each group finishes with a stop-motion explanation of how managing wellbeing can support learning. Frame-by-frame capture makes processes that happen inside the body visible and discussable.

Students post realistic school scenarios involving stress, friendship, sensory needs, setbacks or learning pressure. They respond to classmates' scenarios with possible regulation strategies and explain why each one might help. Students can add more than one response because wellbeing strategies do not work equally for every person. Another Year 6 class can read the wall and contribute different approaches, widening the range of experiences considered. The class finishes with a searchable wall of situations, strategies and respectful peer advice. Padlet keeps notes and replies together so students can compare choices in one place.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record an avatar explaining how their brain and body respond during a difficult learning experience. They describe one sign they notice, one possible cause and one strategy that helps them regulate. Students choose whether the speaker represents themselves or a fictional learner, allowing safe discussion of personal topics. Peers listen and suggest one respectful question the speaker could answer in a revised recording. Each student finishes with a short animated explanation that could open a class conversation about neurodiversity. The Animate from Audio feature automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students write scenario-based questions about growth mindset, relationships, brain function, safety and self-management. Each question asks players to choose a helpful response rather than simply recall a definition. Small groups test one another's quizzes and challenge answers that treat wellbeing as the same for everyone. Authors revise the options so more than one perspective can be discussed after each vote. Students finish with a playable class quiz bank for reviewing wellbeing choices. Kahoot's live question-and-answer format gives the teacher an immediate view of ideas that need further discussion.

Students empathise by asking classmates when a quiet, hands-on breathing prompt could help them refocus, then define one clear need without collecting private health information. They sketch several ideas and first prototype a turning breathing wheel from cardboard, paper fasteners and recycled materials. They then build a LEGO mechanism in which pressing the force sensor starts a motor that slowly turns the wheel through a breathing cycle. Classmates test whether the speed, size and instructions are calming and easy to follow, and teams rebuild or adjust the program from that feedback. Each team demonstrates a working physical wellbeing aid and explains how testing changed its design.

plannerText: The Year 6 'Who We Are' unit explores how management of wellbeing impacts learning, focusing on the physiology and function of the brain, the influence of mindset and experiences, and strategies to support health, safety, and wellbeing. Students investigate identities as individuals and as part of collectives, connecting personal reflection with broader concepts of neurodiversity, relationships, and regulation. The unit integrates self-management, research, and communication skills, with learning experiences ranging from brain anatomy and growth mindset activities to wellbeing artifact creation and reflective journaling. Transdisciplinary links include visual art, drama, and health, supporting a holistic approach to understanding self and fostering positive habits for lifelong learning.

Teacher Reflections
From 2024: This unit has gone well.  The documentaries we use to
support the concepts we are introducing worked well and are still
relevant.  Both excursions were great.  This year we did a tour of
Parliament and it worked just as well as the role play.  Perhaps Drama
could incorporate this role play into their curriculum in future. The
personal migration narrative stills very well for this unit.  Perhaps we
could do some deeper case studies of migration that would be helpful
to unpack the concept and expose the students to different migration
stories.  This year we introduced a Persuasive Piece on whether we
should change Australia Day which again directly linked our UOI with
Literacy.  For action this year a small group participated in the walk to
the G.  Perhaps, next year we could make this optional.  The hearts
that were made in the colours of the Indigenous flag were put on
display.  In addition, some students had the opportunity to represent
Year 6 at the MS Reconciliation Assembly and reflected on their
understanding of pre-colonised Australia, the arrival of European
settlers and post-colonised Australia.  In future, we are interested in
finding out more about Marngrook.

ci: People recognise important events through celebrations and traditions.
lo: The traditions of our families and communities; How and why people celebrate; The similarities and differences between celebrations

s.d: Students photograph a family celebration object or their own drawing, add a mouth and record it telling why the event matters. This shows how objects, foods, clothing and decorations can carry family traditions. Children ask a family member for one detail to include, so every talking image brings a real voice from home into the classroom. They swap recordings with a partner and listen for something familiar and something new. Each child ends with a short talking image for a class celebration gallery. ChatterPix Kids makes the photograph talk through a drawn mouth and a recorded voice clip.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a teacher-made floor mat showing steps from a celebration, such as preparing food, dressing, gathering, giving and dancing. Sequencing the route helps children notice how and why traditions happen in a particular order. Pairs exchange route cards and work out which celebration sequence another pair has planned. They debug their button presses whenever the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong picture. Each pair ends with a working route they can demonstrate and explain to the class. Bee-Bot's directional buttons let children enter and test the whole sequence without a screen.

Students record a spoken sentence about a family celebration and build a short piece of music around it. This helps them hear how voices, rhythms and instruments can express joy, remembrance, welcome or togetherness. Children play their recordings to another Prep class, whose listeners guess the feeling before hearing the explanation. They make respectful choices about whether their music should sound lively, gentle, steady or quiet. Each child ends with a short celebration sound recording containing voice and original music. GarageBand allows children to record and arrange sounds in one music project.

Students sort teacher-provided celebration pictures on a shared Freeform canvas and draw lines between pictures that show similar traditions. This makes common features such as special food, light, music, clothing and gathering easy to see. Small groups choose one surprising connection and explain it to a visiting family member or another class. They can move a picture when discussion changes their thinking rather than treating the first answer as final. The class ends with a large visual web showing similarities and differences across celebrations. Freeform's open canvas allows pictures, drawings and connections to sit together in one shared space.

Students arrange paper figures and loose parts to animate two different celebrations from preparation to gathering. This lets them compare what people do while avoiding the idea that every family celebrates in exactly the same way. Partners swap storyboards and check whether each film shows both a similarity and a difference respectfully. They retake frames when an action is unclear and invite a family member to suggest one accurate detail. Each pair ends with a short stop-motion comparison film. Stop Motion Studio captures one frame at a time so children can make physical materials appear to move.

Students empathise by asking what would help every guest feel welcomed at a class celebration, then define one need such as finding the gathering place or joining an activity. They ideate routes and prototype a welcoming pathway with Indi's coloured tiles, cardboard signs, recycled decorations and paper symbols. Children test whether Indi travels through the intended welcome, activity and gathering points, then rearrange tiles when the sequence does not work. Another pair follows the pathway and gives simple feedback about whether its meaning is clear. Each group demonstrates a tested physical pathway that uses movement and celebration symbols to guide a guest.

plannerText: The Prep 'How We Express Ourselves' unit explores the meaning of celebration, tradition, and culture, focusing on how students and their families mark special occasions. Students learn about a variety of cultural celebrations (such as Lunar New Year, Hanukkah, and Aboriginal gatherings), participate in related art, music, and dance activities, and compare similarities and differences between traditions. The unit emphasises sharing personal experiences, expressing ideas through art and storytelling, and building respect and open-mindedness towards others' ways of celebrating. Activities are play-based, highly visual, and often involve family and community engagement.
